title: I bought a cat 3 days ago, she is not eating enough. What should I do?
post_text:
Three days is too long to go without eating anything at all, but it sounds like your kitty is at least eating a little, a good sign. Have you had the cat checked by your veterinarian? That’s always a first step regardless how you acquired your new cat: whether you adopted it from a shelter or breeder; or it adopted you from “the wild.” If you have not had your new “life manager” evaluated, do so. It’s important even if they seem well so your vet can get a “baseline.” And to rule out any issues (even if you’ve adopted from a breeder and are “assured all is well.”) AND you need to get on schedule for vaccinations, which has become a law in many cities. 
 Some kitties, even in perfect health, take a little time to acclimate to their new home. And cats can be sooo picky about food!!!!! Dear Lord, can they be picky!!! It’s been said that a dog will not let itself starve, but a cat will if they don’t like their food. Or where their food is set out for them. Mine doesn’t like the food anywhere near the litter box, and not even next to the water bowl. 
If you already have a cat and are adding this one, the resident cat may be “protecting” his/her turf, which to him/her includes food, water, litter box, sleeping spot(any flat surface), and you, so the new one may be intimidated. Cats can be bullies at times. 
I would certainly let the vet evaluate first. If the cat develops problems caused by not eating, there is food they can prescribe (just a few cans) that’s very appealing and stimulates appetite. I’ve had a cat need that and she loved it.

title: Why does the floor drain in my house smell bad?
post_text: Floor drains in houses are often installed in places such as bathrooms or laundry rooms, in order to prevent damage from flooding should the toilet overflow, or a water line to the washer break. Because these drains are not in constant use, the water in  P-Trap  will evaporate. pictures of p-traps - Google Search The above link leads to a diagram of how a P-Trap works. (The image is that of a sink P-Trap, but the trap in your floor drain works exactly the same. To avoid this being in issue in the future: Pour enough water into the drain to make certain that the drain is free and clear. After checking drain, pour about a quart of vegetable oil into the drain. The oil will replace the water inside the trap. Salad oil will not evaporate, as does water, so this will help eliminate the odor issue from recurring. Alternately, you can just pour water into the floor drain once a week. If you are in a brand new house, it is always possible that the plumbing contractor forgot to instal the P-Trap in the first place. I experienced this kind of error once many years ago when opening a new restaurant. Good luck.

title: Why are there people who absolutely refuse to smile for photographs when there is no obvious reason for them to be unhappy? For the purposes of this question, presume there is nothing wrong with their teeth, and we are dealing with a Western culture.
post_text: Smiling is harder for some people than others, for a variety of reasons. Personally I find it very difficult to smile unless something  makes  me smile. I suppose you could describe this as conscious/wilful smiling vs unconscious or reflexive smiling. I have various theories as to why this could be. Facial muscles are like any other, they develop with use. People who have had less reason to smile may have weaker ‘smiling muscles’. I have lived with anxiety and depression for most of my life. Long-term sadness or pessimism results in a naturally downturned mouth. When I smile what feels like a ‘normal amount’ (so I can feel the muscles around my mouth smiling) I have actually just turned that downturn into a neutral line. So from :-[ to :-| To actually make a beaming smile I have to strain a lot, which of course just looks like a grimace. :-u Anxiety/stress/tension really tightens up your jaw - I can feel this as I type now. Something that makes me laugh will generally stimulate the muscles enough to overcome this tightness, much like a reflexive kick could move a tight leg muscle, but to try to smile consciously would be hard, and therefore the smile would look forced and unnatural. For someone who is quite self-conscious like me, being forced to do a horrible forced smile for a camera is mortifying - especially as the person taking the photo will usually say ‘Not like THAT, do a REAL smile’, which of course I can’t, especially as I am now frustrated and embarrassed too. If the person taking the photo continues to insist or make a spectacle out of it you feel humiliated and deflated. For most people struggling with the issues above they desire more than anything to fit in, be normal and feel happy and accepted. To be singled out and made to feel weird and different just feels like rejection - often the thing that has caused a lot of the issues above in the first place. They’d love to be able to flash a winning smile, they just can’t, and you’re pointing it out to them and criticising them for it (often in public). Facial muscles are also complex, and can be difficult or impossible for some people to manipulate. Some people can raise one eyebrow, wiggle their ears, curl their tongue etc. whilst others can’t. At least one of these (tongue curling) has been shown to be genetic. Perhaps some people are genetically unable to smile in quite the same way as others. It could also be related to bone structure. My face isn’t particularly symmetrical, and my jaw isn’t well aligned, so that may contribute to my finding it harder to smile. Teeth are another related issue but you’ve excluded that for now so I won’t go into it. If you know that you find it hard to smile, and you have experienced a lifetime of people telling you to smile in photos and then ridiculing or getting frustrated with you because you can’t, then photos don’t make you very happy most of the time and it is actually quite a stressful or sad experience. The best way to get good happy pictures of people like this, is to take one whilst they’re at their best without them noticing (obviously this is only a good idea with people you have a good relationship with) - when they’re laughing and smiling at someone or something. Either that or you need to find a way to make them smile or laugh reflexively. The alternative is that you just accept that they are inexpressive or melancholy, and capture that instead. This insistence that everyone be happy and smiley all the time just makes sad/quiet/less expressive/shy people feel unwanted.

title: What are receptor subtypes? What is their significance for drug development?
post_text: I’ll let others go more into the ugly molecular biology of how slight differences in large proteins cause 5HT-2A… vs only 5HT (5HT = serotonin) receptors. I want to chatter about one of the things behind the first law of pharmacology. Which is: A drug will do whatever the hell it wants. Way back around the turn of the 20th century they were getting much better understanding about how nerves conveyed their signals. They had theories about how to name the substances. They had experimental results showing how other compounds from outside the body (exogenous) were mimics of the active substances they could purify from tissue samples (endogenous). All kinds of clues that built up over the years eventually leading to a paper published in 1948 by Raymond Ahlquist in Georgia. In it he came to a theory to describe why scientists were finding the same chemical would cause different responses depending on the tissues used in the experiments. As in, how the hell could the same chemical cause blood vessels to constrict and blood pressure to rise in one experiment but cause blood vessels to relax and blood pressure to fall in another experiment-  in the SAME friggin’ animal ???? * He called one set  alpha  receptors and after he thought long and hard about what to call the other ones, he settled on  beta  receptors, because nothing else really had that special ring to it. [ Yes, of course I’m fooling around here. ] Plus, he knew that if his idea caught on medical science would be forever burdened with using those names so he better make them short and sweet. Those were soooo much better than two different versions of the word  adrenergic . For a better educating read, go here.  Adrenergic receptor - Wikipedia When I was in pharmacy school in the 1980’s they were discussing alpha1 & alpha2 receptors and beta1 & beta2 receptors in the classroom. It was hard enough to keep track of the different things each receptor did and then we heard of the possibility of beta3 receptors. Eeeek! Now it turns out there are like 27 different types of alpha receptors with practically their own taxonomy. Thankfully the beta receptors haven’t yet been found to be so varied, but that’s only for the students trying to learn about them. Okay, I’m exaggerating but this is how the field’s knowledge grows as new technology comes into play to sort out this stuff. Plus, biological systems evolve, maybe not so quickly in large animals like humans so protected from natural selective forces, but they do change with time. I mention evolution here with the understanding that it isn’t a conscious process - it just happens. It isn’t designed, no matter how cool one might think the way the receptor subtypes are arranged to do so many different things with the same neurotransmitter. Because of this diversity in receptor subtypes there are incredible discrete actions due to high-affinity selective binding in one place along with tremendous flexibility and quick broad influence in other situations - all with the same molecule messenger. Some changes worked great and that example of the species thrived with this new characteristic. Other changes weren’t ready for prime time and the organism didn’t fare so well when it came to reproducing. Although, we are diploid and we’ve all heard of recessive genes that still live on in us as a species. Well, the same kind of pattern exists for acetylcholine, dopamine, glutamic acid, serotonin, endogenous opiates and more. This abundance of receptor subtypes presents BOTH challenges and opportunities for drug development. If scientists can better characterize the regulation of a receptor’s activity by all the other tiny actors around it, the medicinal chemists can use that information to come up with drug molecules that can work with them to exert different modifications to the system’s behavior. Turn it up. Back it off. Stop it cold. Jump start it. Focus it on this one effect - or block just that one effect but leave the others alone. Sounds so simple but it isn’t, with a capital AIN’T. And even if they come up with compounds that reasonably achieve the goals in the petri dish, then they have to see if it works in whole animals, and then in actual humans. And then they gotta make sure it is safe, a whole long process in and of itself. Then can it actually work as a drug product (biopharmaceutics and pharmacokinetics) well enough to treat a disease? Will it even be economically feasible to develop and manufacture it? [Gee, sorry all you folks with truly rare diseases. I mean, we’d love to help but we’re a business here.] Fun fact here. ‘Friggin’ was first used around that time because of those experiments. And it was in the South so that’s why it isn’t spelled with a ‘g’ on the end and rhymes with ‘din’ instead of ‘ding’.

title: What are the healthiest vegetable oils for cooking and how do they affect the flavor of the food?
post_text: I really like virgin coconut oil   and it's surprisingly healthy .  AFAIK coconut oil is the only fat that will actually cause fat loss.  (Early hog farmers in Hawaii tried feeding coconut to pigs only to find they got more lean.)   The "surprising" part is coconut oil is very high in "saturated fat", which we all identify as the "bad" fat, but there's two types of "saturated fat." The short-chain saturated fats in coconut oil actually increase HDL or "good" cholesterol.  Unrefined coconut oil is sightly sweet and aromatic.  It can be used like butter or to coat pans to keep things like cookies from sticking.  (Coconut oil comes both refined and unrefined.  The refined is more savory and because it's slow to spoil can be used to treat cutting boards.) A note on olive oil : I also like olive oil for raw use and as other have mentioned it's healthy.  You have to watch the olive oil you buy, because to be labeled "olive oil" for export an oil only need be 51% from olives. (Italy exports something like 50% more "olive oil" than they produce domestically.)  Typically olive oil is cut with canola oil or vegetable oil. Not only does this reduce cost for the producer, it also makes the olive oil appear more clear.   It's not a sure bet, but if you buy cold-pressed unfiltered olive oil that looks cloudy (and may have bits floating around in the bottom) you're more likely to be getting 100% olive oil.  Taste is another indicator.  100% olive oil is much more flavorful than an olive/canola  blend. I avoid "canola" oil.   People think this is a healthy oil in the US because of the large amount of marketing dollars spent by producers (it's major cash crop).  There is no "canola" plant.  The "Canola" name comes from "Canada Oil", and it's an engineered (bred) or genetically-modified rapeseed oil.  The smoke from rapeseed oil is carcinogenic and rapeseed oil contains erucic acid which is toxic.  Canola's modified rapeseed lowers the level of erucic acid to "levels that are not believed to cause harm in humans."  With so many other oil choices why choose something with a root that was discovered to be toxic but has been modified to a level "not believed to cause harm in humans."

originally_answered: What points should I discuss in performance appraisal?
post_text: With changing times, what’s changed the most in Performance Appraisals is the way its done (obviously). Which brings us to, what points should we discuss on? Here is a brief overview - Get feedback from employees on their performance. Give them a chance to answer for their achievements and assess their areas of strengths & development. originally_answered: What factors affect productivity?
post_text: Productivity refers to the efficiency with which resources are utilized to produce goods and services. Several factors can affect productivity, including: Workforce:  The quality and skill level of the workforce are crucial factors in determining productivity. A highly trained and motivated workforce is likely to be more productive than one that is poorly trained and unmotivated. Technology:  The use of advanced technology can significantly increase productivity by automating tasks, reducing errors, and improving efficiency. Work environment:  The work environment can have a significant impact on productivity. A well-designed workplace with proper lighting, temperature, and ergonomics can improve employee comfort and reduce fatigue. Management practices:  Effective management practices, such as setting clear goals, providing feedback, and recognizing achievements, can motivate employees and increase productivity. Infrastructure:  Adequate infrastructure, such as transportation networks, energy, and communication systems, is essential to support productive activities. Access to capital:  Adequate access to capital can enable businesses to invest in technology, research and development, and other productivity-enhancing activities. Government policies:  Government policies, such as taxation, regulation, and trade policies, can impact productivity by creating incentives or disincentives for businesses to invest in productive activities. Overall,  productivity is a complex phenomenon influenced by a variety of factors that interact with one another in complex ways.

title: What habits have the biggest impact on long-term health?
post_text: Maintaining long-term health is a result of consistent habits that promote physical, mental, and emotional well-being. Research consistently shows that certain habits can profoundly impact longevity and quality of life. Let’s explore these habits, supported by relevant studies and expert advice. 1. Regular Physical Activity Staying physically active is one of the most important habits for long-term health. Exercise strengthens muscles, improves cardiovascular health, and helps regulate weight. It also boosts mental health, reducing the risk of depression and anxiety. Fact : According to the  World Health Organization  (WHO), adults should engage in at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic physical activity per week to reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease, diabetes, and some cancers. Research : A study published in  The Lancet  found that 30 minutes of daily physical activity reduces mortality risk by 31% and the risk of major diseases by up to 15%. Actionable Tip : Incorporate a mix of aerobic activities like walking or cycling and strength training exercises into your routine. Small habits like taking the stairs and daily stretching can also make a big difference. 2. Healthy Diet A well-balanced diet provides the essential nutrients for the body to function optimally. Focusing on whole, unprocessed foods and reducing sugar, salt, and unhealthy fats lowers the risk of chronic conditions such as heart disease, obesity, and diabetes. Fact : The  Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health  recommends a diet rich in vegetables, fruits, whole grains, and healthy fats, like those found in olive oil and fish, as part of a heart-healthy approach. Data : A Mediterranean diet has been shown to reduce the risk of heart disease by up to 30% according to a study published in  The New England Journal of Medicine . Actionable Tip : Focus on portion control, meal planning, and incorporating more plant-based foods into your diet. Avoiding processed and sugary foods can significantly improve long-term health outcomes. 3. Adequate Sleep Getting enough quality sleep is crucial for maintaining long-term health. Sleep affects almost every tissue in the body, including the brain, heart, and immune system. Lack of sleep can lead to weight gain, impaired cognitive function, and increased risk of chronic diseases. Recommendation : The  National Sleep Foundation  suggests that adults need 7-9 hours of sleep per night for optimal health. Research : A study from  Harvard Medical School  found that chronic sleep deprivation increases the risk of hypertension, heart disease, and stroke. Actionable Tip : Create a relaxing bedtime routine, avoid caffeine late in the day, and make your sleep environment conducive to rest by keeping it dark and quiet. 4. Stress Management Chronic stress can lead to long-term health problems, including high blood pressure, heart disease, and weakened immune function. Learning to manage stress through mindfulness, meditation, or relaxation techniques can promote mental health and improve overall well-being. Fact : According to  The American Psychological Association , chronic stress is a major risk factor for the six leading causes of death, including heart disease and cancer. Research : Studies have shown that regular meditation or mindfulness practice can reduce symptoms of stress and anxiety by up to 30%, according to research published in  JAMA Internal Medicine . Actionable Tip : Practice deep breathing, take breaks during stressful periods, or engage in activities like yoga or meditation to manage stress effectively. 5. Social Connections Strong social relationships are essential for both mental and physical health. Studies show that people with meaningful social connections live longer, healthier lives. Loneliness, on the other hand, has been linked to an increased risk of premature death. Fact : A study from  Harvard University  found that close relationships, more than money or fame, keep people happy throughout their lives and are vital for long-term health. Data : Research from  Brigham Young University  reveals that strong social relationships can increase the likelihood of survival by 50%. Actionable Tip : Nurture meaningful relationships with family, friends, and community members. Make an effort to stay connected with loved ones and seek out social activities. 6. Avoid Smoking and Excessive Alcohol Consumption Smoking and excessive alcohol consumption are two of the most detrimental habits to long-term health. Smoking is linked to cancer, heart disease, and lung disease, while alcohol abuse can damage the liver, heart, and brain. Fact : The  CDC  reports that smoking is responsible for 1 in 5 deaths in the U.S. each year. Data : According to the  National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism , excessive alcohol consumption is associated with 95,000 deaths annually in the U.S. Actionable Tip : If you smoke, seek out resources to help you quit, such as counseling or nicotine replacement therapies. Moderation is key for alcohol consumption—limit it to one drink per day for women and two for men. 7. Regular Health Checkups Preventive healthcare is a vital habit for maintaining long-term health. Regular checkups can detect potential health issues before they become serious. Staying up to date with vaccinations, screenings, and physical exams can help prevent chronic diseases. Fact : The  CDC  recommends that adults receive regular screenings for blood pressure, cholesterol, and cancer. Research : A study published in  The BMJ  found that individuals who regularly participate in preventive health screenings have a 20% lower risk of developing major diseases. Actionable Tip : Schedule regular health checkups, including dental visits, eye exams, and screenings like mammograms and colonoscopies, based on your age and risk factors. Conclusion To achieve long-term health, it’s important to develop habits that promote physical, mental, and emotional well-being. By staying active, eating a balanced diet, managing stress, nurturing social connections, avoiding harmful substances, and getting regular health checkups, you can significantly reduce the risk of chronic diseases and enhance your quality of life. Key Takeaways: Regular physical activity and a healthy diet are foundational for long-term health. Adequate sleep and stress management are crucial for both mental and physical well-being. Strong social connections and preventive healthcare can extend your lifespan and improve overall health.

title: Has there ever been a president elected who did not receive the greatest amount of electoral votes?
post_text: Yes. John Quincy Adams, for one. 1824. There were 4 candidates. Andrew Jackson got the most electoral votes, but not a majority. The other 2 candidates were William Crawford and Henry Clay. The election moved to the House, since nobody won an EC majority for president. (John C Calhoun won the VP position with no problem.) The House had to choose a president from the top 3: Jackson, Adams and Crawford. Clay, out of the running, decide to throw his support to Adams. As president, Adams then chose Clay as his Secretary of State, and at that time, that was the office that usually produced the next president: Madison had been Jefferson’s Secretary of State and Monroe had been Madison’s. Jackson declared it a “corrupt bargain,” but there wasn’t anything he could do about it. He ran against Adams in 1828 and won the EC decisively.

title: When someone is stopped by a police officer or State Trooper, how does the driving record they pull up differ from what an insurance company sees?
post_text: I can only speak to California and Nevada records, as those are the ones with which I am familiar. Insurance companies get pretty basic information: dates and types of violations, possibly the court of conviction, and the data goes back only five years. If your insurance company knows about anything from before that time, it’s because they preserved previous record requests. The record that law enforcement gets usually goes back to whenever you first obtained your license. Depending on the state and the nature of the violation, it will show the date of violation, date of conviction, court of conviction, penalty imposed (especially if the penalty include a license suspension or revocation), and even the license plate of the vehicle associated with the violation. Some states (California is an example) preserve and show other names associated with that driving record, so women’s unmarried and previously married names often show up in the record. So, if the officer asks you how many tickets you’ve had or whether your license has been suspended previously, don’t lie, thinking he won’t have access to the full file. The notion that old suspensions and violations “drop off” your record after a time is a myth. Your insurance company may not see them, but law enforcement will.

title: Why do a lot of British people move to other countries?
post_text: I can only speak for my own experience. I left university in the middle of a recession, and with a middling degree in English Literature. It wasn’t the best combination. I moved to London, and tried to find a job I liked. I tried selling financial products (awful), media marketing (awful) and working in a bar (OK, but not a career). Then a friend told me she was doing a course in Teaching English as a Foreign Language (TEFL). This was pre-Internet, and so I looked in Tuesday’s Guardian for jobs. There were teaching jobs in Spain, and Italy, Mexico and Poland, Turkey and many other places. Suddenly, the world seemed like a much larger place, with many more opportunities. So, I think it was, if this is not too overblown, a search for adventure that took me overseas. Deliberately or not, I avoided the more common destinations for TEFL, and worked in places like Poland, what is now North Macedonia and post war Bosnia. I met new people, ate new food and learnt a bit of new languages. At the start of my career, it wasn’t about the money- you don’t make much as a TEFL teacher. 250,000 old Polish Zloty might sound a lot, and gave me a nice lifestyle- but it didn’t go very far outside Poland. Later in my career I moved back to the UK (for a girl). It didn’t last, and I was itching to move away again. I found working in the UK quite oppressive; endless meetings about KPIs and Health and Safety didn’t stir my soul. So I left again. It’s not all expat lifestyle and cocktail parties at the embassy (although I did go to one once*). There’s bureaucracy to deal with, crowded buses and a general sense of alienation and disorientation. Learning new languages gets harder (for me at least) as I get older. And I don’t have the long term friendships and deeply embedded social networks that UK based friends have. For family reasons I moved back to the UK a while back. But a few years later, I was offered a job in China. The money was better, the job was bigger and I was desperate for a change. The sense of adventure kicked in again. I signed the contract in Jan 2020, just as we were starting to hear of a SARS-like disease bubbling up in somewhere called Wuhan. But that’s a different story.

title: Throughout history, how do mines ensure that their miners weren't stealing the ores?
post_text: Well, ore rocks tend to be big and clunky, and it was not like ancient Roman miners in Hispania wore canvas pants with giant cargo pockets to hide them. In order to really steal from the mines, you had to steal a LOT of ore; once smelted, the majority of the ore rock is discarded as slag. And I’m pretty sure the miners don’t just go home carrying giant conspicuous sacks of rocky stuff without the foremen and reeves being none the wiser. Which in turn also kind of requires the miners to, somehow, operate a clandestine foundry to smelt the ore and produce their own ingots. Iron requires about 1538 degrees Celsius, or ​2800 °F to melt down; a very high temperature that only existed during the Iron Age, after centuries of Bronze being the prominent accessible metal. So we’re not talking a tiny fireplace at the corner of your hovel, we’re talking large bloomeries requiring huge amounts of fuel and heat to operate. So the difficulty of profiting from the mines yourself pretty much ensures no one bothered to try. It’s kind of like how we don’t have a Nuclear Police that goes around checking to make sure none of us sketchy types are making thermonukes at home: the resources and expertise required is way beyond the means of any average individual.

title: Is Brazil an expensive place to live as compared to places other than it abroad?
originally_answered: Is Brazil an expensive place to live?
post_text: Yes and no. For 90% of the people living in Brazil, and the products they consume daily, it is actually cheap in absolute terms. But for higher classes and richer neighborhoods, Rio and São Paulo rank among the most expensive places in the world (http://www.csmonitor.com/World/Americas/Latin-America-Monitor/2011/0712/Sao-Paulo-and-Rio-vault-up-list-of-most-expensive-cities-for-expats). Luxury consumption and electronics, imports, restaurants etc. are very expensive. Most entrepreneurs in Brazil attribute high prices to high taxes. Although they're high when compared to US taxes, they're somewhat lower when compared to taxes in northern Europe. The only decent explanation I found was given by piracy researchers (http://piracy.ssrc.org). They state that income disparity is so high that it doesn't make sense to have a lower pricing for a small elite. Pricing for most consumer goods in the US/Europe/Japan aim to be acceptable for 70%-80% of the population, while in Brazil it is useless to try selling any quality goods to more than 10% of the population -- people that are not among these 10% have little disposable income. Thus, products and services are priced so that they'll return an ENORMOUS profit per unit in a relatively small volume, while in developed economies they'd price most items as to make small margins and reach a larger part of the population. If you want to enojy a middle-class lifestyle (in US terms) you must have A LOT of money in Brazil.

title: What are some of the most underrated travel destinations in Asia?
post_text: Since Asia is a very big place, I can only speak from my own experiences living/working/travelling in SE and NE Asia for 4 years, but here are 3 “under-rated” or less known places, which I thoroughly enjoyed. (Disclosure: For travel, I prefer quiet but interesting places with authentic local feel, culture, food and landscape, rather than those with an advanced tourism infrastructure and the crowds that that brings) Phetchaburi town, Thailand - 3 hours bus ride outside of Bangkok. It’s a small, somewhat sleepy town with a series of Buddhist Temples and a royal house perched on a hilltop with lovely walking paths. The town also has a cave temple 2 kilometres by bicycle or motorbike to the North. Very few international tourists, and worth at least a day trip on the way to Hua Hin or Cha Am beaches. The tea plantation hills around Ali Shan National Park in Taiwan. There are B&B lodgings within the tea plantations that overlook the ravines along the entry road between Chayi and Alishan Park. May need to speak a few words of Mandarin. Quiet and off the beaten path. Friendly locals. Nice food and local culture. Access via the High Speed Rail from Taipei to Chayi, then change to Alishan bus. Kumano Kodo pilgrimage trail, Wakayama Prefecture, Japan - a system of ancient pilgrimage trails connecting small hamlets within the verdant mountains. Some distant and strenuous hikes. Many nature worship shrines along the path. Peaceful and spiritual. Natural hot springs. Must be planned ahead, as there is limited lodging in this rural area.

title: My daughter told me that she kissed a boy. She’s only 14, how long should I ground her?
post_text: Be grateful that she told you that piece of information! I didn’t tell my Mum hardly anything, because she made me feel embarrassed about it. So I hid anything remotely like that. And it really hurt in the long run. I feared judgement and when she was supposed to be the person I could turn to about ANYTHING, and she ruined that trust - then she lost everything. She lost me. Even now, there are things I just don’t bother talking to her about because I just can’t stand the judgement. If you don’t want to lose your child - the best thing you can do at this age, is find that balance between best friend and parent. And just be there for her to come and go to. Teenagers have totally different priorities because that’s their time in development. Their brain, their body - literally everything about them is changing. Their place in society. Their need to be accepted as part of the tribe. It dates back to the caveman societal and independent needs - so don’t push her away or think it’s a bad thing. Research where she should be in her development before you judge her. I’m not saying it will be easy - but be the bigger person and don’t push her away. If you want all those special things, like being included when she does get married, and having kids - then you need to be there for her right now too. Good luck xxx

title: How can I do exercise every day?
originally_answered: How do I exercise every single day?
post_text: Start small! Begin by doing just 5 pushups a day. If you can’t do pushups, do a plank for 10–30 seconds, depending on your starting strength. Then, when you feel unchallenged by this, do 5 pushups/10 -30 sec plank and 5 squat jumps or maybe 10 pushups/30–60 sec plank. Then, start incorporating other exercises in small increments and/or increase the repetitions of your current exercises. Start holding weights while you do squats and lunges. Learn how to do more dynamic plank exercises. Do this over many months and keeping working towards heavier weights or more reps (don’t overdo the reps though - that can lead to repetitive strain injuries). If you feel tired one day, just do 5 pushups or a plank or whatever you started at. By giving yourself an opportunity to ease into it on your tired days, you may surprise yourself by pushing a little farther just because you feel warmed up and motivated by your resolve. Give yourself opportunities to succeed and exceed your own expectations! That’s how you can exercise every day, without fail. Keep building out and switching up your workouts and, even if you are injured, you will have something you can do every single day, even if only for a minute or two with your own body weight.

title: Which site is more important to you, Quora or Wikipedia?
post_text: Well, look at my biographical/credential string, currently “Wikipedia administrator for over a decade”, and you can probably guess which is more important to me, hah. There are many reasons I find Wikipedia important or personally value it, but I’ll mention just a few of the big ones: Wikipedia’s mission to make knowledge available is important.  I think that an educated world has better potential to be peaceful and prosperous, and Wikipedia’s mission helps educate the world. Wikipedia’s set up to be around in the long term.  It makes database dumps available, it’s freely-licensed, it relies  exclusively  on free and open-source software and non-patent-encumbered file formats (MP3’s patents  finally  expired in 2017!), and so on. Its parent non-profit organization keeps careful financial reserves, has a huge pool of small independent donors from the public (rather than relying on fewer large grants) and is in the process of setting up a small endowment to help guarantee the most core costs (servers etc.) in perpetuity. I stress the non-profit angle here because that implies the organization’s not chained to the profit motive, which can imply needless risk. Participating in Wikipedia is inherently political.  Wikipedia makes a very careful attempt to take a neutral point of view in its content, and that’s very important, but that to some degree conceals some values of Wikipedia that are  highly  political: free speech, equality, strong exceptions and limitations to intellectual property laws, valuing knowledge, and so on. While it uses its power sparingly,  its 2012 blackout over the (now failed) SOPA and PIPA legislation  in the US is widely cited as one of the larger factors that sunk the acts. Wikipedia is dependent on, and may help encourage, liberal democracy. That’s frighteningly big-picture when talking about a  website . Wikipedia sets good epistemic expectations.  In an era where “fake news” is a buzzword, Wikipedia’s already spent years building up a reputation for reliability despite not formally* using “experts” to write and edit its articles. (*Many editors are, formally or  de facto , experts in their fields, but they don’t have special authority on Wikipedia from that.) Rather, Wikipedia makes the unusual point of admitting its fallibility up front and encouraging readers to judge and follow up on the sources it cites—and correct it if it’s wrong. Sure, traditional sources have a point in seeking to be reliable  per se , but on the other hand, they risk being or becoming epistemic black boxes, dead ends in tracing back the game of academic-Broken-Telephone. Wikipedia makes a point of showing where its facts came from, of encouraging doubt and critical thinking and advertising its faults. That’s important.

post_text: The language of Austria is obviously German. There are some differences between German in Germany and German in Austria - one that springs to mind is  Jänner  instead of  Januar  for the first month of the year - but those are trivial differences. Spoken Austrian German can be heavily dialectal, but most Austrian dialects are quite similar to the dialects of Bavaria in Southern Germany and are indeed classified as Bavarian dialects. In Vorarlberg, the province that is nearest to Switzerland, the local dialect is Alemannic, i.e. more similar to Swiss German dialects.
header: What language is spoken in Austria?

originally_answered: What does Thomas de la Marnière think of the movement for independence of Southern Brazil?
post_text: That’s the first time I’m being addressed a question directly. Perhaps  Habib F  will award me with a Sockistan nobility title for this reason. :D Unfortunately, while I try to follow various independence movements across the world, I’m not very good with South America about this and I think I have heard about Brazil, but I would not be able to have any opinion about this. The only thing I am aware of about this area is this trilateral war between Brazil, Argentina and Paraguay I think, that is much controversial in its memory. Perhaps this is related ? I have however general guidelines : If this population is allogenous to the place, they should try to agree with the local indigenous to define how each sovereignty is going to be defined, and the rights and duties of each. The quality of being allogenous doesn’t make them disappear from the map, and it’s stupid to say that just for this reason they have no rights at all and that the current geopolitical arrangement would be any less or any more legitimate than an alternative one. You cannot criticize anybody on the grounds of being allogenous if the end result is to endorse the status quo. They must not be a diaspora or immigrant community from a nation that is already independent and that they always have the option to go to. However this does not always work. By this standard, Catalonia would not have any legitimacy to ask for independence because Andorra exists. By these standards, indigenous Abenaki in Québec would not be due anything because this is not the region there were originally from. So obviously this idea would therefore need to be refined to be adapted to these problematic exceptions. Ideally, they must have had a national identity for a few centuries. I don’t take much seriously movements that are exclusively based on notions they don’t want to share ressources with other of their own nationals. However, genuine independentist are often accused of being that (again, Catalonia). In my views, if Alberta does have an actual national identity, I would not question their independence movement, but if it’s only about not sharing, then it’s difficult for me to take them seriously. So far, all I’ve ever seen from them was complaining about liberals. This is not serious enough in my opinion. If they have an independence movement, it’s in its infancy. I don’t care much wether you’re oppressed or not ; it might help, but that’s not the only point. I don’t much care if you’re resourceless or resourceful. Look at Iceland or Japan. They don’t have much ressources and still do wonders. I do not believe this is a major issue as long as you know how to compensate for it. I don’t see much favorably the Soviet idea of redrawing the borders to equalize the availability of resources, it just creates more problems. I prefer cooperation, treaties to solve that. Condominium can be an option. The point should be to resolve a geopolitical problem in order to achieve a lasting and more durable peace, that would create respect where previously due respect was not given. If an Islamic State or a Boko Haram state, in the current meaning, managed to exist, I would support to encroach their sovereignty because there is no hope for them to coexist peacefully. You get a lot of points if you have a distinct language. Don’t contact uncontacted tribes, leave them alone. Wait for them to contact us. This is a Prime Directive, basically. So draw your own conclusions.

title: Do I have to bring my watch to a jeweler to replace the battery or can I do it myself?
post_text: You can do it yourself, but it may take special tools. There are essentially two styles of watch cases, one that screws in and one that snaps in. The former can be difficult to open without a case wrench. Here’s a generic case wrench: There are also much simpler ones designed for a single case size. Snap on cases can be pried off, but again it works much better with a special knife with a rounded rather than sharp blade. When you remove the case off take care not lever against the part of the case where the watch band is attached. There will be a tab on most watches where you should insert the knife and exert pressure. You can buy inexpensive watch tools online, on Amazon, for example. Some watches, like a Rolex, may require a special tool to open. Before removing the back, make sure to clean the area carefully so that no debris will fall into the movement when you open it. The next problem is to get the correct battery. Once you open the case you can read the battery type off the battery itself. Let me plug  Battery Bob  here, a website that has really good information and deals on batteries of all kinds. You’ll typically want a silver oxide battery rather than an alkaline battery. The final problem involves replacing the battery itself. You can typically pry the battery out and slide a new one in. You could find it necessary to remove some screws and that will take a special small screwdriver and it poses the very real risk of losing a tiny screw (after which you are literally screwed). title: Why do Hindu kids know very little about Hinduism compared to Muslim and Christians kids?
post_text: Balinese Tradition From my experience as a person who is born from Hindu family in Bali, I really never being taught in depth about Hindu in my family.  Up until high school, I only do what my parent do  (the orthodox version of Hindu Bali).  We go to temple, pray, and then eat the fruit from offering at home. Gebogan As you can see, there are many fruit. After we offer it at temple and got back home, we eat it and share it with all family member. The most common fruit are banana, apple, orange, and pear, also cake and crackers.  My favorite is the crackers with banana. We don’t really pray everyday, just occasionally.  On full moon (Purnama) which come once a month (both at home and temple). And on Piodalan day on local temple which come once or twice a year (there are four temple in every village which have their own Piodalan day, so a total of up to 8 times a year). What we do every day is offering which is like this. Canang By the way, as part of ritual in Piodalan day in temple, there is dance and music performance in which kids can also participate. I also participate to play  gamelan  while my sister she learn how to dance and have perform dance in temple until she lost the interest and stop. This is called  ngayah,  somewhat similar to volunteer. The biggest event (festival) would be Galungan day  which come every 210 day (once or twice a year). It is a 2 weeks long celebration. There are many preparation to do. On the first two days my mother often have to stay up late. Mejejahitan, making prepation for Galungan celebration Penjor, symbol of majesty and abundance Mebat, Balinese tradition to cook together Decorating the family temple As you can see, the preparation often involve the whole family. The wives and daughters prepare more or less all the offerings. The husbands and sons do other preparation such as decorate the family temple, cooking and other things. On the third day (Wednesday) we all pray at the village temples and on the fourth day (Thursday) on family temple. And on Saturday on the following week, we pray at both village temples and family temple. I never read any holy scripture. The closest I ever read are Mahabharata and Ramayana epic  (also its TV series and its shadow puppet “wayang” version). I have deep interest in this. In school curriculum, there is religion subject but it just give general explanation but not in depth knowledge.  Unlike Islam and Christian which is somehow compulsory to learn Arabic or Hebrew even in class, we never learn Sanskrit.  Also there is no further learning outside of school, Christian have Sunday school, Islam have Madrasah and Pesantren, Hindu have none. Each family temple also have their Piodalan day. On this day the whole family gather, include my aunts, her husband and their children. The bigger family may have more than 50 people gathered on this day. Beside family temple ( sanggah / merajan ) at home, village temples ( Pura Dalem, Pura Puseh, Pura Desa and Pura Kahyangan ), we also go to ancestry temple ( Pura Kawitan),  only on Piodalan day though so once or twice a year .  If you wondering what is Piodalan day, it is a day when the temple is built (more or less like birthday), usually celebrated once or twice a year  (either every 210 days or 360 days, there are two calendar system that are commonly followed). More closer to India version When I reach high school somehow my mother join some Ashram and my father learn about meditation. Both of them got in depth in their respective way. My mother invited me to join her to Ashram in which I learn more about Hinduism especially about Sarasvati and Ganesha. She is a devotee of Lakshmi ever since. She also invite my father, but he somewhat reluctant and not that interested.  She do Lakshmi Pooja every morning before going to work. My father leaning more toward meditation.  At first he join an inner power self-defense school (local) to self-healing therapy (Reiki & Ling-Chi) but somehow learn about meditation (Kundalini). title: Is there a World War Two movie made from the Nazi's point of view?
post_text: Many films have been listed by other answers primarily involving Germany, so here’s a few about the other Axis powers. The Battle of El Alamein  (1968) was an Italian film about their role in the operation that saw the beginning of the Axis being expelled from North Africa. It’s unusual for it’s production time period by showing the Italian Army in a positive and heroic light, unlike most films of this time which always depicted them as buffoons. It’s generally faithful to the battle, but the low budget of it is noticeable, as it depicts the valour of the  Bersaglieri  and the parachute  Folgore  division during the fighting and seems to be basically historically true to fact. There are a few dramatic licenses, particularly showing the British as the bad guys and committing a war crime by executing German prisoners, but it is refreshing to see the Italians portrayed well. Another Italian film about this battle is the 2002 production called  El Alamein: The Line of Fire.  This is a more hard-hitting picture, unlike the  Boys Own  feel of the above one, which shows the trials and tribulations of the Italian soldiers in events leading up to, and during, the battle. It very much has an anti-war feel, and particularly follows a young soldier, who, believing the Axis propaganda, reckons that the Italians and Germans will soon be the conquerors of Egypt, and his growing disillusionment when he realises that this will not be the case. An excellent film, and again, very interesting to get an Italian perspective. So OK, Finland was not, strictly speaking, an ‘Axis’ power in WW2, but to all intents and purposes it was an ally, as it fought it’s Continuation War against the USSR, from 1941–44, to regain the territory it lost in the 1939–40 Winter War. During the massive Soviet summer offensive of 1944, the Finns desperately tried to repel the Russians’ attacks, and the Finnish film  Tali-Ihantala 1944  (2007)   faithfully recreates the battle of that name which stopped the Soviets from occupying Finland, like they were doing with Germany’s Eastern European allies. Despite being pushed back by the Red Army, the Finns gallantly fought their opponents to a standstill, and this film tells the story of this heroic struggle. Brilliant movie. As a footnote, there’s a Japanese film, excellently done, about the last days of the Kwantung Army in Manchuria, also fighting against the Soviet’s, part of  The Human Condition  trilogy,  The Road to Eternity  (1959).

title: Do protein shakes help repair muscle?
post_text: Yes, protein shakes repair muscle. Muscle tissue is 100% made of amino acids. Protein shakes too are made of amino acids, therefore, protein shakes are essential for muscle growth and repair. When you work out, you literally destroy muscle tissue. However, following your workout, the body temporarily speeds up protein synthesis to repair the torn down muscle. This is the ideal time to eat protein in order to prolong protein synthesis and prevent your muscles from wasting away. If you do not eat protein following a workout, your elevated protein synthesis will last about an hour and your muscles will eat themselves to shrinkage. Because protein shakes are predigested, blood levels of amino acids spike within 45 min upon ingestion. That means your blood amino acid levels will meet the 1 hour window you have before your muscles break down. That's assuming you drink the protein shake immediately following exercise. The growth happens during sleep though, but is piggybacked on the protein you ate earlier. The best way to kick start protein synthesis is consume 20gm of whey and 5–10gm of BCAAs (branch chained amino acids). Or, just 35 gm of whey protein. title: Why are Apple devices so expensive? Are they worth it?
post_text: Although people love pointing out Brand Loyalty and Marketing as the main reasons for Apple prices with Apple buyers for some reason been blind or not educated or just wanting to pay money to have what seems to be a culture symbol these are not actually the reasons why the Apple devices are so expensive.  Dave Haynie's answer to Why are Apple devices so expensive? Are they worth it?  does cover a lot of the concept nicely and be sure to read it as well but there are some oversimplification on the ‘specs are the same’ or the Luxury brand approach. There are actually two main reasons for the price. 1. Apple has zero low end devices. There is no ‘One Laptop Per Child’ clone, no Low spec tablet for the poor nor a barebone barely usable phone for a teen/child to hopefully try to socialize. It’s easy to say how a MacBook costs thousands of dollars when you can buy a decent PC for less than $400 (and I have a few of these and are indeed fine) but the MacBook Pro is not just a decent PC. It’s a high end behemoth that is priced comparably with any other Windows laptop that is on the same spec sheet and has comparable size/weight (miniaturization costs a lot you all!) Of course if we forget the size sure there are Windows PCs that can have better specs for the same prize or cost quite less but there’s always a catch for the less. Worst screen? (there were no Retina displays on any PC until a couple of years ago) SSD that is a lot slower? (1TB of a SATA 3 SSD is a lot cheaper and a lot slower than a nvme SSD). They also use old laptop chassis with new CPUs so there are times where you can see a Dell with new Intel CPUs for less than the Macbook Pro with the previous one. But first this happens on any vendor (just check all the dual core i7 U laptops the same price as the quad core i7 u ones). What does happen though is that other OEMs update to new components faster nowadays. Which creates weird Frankenstein laptops with old screens, old ports and a dedicated GPU that is slower than the integrated GPU packed with the CPU since Asus/Lenovo/Dell simply had those in stock and they could sell it as a feature and indeed you pay for it. If we compare the same products they are not really that different price wise. Even accessories. Sure you can find chargers for lower-end laptops for 30 or less but have you seen the cost of Chargers for high-end HPs or Dells? They are $90–110. And this is not a new trend. The only thing that was a decade ago ‘new’ is the Ultrabook category which sure started with the MacBook Air, a laptop that was a lot slower compared to the 3kg laptops of same age that cost half the price but the difference in portability was insane and hence it sold well. I found it hard to carry my normal sized fast laptop around so rarely carried it when someone that bought the slow Air just threw it in a bag every day just in case (I speak from experience). 2. Retail Price. A second issue which is due to the demand of the devices (as covered by most of other answers) is that an Apple Product stays closer to its asked Retail Price (MSRP) for a lot more. You can see a new Samsung device priced exactly the same to a comparing iPhone when released and then after a couple of months costing $200 or more less. So 6 months later you can see the Samsung or the LG costing 2/3 of the iPhone. But this is the price to the store. The asking price usually is the same for the remainder of the self life. Apple at least does change the MSRP when a new phone is released when I’ve never seen an old Galaxy S ever displaying a lower MSRP since the retailers have already lowered it. Sure there are products Apple Sells that are highly outdated and keep selling them for the old MSRP (hello MacMini with 4th gen Intel CPUs) and the pricing there is at least weird. But there are always on products with no real alternative. You can get some Atom based small PCs for a lot less but if you go for i5/i7 then you will most probably reach similar prices (Update: you can go for a Chinese NUC alternative and spend the same or less). And about demand we can see how the iPhone 8 series became a bit more affordable and faster due to not selling as much. The MSRP stayed the same but on retailers they weren’t a lot more expensive than the other with similar MSRP Android devices. Now is it worth it? For most people, no it doesn't. Do you really need the fastest phone to get a selfie or send a message to your friends? You probably don’t. Does it really matter to you if the device will stutter a bit or some times hang up for a millisecond? Of course it does not. So a mid-range Android device from a company that doesn't boggle the device with stupid gimmicks and tries to optimize the software a bit is more than enough for most people (Something like Sony). Even if you want an iPhone since all your family use iMessages etc you can get a second hand for the price of the mid range Android or even less. As stated by the other answers most Apple devices really last long (save for some defects that any device can have) and they are really supported for years with Apple still having battery replacements and screens etc so you can use it for long. But if you want something new and shiny every now and then why not get some of the respected Chinese Android vendors? Having an iPhone is all about the synergy of using all its devices together but if you only want one phone to use and don’t care for syncing etc Android will get you there. And can also help you with some computer like tasks not allowed on the iPhone (torrents for example. You can do pretty much everything else just fine on both) The same for Computers. If you work on your computer and reliability is the most important for you, maybe a Mac is not that bad of an idea. Not because they are super difficult to break, since everything breaks eventually and randomly but because Apple is everywhere and you can most probably fix it and have it using the latest OS for years. But then the new ones have everything glued together so if you can find something that can be upgraded without been really heavy might also be a better option if you travel a lot and you can not wait for someone to try to unglue stuff etc or find a new motherboard. Also now ultrabooks have come a long way so there are not just super slow machines that aren’t expensive but there are some quite small but capable and even convertible to tablet devices that you can get for a manageable sum. Also let’s be real unless you are a designer/cinematographer or a developer or an engineer/scientist (or any other profession that uses really heavy software) 2 CPU cores and 4 or 8GB of RAM is more than enough. You can do everything most people do and never feel that something is slow and there’s really no reason to upgrade from something that was not slow when you bought 3–5 years ago if you only use it to Browse and use Office type software and email as long as it has an SSD. If you are a gamer then the ‘it’s too expensive’ does not matter to you since the $700 GPU card you just bought will not run the new games at ‘acceptable’ quality in 2 years and you need Windows anyway so why not go the Desktop PC mode anyway and skip the Apple Devices. TL;DR: If you want something that is fast and reliable since you use it constantly, every day, you want to be sure it will never let you down (at least that it will be less likely) and you want to stay with it for quite some time an iPhone or a MacBook is a good choice but if you want something to just do simple stuff try any other vendor. Just wait for some good sale and go with it.

title: No student wants to become a teacher. Why?
originally_answered: Why don't most people want to be teachers?
post_text: There are (or at least  were ) two reasons why people became teachers in Greece: It was a stable well (for middle class) paying job with 15 days off at Christmas, 15 at Easter and 2 months of in summer It was a person’s vocation, they really wanted to teach, to open people’s minds After 2011 and the austerity that hit Greece, with the huge pay cuts in every civil servant’s paycheck (almost all schools in Greece are public and teachers are paid directly by the government, like doctors in public hospitals are and other employees in various government jobs, from cleaning personnel to executives), most people turned away from teaching jobs. Until then, the supply was much greater than the demand. As years go by, with so many “counselors” and “advisors” who have never set foot inside a greek classroom (especially a rural one) since they were students themselves making the policies and rules for teachers to follow, there are too many loopholes that can be exploited by students and parents to make teaching a difficult and often thankless job today. We have the blind not leading, but forcing everyone down a path to destruction. And the paycheck doesn’t make it worth your while anymore. As a high school teacher for the past 20 odd years in the Greek education system, there are a few things the government can to to make the whole system much better and more substantial: fire all their “advisors” that haven’t taught in actual classrooms in various parts of Greece: from the rural mainland areas, to the tiny islands that are cut off for months at a time from the rest of Greece to the big cities with the huge and chaotic classrooms and in both general education schools and technical school (trust me, it’s not that extreme an idea or condition: almost every teacher in Greece has done their “tour” of Greece before they got tenure, it’s a fact of life). Most advisors today - IF  they were ever appointed to a school, they spent their time behind a desk in some Minister’s office, not a classroom Pass laws that improve students’ accountability: there are too many things that students get away with (including “seizing” the school building for days with zero demands or reasons for doing so. it’s become a country wide tradition that commemorates absolutely nothing) Give teachers decent salaries that can cover everything they are expected to provide, not to their students, but to the Department of Education And pay them their damn overtime

title: Why can I get items cheaper by ordering pickup online than just buying in store? I have seen this at three different retail stores.
post_text: This really could be for several reasons. It could have something to do with the store trying to boost sales on the website especially if it is something that they recently implemented. More often than not I would say that it really comes down to the simple fact that they haven't had to pay to have the item transported to the store so there's less cost associated with that item for the company. If you think about it if you order something online and you get it shipped to your house instead of buying it in store you're really just cutting out the store as the middleman for the product. Instead of the store buying it from their supplier, and then it being shipped to their warehouse, and then being shipped to the store (all which needs to be paid for), it just gets sent from the supplier to the warehouse. Then if it's purchased online before it is sent to the store then that step is essentially just removed from the supply chain process. However, even with a lot of places offering free shipping on most items these days chances are you are going to pay some kind of fee to have the item sent to you, or some kind of processing fee for ordering it online. Which more often than not would be more than the difference in price between the website and the store. So if that is the case in all reality you are really paying more for the item instead of paying less for it. Even though it is listed as a lower price point on the website and it is on the shelf in the store.

title: What would happen if cars didn't have grills?
originally_answered: What will happen if cars didn't have grills?
post_text: Q:   What will happen if cars didn’t have grills? A:  Cars are transportation machines. The only reason that they have “grills” is because for the first 100 years of cars, internal combustion engines prevailed, and internal combustion engines needed to be cooled, and “grills” let the air into the radiator to do so. Not all ICE cars had grills. Note that the VW Bug and the Chevy Corvair, being air cooled engines didn’t have a grill. But every other car did. So time for a story. Before cars, there were horse-drawn buggies, and they were the primary mode of transportation. So when the first cars came out, they looked a LOT like a horse drawn buggy. Finally, cars began to look like cars, and not buggies. And in the same way, the first electric vehicles look a lot like gas cars, and self driving cars will look a lot like gas cars. But eventually, a new paradigm will emerge, focused on the inherent idiom of self-driving electric transportation systems. And they won’t look like “cars” at all. (Notice the “grill?”) (Notice that the “advanced future” EV cars mostly still have a “grill” even though it has no real function.) But in the future, there will be no need of it, and it will go away.

They have an open marriage to which they invite “spiritual wives”, meaning unmarried women who pretend to be and behave as if they were married to the man but know that they have no legal rights, privileges, benefits, duties, or protections as wives by secular or canon law. They claim to be married only in the eyes of their God (theologically questionable), not in the eyes of the law. Spiritual marriages are not illegal in the United States. post_text: It depends who gifted it to you and why. title: Why does it always seem that people with a high IQ (140+) have reached some sort of ultimate truth that makes them not care about their high IQ?
post_text: Why does it always seem that people with a high IQ (140+) have reached some sort of ultimate truth that makes them not care about their high IQ? Thanks, Darius, for the A2A. This is a tricky question for me to answer not because I don’t have an answer, but rather because Quora is a platform of echo chambers extraordinaire. It’s easy to get wrong ideas about subjects such as high-level IQ because so many people, many of them psychologists, that don’t have high-level IQ set themselves as subject matter experts. How dare I disagree with the consensus of “experts?” I’ll answer this question personally, because it’s not necessarily fair for me to speak for everyone with IQ >140. With that said, the profoundly gifted people I know tend to share some of the same sentiments. The reason it seems that way is because we need to watch our words very carefully. An intellectual variant of  Tall Poppy Syndrome  applies, and the taller the poppy, the more careful it must be to not get cut down. To not care about something means to not feel concern or interest, or attach importance to something.    Now, I don’t know any of us that is so much of a jerk that s/he will imply something along the lines of, “You need to have an IQ above such-and-such a level in order to be my friend or associate. If you haven’t been tested on the Stanford Binet or Wechsler Scales and have an IQ above [a certain number] then go away.” This is complete bullcrap, and no polite person has any business doing such a thing. At the same time, if we do know our IQ, it does actually concern and interest us because the concept of IQ and all the research done surrounding it helps us to better understand ourselves and our relationship to the world around us. So, we do care, but not in the self-aggrandizing way that people who just want to go around cutting off the tops of tall poppies would accuse us of doing. Additionally, there are many other metrics to measure ourselves by than just IQ. We are multidimensional human beings. We aren’t stupid, and most of us have more than a modicum of self awareness, so why would we attach a disproportionately high weighting to one metric over another? So, between not attracting too much attention to ourselves by poppy choppers, and having at least somewhat of a realistic perception of ourselves, there is no reason for us to blow one aspect of ourselves out of proportion.

title: Why do some people say that BTS is just as revolutionary as The Beatles?
post_text: Because if you compare the early Beatles (up to say 1965) and BTS, the similarities are striking. The Beatles were the headliners of a new kind of sound (Merseybeat) that first swept England and then the world. They were rough leather boys that were ‘cleaned up’ by Epstein and presented in a compact formula (cute boys with longish hair who had clever quips for the cameras) and who performed their own songs along with covers. The girls of the world fell at their feet, and they made British Rock fashionable. BTS are a group Big Hit CEO Bang Shi Hyuk (PD Bang) wanted to form as a hard-core rap group. He signed RM, Suga and Supreme Boi as the core (although Supreme Boi decided not to continue when the concept changed - he’s now a producer for BTS). JHope (street dancer supreme) got signed on early as well. The concept changed a bit however, as the boys got ‘cleaned up’ and other more idol-like trainees were added (Jimin, Jin, V, Jungkook). They had their own style and wrote a lot of the lyrics (the raps - RM, Suga - especially). This style became gradually popular, first in South Korea and then the world. BTS are currently THE biggest boy band IN the world, and have been for about 3 years. They have brought KPop to the attention of the West (KPop already ruled in Asia, since TVXQ) and this has allowed a lot of other KPop groups access to Western audiences. Now, the Beatles went on to become musical icons who changed the sound of pop music, because of the outstanding talent of Lennon & McCartney as song writers, and the innovations the later Beatles showed (starting with Revolver). I have no idea if BTS will ever reach these heights. I haven’t seen anyone seriously compare BTS to the LATER Beatles.

title: What are the chances that I, being 17 years of age, will live forever, or at least for a very long time based on the ever more frequent technological advancements that are taking place?
originally_answered: What are the chances that I, being 17 years of age, will live forever, or at least for a very long time based on the ever more frequent technological advancements that are taking place?
post_text:
I would say your chances are "decent."  My personal opinion is that there is a nontrivial chance that the speed of advance in the relevant areas of science and technology will DECREASE due to poor choices by governments and other large institutions regarding the structuring of society in ways that incentivize this work.  But, assuming this possibility is avoided, by the time you reach traditional "middle age" -- 40-50 years of age -- advances in life extension and rejuvenation will have been made that will extend your lifespan so significantly that you might "make it" into an era where life span becomes effectively indefinite.
 
In the 1990s I was MUCH more optimistic that someone born in the 1990s would "make it" as I describe above.  Now, I'm significantly more pessimistic.
 
As for the idea that people won't WANT to live such extended lives, I heartily disagree.  So much of the weariness that comes in middle age and later derives from the slow, steady decay of the body.  I'm 57 -- I know what I'm talking about.  I think those who make such arguments lack imagination about what life as a 200 year old in the body of a 20 year old might be like.

title: Should Bhutan grow out of India's shadow and initiate direct official diplomatic ties with China?
post_text: Let me highlight that Bhutan is an independent and sovereign nation that is totally free to choose its allies or to diplomatically engage with any country in the world that it chooses to. If there is a general impression that Bhutan only supports India and it is India that controls the external relations of Bhutan, then it is a very  misguided impression. Bhutan is opening up to the world and its relations are already diverse and spread out: Bhutan is a member of the UN since 1971. It maintains diplomatic relations with  52 nations  and the  EU , but it doesn’t have such relations with any of the 5 Permanent Members of UNSC (which includes China). It is a founding member of the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation ( SAARC ). It is also a member of  BIMSTEC, World Bank, the IMF, Group of 77  and others. Can you still say that India controls Bhutan’s relations? Friendship with India:  Historically, the relations between Bhutan and its southern ally India is exemplary of the bonhomie and true friendship shared between good neighbours. Bhutan was the first foreign nation to be visited by PM Modi after taking office The cornerstone of the relation was the Indo-Bhutan friendship Treaty signed all the way back to 1949 and since then, India has been a friendly ally to this Himalayan nation through thick and thin. 80% of Bhutan’s imports come from India, and India buys 90% of Bhutan’s exports; and is also committed to the development of Bhutan and has invested heavily in infra projects worth millions of dollars. Why not China? :  The Tibetan issues of 1950s made Bhutan anxious of its security from China, which further cemented its strategic partnership with India. Even though this issue has faded, there is still an undemarcated border and unresolved territorial disputes between Bhutan and China. The latest issue of the  Donglang  plateau (Bhutanese territory claimed by China) in 2017 that stretched over 70 days and even made a dent in Indo-China relations shows the complexity of the situation faced by Bhutan, and may show why it is still uneasy about China. But Bhutan has directly engaged with China and held formal talks and exchanged visits on many occasions, which shows that today Bhutan is more close to PRC than it ever was: Bhutan and China started annual direct talks to settle border disputes in 1984. They arrived at an agreement of peace and respect for territorial integrity in 1998. More Chinese tourists now visit Bhutan. Tibet is getting massive investments in infrastructure, which enhances trade and commerce opportunities for Bhutan. There have also been official visits between the two nations. Therefore in the modern times, nothing is stopping Bhutan from developing its ties with other nations. It is only the anxious history and the disputes of the present that stress the development of bilateral ties between Bhutan and the PRC. India would be happy as long as any relation promotes peace in the Himalayas and satisfies our security concerns and respects the territorial integrity of both India and its ally Bhutan. Bhutanese King Jigme Namgyel Wangchuk and Prince Gyalsey meet PM Modi, Nov 2017. title: Do any religions believe in god(s) who are not immortal?
post_text: The Norse deities certainly weren’t immortal. They could and did die - and many more of them will die in the future, at Ragnarök (‘fate of the gods’), the apocalyptic battle at the end of the present world that will ultimately destroy the planet, submerging it under water. ‘Battle of the Doomed Gods’ by Friedrich Wilhelm Heine (1882) The Norse deities exist purely to avert Ragnorok. They keep the outer darkness at bay by constantly battling with monsters; indeed, much of their interest in humans is in gathering enough warriors to help them fight this last battle. But in the meantime, they must regularly eat the apples of Idun - (‘the rejuvenating one’) - the mysterious fruits which enable them to retain their youth and ward off the process of ageing. Once, through the trickery of Loki, Idun was captured by the giant Tahzi, and the gods began to age rapidly. The gods then informed Loki that if he couldn’t rescue Idun he would be put to death. The goddess Freya lent Loki her hawk feathers, with which one can shift his or her shape into that of a hawk. Once he found her, Loki turned the goddess into a nut and sped away with her in his talons. For a while, the gods became immortal once again. Loki's flight to Jötunheim, illustration by J Collingwood c. 1908. But time - and Ragnarok - can’t be postponed indefinitely. Like the Christian apocalypse, Ragnarok sets out a series of signs that will ultimately define the end of times. The first sign is the Fimbulvetr, a winter with constant snow that will last for a year. The crowing of three roosters is foretold to signify the beginning of Ragnarök: the third red rooster, Gullinkambi, will warn all the gods about the beginning of their end. The god Heimdallr will use the horn Gjallarhorn to play a specific tone that will be heard in Valhalla, and this will bring these warriors back to life and they will march to the realm called Vigrid (the place of battles), where the final battle will take place. The cock Gullinkambi atop his head and the burning rainbow bridge Bifrost in the background, Heimdallr blows into Gjallarhorn to announce the arrival of Ragnarok. Thor kills the world serpent, Jormundandr, but then dies from his poisoned wounds after taking nine steps. Garm, a giant dog associated with the forces of destruction, bites off the other hand of Tyr, and he bleeds out, but not before he gives Garm a mortal wound. Heimdall and Loki inflict fatal wounds on each other, but Loki will refuse to die until he sees the destruction of the worlds which happens soon after. They will then both die next to each other. And although Odin selected the finest of the fallen to join an him in preparation, he too is fated to go down fighting, swallowed by the great wolf, Fenrir: Ragnarok (Franz Stassen, 1920) Vidar will kill then Fenrir by stepping on his jaw and splitting it all the way down through his tail. That's when Ragnarok ends: Surtr will alight the world in flame, and a a flood will finally cover the world. Creation will be completely undone, as if it had never happened. The gods will decide to go to battle, even though they know the prophecies have foretold their deaths as the outcome. Humans too will die; but they are simply ‘collateral damage’, which is what distinguishes Ragnarok from the Christian apocalypse, in which humans are specifically punished for not being faithful to God. So it’s clear that immortality is not a part of the Norse religion for either humans or gods. Being a god might bring you a wilder, more ‘interesting’ and longer life - but immortality is certainly not part of the deal.

Genre Blending : The lines between genres continue to blur. Rock is increasingly fused with pop, electronic, and hip-hop elements, creating hybrid styles that resonate with a broader audience. This blending can make rock more accessible and relevant. Emerging Artists : New rock bands and artists are gaining traction on platforms like TikTok and Spotify, where they can reach younger audiences. This grassroots approach can help rock regain its footing in the musical landscape. Nostalgia and Legacy Acts : Established rock bands are still touring and releasing new music, tapping into nostalgia. This can inspire younger generations to explore rock music, leading to a resurgence. Cultural Shifts : As societal issues evolve, rock's traditionally rebellious and countercultural themes may resonate more with younger audiences seeking music that reflects their experiences and challenges. While it may not return to the dominance it once had, rock could certainly evolve and find new life in the 2020s, potentially taking on forms that blend its classic roots with modern influences.
