title: If a South Korean and a North Korean teenager meet, would they understand each other?
post_text: Yes, with goodwill on both sides. The northern dialect is archaic. This was true before North Korea existed. For example, northerners say “rodong” for labour, while southerners say “nodong”. (This is why there were two presidents of South Korea who wrote their names Roh, while pronouncing it “No”. They didn’t want to be Mr No.} The language of South Korea has taken on a lot of English words, which are unknown in the North. North Korea does not use Chinese characters (hanja) which South Korea does. The political divide has lead to a linguistic divide: South Korea does not use words like “comrade”.  Juche,  the North Korean slogan, is not found in any South Korean dictionary. Culturally, the two countries are worlds apart. In the South, they have K-pop, while the North has the Moranbong Band. One side is dominated by a ridiculous personality cult centred on a plump man, but in the North they have never heard of Psy. This cultural divide might be difficult to cross at times. Overall, there would be various obstacles, but they could be overcome by goodwill.

title: How common is post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) among Navy SEALs?
post_text: This is a very difficult question to answer because it is clearly very inherently different to each individual person. I, personally have no PTSD whatsoever. I am very at peace with every decision I made. I am at peace with every round I fired from my rifle. I am at peace with every room I entered and cleared. I am at peace with everything I had to do. Second guessing decisions will not change a damn thing. Reliving events over and over wondering what could have gone differently will not bring anyone back and will not alter any resulting situations. I say all this having been involved in some very hairy situations. I knew that every single operation I was on could have been my last and I was ok with that. That said, I was never seriously injured in combat. I never was awarded the Purple Heart. I never had a teammate due in my arms. I never witnessed anyone lose any limbs. I never accidentally killed a non-combatant. I’ve experienced friends who did not make it back (but I was not with them when tragedy struck). I do also know guys that do struggle with what the doctors call PTSD for a myriad of reasons. Why are they affected and not me? Especially when we experience md some of the EXACT same things. I don’t have the answers for that. I wish I did. 🤷🏻‍♂️ I don’t know what it comes down to in determining who is affected by PTSD and who is not. Very early into the GWOT, I had an old crusty Master Chief tell me something that stuck with my over many years. He said, “you must not get any joy out of killing the enemy (if you do you are psychotic and need to seek medical assistance immediately). You also do not get any sorrow out of killing the enemy. Your enemy is willing to kill you WITHOUT hesitation. He wants to make your wife a widow and he wants to make your children fatherless. He wants to kill you. You must act before he does because he will not hesitate.” That sticks with me even to this day. Like with fear, your emotion is not the absence of empathy but the control of it. I say this all the time: control your emotions or they will control you.

title: What is an unpopular opinion you hold?
post_text: A government should not be able to dictate what a person does with their body. This includes, but isn't limited to recreational drug use, prostitution, and the choice to end your own life. Counseling should always be an option (and should be encouraged) for those who need it, but it should not be the government's job to protect a person from themselves. Recreational drug use: Let me start by stating that I'm speaking only about these activities in and of themselves, because self-destructive behavior is just that; you cannot be your own victim, and I've always felt that if there isn't a victim, there isn't a crime. If a person under the influence of drugs harms someone else, that's completely different than someone just using in the privacy of their own home. The biggest arguments I usually hear in favor of criminalization are that these substances can destroy a person's life, and that they can be deadly. Well, so can plenty of legal substances. Most people are aware that alcohol can cause most of the same personal and relationship problems that other drugs can, yet no one is advocating for a return to prohibition. We're also aware that common, over-the-counter medications can, and will kill you if you take too much. Those substances are perfectly legal to use, up until a person under the influence endagers someone other than themselves (drinking and driving, for instance). Why not do the same for other substances? I feel like it would likely prove beneficial in some ways, the most important being that it would make it much easier for addicts to get treatment. Many addicts are reluctant to do so because they could get in trouble for having used in the first place. Decriminalize it, and it becomes no different than a recovering alcoholic going to AA. Prostitution: To quote the late, great comedian George Carlin, “Selling is legal, fucking is legal. Why isn't selling fucking legal? Why should it be illegal to sell something that's perfectly legal to give away?” Think of it this way; it is perfectly legal for someone to have sex with every consenting adult they meet, yet illegal to have sex with one person once a dollar changes hands. The same risks apply in both situations; the only difference is financial. This is just more of trying to legislate morality and make people feel bad about enjoying or craving sex, and it needs to end. Ending one's own life: To be clear, I'm not necessarily talking about suicide (though, no one should be arrested for that, but offered counseling), but assisted suicide; human euthanasia. I firmly believe that bodily autonomy is the most fundamental right we have, and it should include death. There is just no reason to force a terminally ill patient to endure excruciating pain until they die naturally. We euthanize animals when they're suffering and have no hope of recovery; in fact it's considered to be the humane option. So, why is it not acceptable for humans to make that decision for themselves?

title: What is interesting to know about Japanese culture?
originally_answered: What are the things to know about the Japanese culture?
post_text:
Whenever we think of Japan, we think of sushi, sumo wrestling, and samurai. But here are some lesser known facts of Japan....  
  While China may be known for its tea consumption, the Japanese are more into coffee.  The literacy rate of Japan is one of the highest in the world, at almost 100%. Many think that Japan’s rigorous education system is the reason behind it. Japan’s unemployment rate is less than 4%.     Speaking of reading and writing, there are four different writing systems found in Japan: romaji (Romanized spelling used to translate Japanese), katakana (foreign words and names, loanwords, and scientific names), hiragana (used with kanji for native Japanese words and grammar), and kanji (adopted Chinese characters).  Japan’s national sport is sumo. Dating back to at least the 8th century, sumo began as a prayer for a fruitful rice harvest, then evolved into a public sport in which two men fight in a circular ring, with one winning when the other was either knocked out of the ring, or any part of his body besides the bottom of his feet touched the ground. Sumo is a living Japanese tradition, containing ancient customs and dress.    Japan is crazy about vending machines, which offers customers a multitude of convenient buys, including beer, Pringles, raw eggs, fried chicken, and even entire Smart Cars.    Sushi started off as a way for fish to be preserved in fermented rice evolved into the culinary delight we know and love today.    Also popular in Japan is horse meat. The most popular way to serve it is raw and sliced thinly, which is called basashi, where it’s dipped in soy sauce and eaten with ginger.      In Western countries like the U.S., slurping your food, such as a soup, or noodles, is seen as annoying, and you’ll get weird looks. But in Japan, if you slurp, it’s seen as complimentary to the chef, so slurp away if you find yourself enjoying soup in Japan.     Japan has produced 18 Nobel Prize winners, coming from the worlds of chemistry, medicine, and physics.     Anime is huge in Japan, and their animated output, both for films and television, accounts for about 60% of the world’s animation. There are also around 130 schools for anime voice acting in the country.     While slurping your soup is seen as a compliment, blowing your nose in public is frowned upon.     Taking your shoes off in Japan is a widely practiced custom, but may confuse foreign visitors. If when you enter a home, and the floor is raised about six inches, that’s an indication that you should take off your shoes and put on slippers. If the house has a floor that is covered with tatami mat, and raised only one to two inches, that indicates that you should take off your slippers. There are also special toilet slippers that must be used when going to the restroom, then removed when finished.     Containing the highest proportion of elderly people in the world, about 23% of Japanese people are over the age of 65. Older people are revered and honored in Japan, even being the first to be served food and drinks at a meal.     There are many subtleties involved in meeting someone for the first time in Japan. One usually waits to be introduced, as it’s seen as impolite to introduce yourself. For foreigners, it’s acceptable to simply shake hands upon meeting, but the traditional form of greeting is a bow, with how far you bow being relative to the respect shown to the recipient.     As you would expect, table manners are many and stringent in Japan. Always wait to be told where to sit, and remember that the guest of honor, or the eldest guest, is usually seated at the center. Chopstick use is important and comes with its own set of rules. Never point with them, never pierce your food with them, and lay them on the chopstick rest when chewing, making sure not to cross them. Eat a little bit of everything, and make sure to not mix rice with other food, like many Westerners do – try some of the food, then the rice.

title: Which country is better for an interesting life, Sweden or Ireland? Are Swedens cold and closed? I don’t like it.
post_text: Both Sweden and the Republic of Ireland are EU countries. The Swedes are not particularly difficult to get on with, but if you live in Sweden you will be expected to speak Swedish. The main drawback with Sweden is extremely low winter temperatures and long winter nights. Summers, on the other hand, are hot and sunny. The main drawback with Ireland is heavy rainfall all the year round - you’ll walk around with a plastic mac on your back most summer days! Winter temperatures are mild, but expect plenty of wind and rain in your face! Although Ireland has its own language - Irish Gaelic - you won’t be expected to speak it at all with English being universally understood. If it is humour you are after, Ireland is the place. Sweden does not have a Blarney Stone, and even if it did the Swedes would not kiss it.

title: How do you connect to your home WiFi from anywhere?
post_text:
Your home WiFi has a limited range, so you cannot connect to it from anywhere. No way. However I think you mean: How can I connect to my home network from anywhere? If this is your real question, there is more than a possible answer, depending on what you want to do. 1. VPN. If your modem/router allows to, you can enable a VPN server. On your remote device, you must configure a VPN client and connect to the VPN server on your modem/router. When you are connected, your device will be on your home LAN, and you can work as if you were at home.
2. Port forwarding / Virtual server. On your modem/router, you can forward one or more (or all) ports to a computer in your LAN. Then, from anywhere, you can connect to your computer through your public IP. For example, if a computer in your LAN is hosting a web server and you forward port 80 of your modem/router to port 80 of that computer, you can access the domain through your public IP, like: http://<your-public-ip>
3. VPN and port forwarding. You can mix the above. For example: If you have a Windows server in your LAN, you can create a VPN server on it, and if you also forward all ports ...

title: I’m in a skinny fat position. I have around 17% body fat and not much muscle. My main goal is to reach 10 to 12% body fat and gain as much muscle as I can before November. What should I do?
post_text: Very simple…. Weight train to prompt your body to build more muscle AND eat clean so you can still burn some of that fat while also building muscle. Many argue that you can not build muscle and lose weight at the same time….but it can be done, often depending on the person. There are people who can’t gain muscle to save their lives and even people who can’t gain weight. Making that much of a change by November probably isn’t practical unless you get militant intense. I’d suggest not more then a 20% calorie deficit, when you cut lower it’ll definitely inhibit muscle gain. Hit the gym 3–4 days per week, lift heavy, keep reps to 6–10 and you’ll need to feel some pain to really prompt the muscle fibers to rebuild larger/stronger. Personally, I don’t enjoy the pain, discomfort and agony that goes with weights….but putting a strain and micro-tears on the fiber is what builds muscle… Eat clean, avoid sugar, maybe some a multi-vitamin, plenty of protein…all that good stuff. Good luck.

title: Where can tourists marry with a tourist visa?
post_text: The visa has nothing to do with if you can get married or not. The documents needed to get married in the country you plan to get married are often not linked with a visa. However you still need to leave the country at the time indicated on your visa/entry stamp and then from home apply for a different visa (not a tourist visa) to be able to go back to your partner you have married. Marriage will not be the door opener to receive the immigration visa you would need.

title: What are the pros and cons of retirement with annuity or mutual funds?
post_text: Pros and cons. Well, the pros of an annuity are typically guaranteed income, or guaranteed return on your principal, or guarantees that you won’t lose any of your principal. The advantages of mutual funds, are that you can earn significant returns overtime. The cons of annuities? You’re locking up your money in some cases. You’re not gonna be getting huge gains. The cons of mutual funds? Risk. If the fund plummets, your money goes away. This is why you may want to consider a mix of both. Use annuities to lock in the minimum guaranteed lifetime income you need to meet all of your basic expenses, and then the money in the stock market – mutual funds - is where you get your discretionary income.

title: What is the best liquid (and powder) foundation for oily skin?
post_text: You’ve asked the right gal. Okay, let me get into this. So, if you want an inexpensive one, I REALLY love the L’oreal Infallible pro matte foundation. That is drugstore gold. It worked very well on my oily skin and I normally find 99% of drugstore makeup doesn’t even hold up well on my oily skin. I’ve tried maybelline for me, revlon color stay, etc etc Plus, the L’Oréal undertones are better than other drugstore brands. I believe it costs around $8–13 depending on the store. Now, another good one for oily skin is the MAC Studio Fix Fluid ($31) or the MAC Studio Fix powder foundation($31) I like both formulas. The liquid foundation; you really only need a tad and it give a more natural matte finish but most oily people set their makeup with powder and once it’s set it’ll be matte but I really like how the formula helps smooth texture on the face like large pores which is common with oily skin. The color range is insane, they have like… 60+ shades so you’d definitely find a match. The powder foundation is also a really good product. I like it for days when I want a more lightweight feel, more natural sort of look but the foundation isn’t like other foundations where it’s super sheer and powdery. It’s a  foundation.  It will cover. It’s about a medium coverage. With oily skin, when we use liquids we can normally feel heavier throughout the day because the silicones are sitting on top of our skin and our oils are producing etc but with the powder version I feel the makeup doesn’t feel as heavy throughout the day and doesn’t look as cakey at the end of the day either. I also like that it has a crap ton of shades especially for a powder foundation because most powder foundations has at most like 20 shades while the MAC one has 40+. I do not recommend using this to touch up shine which is a big mistake. You don’t add more liquid foundation when your face is oily nor should that be the case for powder foundation. I normally use a blotting powder compact throughout the day to touch up shine. They come in different tints to prevent looking ashy but they won’t add coverage or cakiness. Setting powder: I’m a HUGE fan of the Mehron loose mineral finishing powder. ($10-14) I personally use the shade “translucent” and “saffron.” But they have other shades as well which I didn’t buy because I just wanted to try it and ended up really loving it. The shades I do not have are light/medium, medium/medium dark & Sienna. Now, this powder isn’t very buttery smooth which is kind of what I like because I know it’s not full of silica. Silica is used in a lot of powders to make it smooth/buttery and because this powder blurs imperfections but I don’t find silica powders are good at setting oily skin. In fact, I don’t think talc powders are that great either. This powder actually includes “corn starch” which is very oil absorbing as is the Aluminum Starch Octenylsuccinate thats in it, it’s very oily skin-friendly and will definitely properly set your makeup. With product that only use talc I had to bake with them to really set my face but with this powder I only need to press and roll or just use a brush and sweep some on.

title: How profitable are crossfit gyms?
post_text: They can be very profitable pending on how much work you put into beforehand and throughout the process. It's much like any small business at start. You have to find an appealing location that isn't to expensive that will still draw your key demographic. Once that is in place, it's time to buy equipment; lucky for crossfit boxes, overhead is pretty minimal here (depending how carried away you get with your shopping cart at rogue).  The goal is to buy just enough equipment, space, and accessories to maximize capacity and profit (i.e. large space + low memberships = barely "making it" vs. small space + large memberships = overcrowded, time to expand before people leave). This is a tricky balance to achieve, but can be done conservatively to keep risk minimized initially. Once the business is up and running it's time to draw that attention (marketing) to get your capacity up. Expect a pretty high turnover of memberships... nature of the gym beast, which makes marketing a 24/7 job for your gym. Do these things and your gym can have a pretty solid basis for high profitability potential. Cannot stress enough on the plan ahead side. If unsure, start small and sign for a 1-year contract with your location lease. Crossfit equipment is easy to move and expand upon, filling up a large location; however, is not as easy to do initially. Good luck.

post_text: Switzerland  is an expensive country. High Swiss prices  are largely down to a lack of competition, one sided, sometimes exclusive, territorial wholesale agreements on some imports, and import restrictions on products in protected industries, farm products in particular. title: What are the health benefits of Baduanjin?
post_text: It is interesting to see Ba Duan Jin, an ancient hobby for senior, appeals to young people in China. Ba Duan Jin is a traditional Chinese exercise routine with a history of more than 800 years. Dubbed “the exercise for longevity”, it has long been popular with seniors. However, in recent years, it increasingly appeals to younger generations. The Ba Duan Jin, as the name suggests, consists of eight movements. It is an old practice honed over time. In ancient China, Jin, aka brocade, and silk were considered luxurious, and kind to the skin. Therefore, Ba Duan Jin is considered a complex and fine exercise. Its moves follow our body’s alignment. Nowadays, young Chinese consider it a kind of fashionable lifestyle. Many universities offer traditional Chinese health courses that involve Ba Duan Jin. After the outbreak of COVID-19, some sports activities were not viable due to their need for venues, equipment and partners. Traditional exercises can overcome all the above. On the one hand, people can practice it alone. On the other, it requires very little space. It can also help regulate the whole body. For example, when we’re not doing entirely ok, maybe experiencing stress or depression, Ba Duan Jin can improve our mental state. There is no need to practice the entire routine; a few moves will do. It helps you focus and nursed your body through the exercise, gaining a better understanding of yourself.

title: I am unable to find my interest. What should I do?
post_text:
Choosing a career is like choosing a life partner. You never get the perfect one, but you start finding perfections in the complex imperfect realities of each. But gradually! 
This doesn't mean you pick a career that "looks the best". Pick the one having a "job description" closest to your best liking. You can start by talking to people in 3 different fields you are interested in and ask them their daily detailed activities. Then ask yourself, "Which one of these will I be able to do for longest time without saturation?" 
Choose that. Easier said than done, but honestly you still have a lot of time to think. I was in the same boat is you few years back when I wanted to study GRE, GMAT, and UPSC at the same time. Consider a few things: Work-life balance : Are you a family person? Or are you a loner? Do you want a work-life balance, or you're okay with a lot of work, anytime of the week/day? Now see which career offers what you want. Diversity:  PhD, like one of the persons said, requires focus and passion. It can get monotonous if you dont absolutely love what you are doing. There are failures and you may have to repeat one thing many times, and often stick to protocols. It will depend what subject you choose though. If you are not passionate about research, don't get into it. MBA is a good option because it offers diversity. Not just a managerial position, but various avenues like digital makering (social media, online marketing strategies, etc.), marketing, sales, finance, International Relations (you get to travel a lot here), HRD, etc.
So with MBA, you can choose a specific specialisation. It's not just about "marketing, and sales" or "management". For now... Before you do anything,  please add meditation to your daily schedul e.
This keeps you calm and eliminates anxiety. Anxiety will be inevitable if you have diverse interests and less time to choose one to major in. By the way, I'm in your shoe, because I am the same. I like everything from marketing to PhD, to travelling, to coding, to graphic design.  And I try to do as much of these as possible, but... Prioritise... What is tomorrow's submission topic? Or the immediate thing you MUST do? Do that. Then in extra time, read.
You sound passionate and ambitious about many things. Try to read as much about ALL of these things on the web. Talk to people and know more because this leads to finding stuff that you dont know that may lead to you getting more inclined to either choose or eliminate that career.
 
 Don't think only $$$$ I am not going to make saintly statements that "hey, money ain't everything". I am nobody to speak about it. But I'll tell you what, when you put money in the front, it is going to lead to confusion. You are thinking CAT, UPSC, etc. which all pay very well if you get admission in good schools and pass out. You say that your colleagues and friends are getting good jobs, and I am sure you mean in terms of money.  I urge you to look at the bigger picture. Don't compare yourself with them. Instead make a road map of your life and see which career will give long term benefits and make you settle down by may be 28, 29, or 30. Start working towards that instead of just applying for CAT and other things that your friends may be doing. As far as you believe in yourself, work hard and smart, you will eventually find your focus on something. There's a lot of time, lot to explore and learn. P.S: Mini-internships and crash courses in specific fields may work better for you than a job at this stage. Consider it. I wish you well!

title: Why does America dislike China?
post_text: There are two reasons, one political, and the other personal. The political reason is that China is a communist dictatorship that overthrew the previous government and intent on spreading communism over the rest of the world. It supported various regimes and military actions in its part of the world, many of which are crminal by U.S. and Western standards. You *might* try to justify some of these as liberating people from colonial oppression, but the reality is that their organized brutality is even worse. China is the country that backs North Korea and other brutal dictatorships. The collapse of the Soviet Union makes it clear that there are better ways to defeat an enemy than military victory. The USA ground the Soviets into the dust economically, aided by some clever ruses like Reagan’s SDI (“Star Wars”) initiative. China is now working to do the same to the USA, but not always wih adherence to international lawy. China has hacked into US and UK banking systems to take billions of dollars through currency manipulation. Their electonic products have been found to include “backdoors” which give them access to proprietary information. Like Russia, they now cast themselves as a “democracy”. Except it is a democracy where opposition leaders end up in prison or dead, and all information is tightly controlled by the government so that the Chinese people only see and hear what the ruling party wants them to hear. China’s quest for world domination has been thwarted by the United States and their competing Communist “superpower”, Russia. Russia has now been exposed as a corrupt bag of [wind], which means China has a chance to expand Northward. With those additional resources, it makes them even more dangerous. On a personal level, there is another problem. It is a cultural difference that few people think of, but it’s quite real. In China, “family” has always been the primary economic unit, living and working together, with everyone contributing to the same household. “Family” is everything. Older members depend on younger members for their support in old age. The older members so their best to assure that the next generation is successful enough to provide for them all as time progresses. There was even a time when female babies were killed because their earning potential was so much less. China’s “one baby” population control edict made it even more important that the younger members of the household are as productive as possible. Suffice to say that this is not typical of Western/Christian societies like the USA, where the children are expected to get out of the house and earn their own keep. Male children were often kicked out at age 16-18, and Female children were pressured into finding a husband. Older people have retirement plans. The governement proivides “social security” to support seniors. For their part, the children don’ want to live with their parents. It’s important to them to live indepedent lives. Given that dichotomy, a different business ethic has developed. The Chinese will likely say or do anything to benefit his family. What a US citizen considers lying and cheating, a Chinese person might consider merely good business tactics. We are so used to certain examples that we don’t really think about the root cause: Chinese products that look good on the outside, but made of inferior materials on the inside that will needlessly rust or break within a short period of time. On a more personal level, we might be promised something that turns out to be completely untrue. From the Chinese perspective, they are making a legitimate sale. From the US perspective, it is deliberate fraud. Of course, it happens in China, too….Milk for babies that is fortified with a poison to fool the vitamin sensors. But the Chinese are used to it and more likely to accept it as a normal business practice. There is a reason for the American stereotype of the “inscrutable Chinese”. The stereotype is sneaky and deceptive., not to be trusted. That’s why Americans typically don’t like China.

title: How can one effectively handle individuals who believe in conspiracy theories and exhibit delusional behavior?
post_text: These are two very different things. Belief in conspiracy theories is often caused by paying attention to how politics and economics really works. Many conspiracies are not at all delusional, and are actually based completely in a rational understanding of how rich and powerful people attempt to manipulate political and economic systems for their own gain. Of course there are rich and powerful people who conspire to increase their own wealth and power - why wouldn’t they? See, for example, Jeffrey Epstein, Ghislaine Maxwell, Clare Bronfman, Anthony Weiner, Roy Cohn, and Assi Ben Mosh. Not all of them were convicted, but all were part of a child sex trafficking ring that sexually blackmailed rich and powerful people - Maxwell and Bronfman were both convicted on criminal conspiracy charges for sex trafficking minors and criminal blackmail. At least in the case of Maxwell and Bronfman, that’s not a conspiracy theory - it’s a conspiracy fact. In the case of the others who weren’t convicted or who were convicted of lesser crimes, it’s still a conspiracy theory, but one for which there’s a mountain of evidence. You can handle individuals who believe in conspiracy theories by letting them present the facts that support their theory and making a logical judgment of how likely that theory is to be true. Some theories, like the theory that George Bush lied to us about Iraqi WMDs and Saddam’s to Al Qaida, are likely to be true - in this case, the theory is that a politician lied and there’s ample evidence of his lies. Other theories, like the theory that the Earth is flat and covered by a glass dome called the firmament, are not likely to be true - in this case, the theory would require you to rewrite the laws of physics, many of which you can test for yourself. Others, like the theory that the moon landing was faked, are possible but hard to confirm or deny - in this case, the theory is based on the idea that the government lied to us, which it sometimes does, but the government has presented far more evidence for the moon landing than for Saddam having ties to Al Qaida (the CIA had closer ties to Al Qaida), and the evidence suggesting the moon landing was faked is not as strong as the evidence for many other conspiracy theories. As for delusional behavior, I try to avoid people who are so delusional that they automatically assume all conspiracy theories are false. I hope that works for you.

title: Where should I be in puberty? I'm 15?
originally_answered: Where should I be in puberty at 15?
post_text: Wherever you are comfortable with. But it wouldn’t hurt to envisage yourself in 20 years’ time and decide what kind of person you would like to be in this world. Keep that in the back of your mind when you are about to make decisions, or simply do an internal check every week or so. Are you not drifting away too much from who you want to be…? If you are, be honest with yourself and see what actions you should take to ditch unhealthy or careless negativity. Life is quite a gift! Remember that, wherever and whenever they live, human beings don’t differ much in the sense that they love people who are kind, helpful, strong (i.e. not giving up when you are doing something good), passionate (whatever it is, never be ashamed of your passion - be it history, birdwatching, dancing, geology, or collecting poststamps, go for it!), and truthful (not rude!), yet humble. Life is one single test and learning process. No-one is ever ‘done’ learning because life throws problems and disappointments at us all the time (well, a lot of times) - the test is how you respond to the problems you face. Many times, life also gives us moments of bliss and happiness, thank God for those! When older people try to explain something to you that you think you already know; do listen to them with an open mind. You don’t have to agree with them, but chances are they know something you don’t and that’s what they are trying to make you aware of. Ask them questions!! No question is stupid!! If the subject they talk about is boring to you, listen anyway. Ten minutes or so won’t harm you and still those words may some day pop up in your head again when you need them. Thank them for their talk. If you can, develop healthy and authentic friendships now, they may last for decades to come and these individuals will be the ones that give you a sense of belonging in this world when you need it. People mature lots in their teens, twenties, even thirties (etc.!) so if the friends you have now seem unlikely future saviours, try looking at photographs of your mum and dad when they were your age. They may surprise the old you in the future! Just keep building your relationships with them and don’t chuck anyone out for a small nuisance they caused. Talk calmly about what disturbed you in what they said or did but don’t expect they will become just like you want them to be. They should make an effort for you too, though, as you do for them. Walk away when you see drugs, violence or group behaviour you know is bad. Don’t explain yourself just say: l’m going home and leave. Everybody DOES differ in the sense that no-one is going to be saying exactly what you agree on all the time, or behave in a manner you love all the time. Accept this. But don’t let yourself be stifled or abused, ever! (That is different from knowing when to stop talking and respecting others.) Go your own way and try to involve good people by telling them about what drives you and listen to what they have been up to themselves. Oh and please take advantage of the curriculum that is being offered to you at school and later on at university or other educational facility. These are the years you can relatively easily learn a new exotic language or learn any other stuff you like. Relatively easy means you still have to put in loads of effort (many study hours in addition to school) but it will stick in your mind “forever” whereas older generations may study as many hours as you but their brains have often been stretched to the limit (24–7 of work, stress, worries, looking after a family member, etc.) so the new info won’t be stored in their brains as easily; they forget. Just do your homework and get your diplomas! Remember that no feeling lasts forever. This is nice and not so nice. Depressive loneliness will pass but blissful happiness too. Above all, be yourself and be kind to the world.

Originally it was an ideology to advocate for the peaceful transition into socialism as opposed to revolutionary means, but that doesn’t necessarily apply to social democrats and their ideology today. title: Why is summer sausage called summer sausage?
post_text: Wikipedia gives a good answer for this. A lot of salamis are good examples of summer sausage. My guess would be that the name originally was to distinguish it from the harder, drier sausages, which could be left to hang all winter. In my grandparents day, if your budget allowed you to raise a pig that year you waited until the onset of cold weather to slaughter and dress it. Parts of it had to be eaten fresh and parts of it could be cured, some of it would go to sausage which would be cured with the hams, shoulders , and bacon in an improvised smokehouse. Most people shared the perishable parts with their neighbors, which would generally be remembered and repaid. As much as possible, lard would be rendered from the fat, the good part for cooking, the less good for soapmaking.

title: What is the role of the military in the development and operation of the GPS system, and how has this changed over time?
post_text: The first global navigational satellite System (GNSS) was the US GPS, started in the 80’s I think. It was the project of the US department of defense which was looking for a secure way for soldiers, ships, planes etc to determine their location accurately anywhere in the world. It required a constellation of expensive satellites costing billions - only a government project could afford such an expense at the time. The initial system had features that allowed encoded military use for those with special military receivers; the unencoded signal capability could be switched off and or made less accurate in event of war to deny the enemy targeting capability for example. However the details of the unencoded signals were made readily available and commercial users found to to be a great assistance as well as civilians personal uses. Ultimately the US government told the Dept of Defense to eliminate the encoded system and make the civilian codes full accuracy so that it could never be denied. Today the Department of Defense still maintains the system but has upgraded all the satellites with multiple generations with improvements and it has become a critical part of both military and civilian national infrastructure. Meanwhile, China, Russia and the EU and partially India have all put up similarly functioning global or regional systems as a matter of national prestige, or national security

title: Is there any difference in quality between Lodge cast iron cookware and generic cast iron?
post_text: Yes, there is a quality difference between Lodge cast iron cookware and generic cast iron cookware. I would like to expand this answer to include all high-quality brand names of cast iron cookware. 1: Weight. The magic of cast iron is heating a massive amount of metal to the desired temperature in order to get the desired cooking results. Heat a high quality cast iron pan to 550F and sear a steak on it. No big deal, just another evening in the kitchen for cast iron. Do the same thing with a light weight cast iron pan and there is a high probability that you will now be the proud owner of a warped pan that did not heat evenly, or cool down evenly. 2: Metal Content. A high quality cast iron pan will be made of one thing and one thing only: Cast iron. This cast iron will be traceable to testing labs and methods proving the cast iron is not full of nasty, toxic metals. A lot of cast iron pans are made from recycled metal. You have to heat that metal enough for the impurities to flow off leaving the iron you really want. Generic, lightweight pans will sometimes not heat the metal enough to get rid of all the impurities. All that extra heating and melting costs money. 3: Seasoning. A high quality cast iron pan will be seasoned at the factory with a pure, natural oil like soybean or similar. There will be no additives or chemical enhancers. I give my cast iron pans a wipe down with a little Crisco after each cleaning. Keeps out the rust. 4: Lifetime: Buy a high-quality cast iron pan like Lodge. You will pay a few bucks and be blessed with a pan that will still be cooking great meals when it gets handed down to your great, great, great grandchildren. BTW: There are horridly expensive cast iron pans out there that are little better in quality than a generic pan. Weight is the best way to judge quality at the store. Lodge cast iron pans do not have a warranty. Just a promise that if something is wrong, they will work with you to fix it.

title: Why do Russians celebrate Victory over Hitler on May 9th, while the Ukrainian regime holds the Day of Sorrow for Hitler's defeat on May 8th?
post_text: If the focus of the question is the difference in dates, then  Alexander Petrov's answer  explains that it was the difference in time zones between Berlin (where the declaration was signed and announced) and Moscow; in Berlin it was before midnight while in Moscow it was already the next day, after midnight. If, however, the focus of the question is why Russia celebrates “Victory” and Ukraine celebrates “Sorrow” it has to do with their perceptions of Ukraine. For Russians, the Ukraine is an appendage which they can use and abuse as they see fit. The Ukrainians are supposed to shut up and grow food to supply the rest of the  Rodina  — the homeland — the Russian Empire, and be grateful that they are allowed to be a small part of Moscow’s glory. For Ukrainians, Hitler offered a brief respite from Stalin’s overbearing domination. Despite the harshness of the  Wehrmacht , the Ukrainians prefererred German military rule over that of the Red Army. While the Germans plundered, they were relatively decent about it, and mostly didn’t massacre civilians (except Jews and Romi! whom the cursed Nazis were dedicated to slaughtering, and did) unless there were attacks or reprisals. The Red Army by contrast, even while “liberating” Ukraine from the Nazis, raped, pillaged, and slaughtered humans and animals alike, and actually made the Mongol Horde look gentle by comparison. (The Soviets did the same thing to Poland.) Buildings which the  Wehrmacht  had left standing were destroyed by the Soviets for no military object, seemingly just to prove that they had been there. Thus it was with sorrow that the Ukrainians saw the Germans booted out of their land, because the “defeat” of the Germans was accompanied by an even greater defeat of the Ukrainians themselves, and even worse they were once again relegated to the mad rule of Joseph Vissarionovich.

title: What are your tips to make ambrosia salad?
originally_answered: How do you make ambrosia fruit salad?
post_text: FREQUENTLY ASKED QUESTIONS: Do you taste the sour cream in ambrosia salad? The answer is no. You really don't. It does cut the overall sweetness so you don't break a tooth - ha. But you don't taste it as a separate ingredient. Do I have to use coconut? No. You can leave the shredded coconut out if you absolutely can't stand coconut but it is a traditional ingredient in ambrosia. Can I use sugar free options? There are natural sugars in the fruits themselves. However, if you want to cut the sugar then try to find the canned fruit that is packed in sugar-free juice. You can also buy sugar free whipped topping. What are some other fruit options? There really is no wrong answer here. You can pretty much add most of your favorite fruits. Raspberries, sliced bananas, blackberries, blueberries, strawberries, pomegranate seeds all work here. How do I store leftovers? Ambrosia is always best the day it's made or the day after. After that it starts to break down and lose its consistency as the fruits release their juices. Store covered and in the refrigerator. Eat within a day. Ingredients 1 (8 oz) tub of whipped topping thawed (In most recipes, you can use whipped cream as a substitute for whipped topping. There will be some changes in texture and stability, which could result in minor changes in the end product. It’s not a 1-to-1 substitution, either: If your recipe calls for an 8-ounce carton of whipped topping, you’ll want to whip 1-1/2 cups of heavy whipping cream to create 3 cups of whipped cream.) 1 cup sour cream 1 (20 oz) can pineapple tidbits, drained well 1 (15 oz) can mandarin orange segments, drained well 1 cup red or green seedless grapes, sliced in half 1 ½ cups sweetened coconut flakes 1 ½ cups mini marshmallows 1 10 oz jar of maraschino cherry halves, drained very well ½ cup chopped pecans Instructions In a medium bowl, combine whipped topping and sour cream. Add in coconut flakes and marshmallows. Then gently fold in pineapple, mandarin oranges, grapes and maraschino cherries and nuts (if using). Once combined, put some plastic wrap on it or put it in a bowl with a lid and refrigerate for about an hour before serving

title: What are some unique things of Mexico City?
post_text: I always recommend this (no doubt because I am very much a film person). Cineteca Nacional, a complex in Mexico City of 10 movie theaters of varying sizes—the three largest have balconies as well as their own concession stands and bathrooms, and the smallest theater having only about 30 seats—showing international films that often don’t get screened in mainstream theaters. It is the largest film complex of its kind in Latin America. The complex also contains numerous places to eat and drink, cafes, (no chains allowed. You definitely won’t see Starbucks or McDonald’s) a bookstore, shops focusing on film memorabilia, a museum with rotating displays (recent ones have been on Hitchcock, Disney and Mexico, Stanley Kubrick). Films not in Spanish are screened with Spanish subtitles (obviously) but non-Spanish speakers will always find numerous films in English on any given day. You could spend an entire day there, going from one film to another and having something to eat in-between screenings. A unique experience that too many tourists miss.

title: How has your attitude toward money changed during your life?
post_text: While in college, I had several jobs. I spent every dime I made, usually before the end of the week. I lived at home so I’d make a sad face every time I needed a bail-out and my mom would begrudgingly pay for other expenses I incurred—including tuition, books, gas, etc. (Tuition wasn’t as high then so I could’ve managed to pay for it myself if I didn’t spend my money on frivolous things.) At the time, I was making quite a bit of money. I taught swimming and music classes, and worked at a bakery. It sounds like a lot, but it was less than 25 hours a week. One day, I decided I wanted to buy my own grand piano. A new tariff was coming so I needed to save as much as I could quickly. Within 5 months, I saved enough to buy my piano in cash. During that 5 months, I saw this money build in my savings account and found it physically hurt to withdraw the money to buy what I wanted. After that, my whole concept of money changed. I realized instant gratification wasn’t necessarily a good thing. Long-term planning became my goal. From that time on, saving, paying off debt—and staying out of debt, was my new mantra. When my husband and I got married, we both set financial goals with the same objectives in mind. Now that we’re retired, our main concern is staying healthy, being active, and enjoying every day to the fullest. Yes, we still worry about money, but we know that we are in control in most situations because we planned ahead.

post_text:
Amazon can predict what you wish to buy even before you buy it! And ships it to you even before you place the order. It is called anticipatory shipping. 
As the name suggests they ship the product to your nearest amazon store even before the ordered is placed.  Amazon even has patent for it, and it is called "method and system for anticipatory package shipping". Source: predictiveanalyticsworld As per the patent, forecasting model uses the historical data of the customer. For instance, If I am a regular amazon customer who buys a fixed list of house hold stuff in the beginning of every month then the smart algorithms collate information of similar users and ships the products even before the order is placed. The sophisticated algorithm also considers instances like:  User spending a lot of time on a product User has added some product in the cart but didn't buy it or any such other factors that are historically mapped to sales

Of course, there is a risk of user not buying a predicted item, but then I think discounts and other marketing tactics covers this part.  
This is merely one of the many smart things amazon does using analytics.

post_text:
Horn  NOT  ok , Please !! Honking unnecessarily, the deeply ingrained practice so ubiquitous that mostly conspicuous only in silence. 
 
 To horn is Ok when the driver ahead, having the entire road for himself, forgets his duty to keep driving or at least barge aside of others’ dutiful rally. Serves the purpose of inventing a horn. But any desired productive aim of orchesting a horn opera in long traffic jams is still a mystery. May be the horn-blowers frustrated by the heavy traffic and forced inability to get moving take recourse to the perceived stress buster. Yet the incessant use of this psychological instinct driven involuntary action undermines the insensitivity towards those forced audience for whom it might not be all that musical. May be was a necessity in past with narrow lanes but on modern multi-lane highways using lights and indicators as a social alternative during overtake is a practice yet to be inculcated on mass scale for the common welfare of we the people. Pakistan and India (also Bangladesh, SriLanka, Nepal and Bhutan) are part of the Indian sub-continent. There is a reason why it is called a sub-continent.

Because of the proximity of these countries and similar weather conditions, the landscape in Pakistan can be pretty much the same as that found in Northern India.

Even though I have dinner quite early for us (8pm), most Argentines, or at least people from Buenos Aires, have dinner later than that and have a hard time finding open restaurants in other places. That happened to me when I went to Europe, our, also Argentine, guide warned us that everything closed at 9pm in a München and we thought he was exaggerating, but he wasn't. In Prague everything closed around 5pm, I mean every kind of museum or tourist attraction, which really surprised me. I couldn't believe either when I went to “the city that never sleeps” (New York) to have dinner at 12am after a long day, and found nearly everything closed near Times Square, we ended up going to a Friday's that seemed to be our only option in the area. Another thing I miss is  being able to pet dogs without asking their owners if I can , when it's considered rude in the country I'm at, or considered to pet other people's dogs in general. Here most people either go for it or ask “Does it bite?” and then go for it. So many people have dogs here too, that I miss seeing that many when I'm abroad.

title: What's a reason that China supports Pakistan more than other countries having a good relationship with China?
post_text: TLDR: Maoism, surprisingly enough. The “Enemy’s enemy is my friend” theory that places ‘common opposition to India’ as the basis for Pakistan-China friendship holds almost little to no water among serious foreign policy circles. I mean, politics among world powers is messy enough as it is without following any clear algorithmic rules to determine their interactions. The US remains committed to the KSA despite 9/11 hijackers origins and opposed to Iran despite the fact that Iran makes a more logical ally to the US and more supportive of its anti-terror efforts during the early stages of the War on Terror. Or consider the US-Russian relationship: stretched thin to the point of contention between Imperialist expansionist expanding NATO to Russian borders and White Nationalists embracing Russian machismo in response to increasingly vocal minorities, economic displacement and cultural shifts. India and China have long been cooperative powers on the Global arena, at least up until the recent Trump-China tensions, and used their collective bargaining powers as Asian giants to advocate the cause of the developing world vs the developed world on the international platform. Usama Ahmad's answer to Have China and India ever been friends during any point in history? When Pakistan was first formed, our initial embrace of the US firmly placed us within the SEATO-CENTO alliance structure designed to combat and contain Communist expansions across Asia. Hence, Pakistan was on the side of the US led UN mission in Korea against the North Korean and Chinese militaries and provided logistical support in the form of sandbags and other infantry equipment to the US side during the Korean war and one can still travel to Korea to war memorials where the flag of Pakistan can be found along side others like Turkey and so on as some of the parties that fought alongside the US lead UN mission to combat the North Koreans. Granted, our role was extremely limited and mostly restricted to providing make shift fortifications for infantry defenses. And Pakistan sent no combat troops or equipment to fight the Chinese besides sandbags. Not exactly a country seeking China as a counterbalance to India, right? Pakistani leadership, particularly its military remained cool to the idea of warm ties with Communist China despite the looming threat of war with India. The US, was always relied upon as the foreign power that would tilt the diplomatic and military balance in our favor during any military adventurism against India (or to ward off a catastrophic defeat at the hands of Indian forces in West Pakistan). So when the first border disputed between China and her southern neighbors flared up culminating into the 62 war between India and China, Pakistani leadership under President Ayub didnt take this as some sort of automatic opportunity to open diplomacy with China to forge a united front against India. In fact, Ayub remained bitterly opposed to ceding any disputed territory or peaks to China. The wild card here was Bhutto and his infatuation with socialism in general and Maoism in particular. Bhutto, Pakistan’s foreign minister at the time of the early 60s, was the one who prevailed upon Ayub to cede the peaks in northern Pakistan to China and prevailed upon him to pursue warmed ties with our neighbor to the north. It was only under his pressure that Ayub conceded and allowed the territorial adjustment to take place which would form the foundation of Pak-China ties. And only under Bhutto’s tenure did military, economic and strategic assistance pacts get signed between Pakistan and China that deepened the relationship. The Pakistani military was firmly anti-communist at the time and were very clear in their desire to ally with the US lead capitalist block. If anyone was looking for a major power to help them balance the scales against India, it was the military. They, however, never looked to Communist China though. But Pakistani politics was complex enough back then to permit Bhutto’s infatuations with Mao to rule the day since he was careful to veil his Maoist entryism with populist slogans, nationalist zeal and even Islamic rallying cries. He called upon all Pakistanis to espouse every Afro-Asian cause and struggle, insisting in language he had picked up from J. A. Rahim and Mubashir that “we are the proletariat of the world....therefore, we have to cooperate, collaborate, get together, assist one another ... and finally the right cause and justice must prevail. . . . Our people deserve it. For centuries they have lived in misery, squalor, filth and poverty.” Zulfi was aware by now that Ayub and his closest colleagues considered him most “dangerous,” a “Maoist” as well as a “madman.” “Must we be labeled as communists and various other things merely because we fight against domination, because we rise against exploitation?” he asked the cheering students. “Must we be blackmailed and must we be slandered in this fashion merely because we say it is not the law of God that people should not have a better life . . . just because we want to defend our sovereignty and integrity and our national independence and give our people a more egalitarian future?” - Zulfi Bhutto of Pakistan, Stanley Wolpert Beijing, in turn, was quick to reciprocate the love stemming from Bhutto, the curious feudal lord turned Mao enthusiast. It was during this era that Pakistan developed its own Maoist movement which famously splintered from its Leninist Left Wing allies after the Sino-Soviet split and these Maoists would side with the Pakistani military during the 71 war as opposed to their Leninist former allies who were more sympathetic to the Bengali resistance. Curiously enough, these Pakistani Maoists never really sided with Bhutto once they rose up against the feudal lords in the after math of the 71 war, engaging in gun battles with police forces and feudal lord thugs during their attempts to over throw the land owning gentry. Bhutto was quick to secure his land lord supporter’s interests as they were the primary backers of his PPP political party and thus cracked down heavily on the Maoist movement of Pakistan, either defeating them in gun battles or channeling their energies towards religious madrasahs that would turn them into some of the first Jihadists crossing over into Afghanistan once the Afghan Jihad began. Once Bhutto ascended to the Prime Ministership after the 71 war, he was quick to begin formally materializing his Maoist tendencies into a diplomatic relationship between Pakistan and China. Bhutto began wearing Mao style pantsuits and introduced a land and agriculture tax against his own feudal lord constituents that were decried as the “great betrayal” by Mustafa Khar, one of his old feudal lord supporters. Zulfi dressed like Mao on the campaign trail, wearing a plain green jacket and a Mao cap, which gave him instant identity both with China and a “people’s” revolution. It was the closest he came in trying to compete with the Awami and National Awami Party leadership of Bengal. At times he was more specific in identifying his party and people’s movement with Mao, though he was always careful to deny any imputations by his opponents that he was a communist. “We need a long march,” Zulfi told his cheering audience at Abbottabad. “When I say that we would undertake a long march I am dubbed as a communist. I say that the first long march in history was undertaken by Imam Hussain.” - Zulfi Bhutto of Pakistan, Stanley Wolpert Bhutto also drew inspiration from Mao’s advice to begin the creation of a People’s Army styled along the lines of the PLA that would compose of 1.5 million troops and would be trained in the PLA style of tactics that had been tested during the Korean war. The army would be a village based army similar to the PLA during the Korean war and a far cry from the professional, western trained Colonial army left behind by the British. He even began making grandiose plans of his own Long March similar to Mao’s long march in the Chinese Civil War and had dreams of a Long March invasion into India that would cut the Delhi-Mumbai link and split the country’s political center from it’s financial center. A plan that was quickly dropped once his military advisers illuminated him of the fact that even 20–30 km pushes into India would stretch supply lines, let alone a dash to the Mumbai-Delhi link. Bhutto’s memorandum went on to detail the possible military strategy and tactics that might come into play in his envisioned people’s war against India: a northern “Panipat offensive” against Delhi, or a southern “Somnath offensive,” thrust, cutting off Kathiawar and Bombay. The village-based people’s army would be a “massive wave of raiders” that would always be ready to carry out V. P. Menon’s warning to his Indian government in 1947: “The raiders are a grave threat to the integrity of India. Ever since the time of Mahmud of Ghazni . . . Srinagar today, Delhi tomorrow! A nation that forgets its history and its geography does so at its peril.” Whatever Tikka Khan’s reply to Bhutto’s memo may have been, Pakistan was never to be “prepared” for the people’s war Zulfi Bhutto visualized against India—at least not in the remaining seven years of his lifetime, nor during the decade and a half that followed his death. - Zulfi Bhutto of Pakistan, Stanley Wolpert Nevertheless, it was clear that Bhutto’s intentions to begin molding the Pakistani state institutions into a distant mirror image of the Maoist institutions of China was being pursued with earnest intent. The Pakistan Ordinance Factory and Aircraft overhaul facilities were set up with Chinese assistance to make Pakistan self sufficient in military gear rather than dependent on US supplies. A key tenet of the PLA has always been that the PLA must be self sufficient in it’s military armament and ammunition which was why China was always technologically somewhat challenged during the 60s-80s period albeit fairly self sufficient in terms of arms production. A total of 8 military factories and 5 civilian factories were gifted by China to Pakistan during his tenure to promote his idea of a Mao style industrialization and self sufficiency. Bhutto, clearly admired this model and thus Chinese armament imports into Pakistan were made with the intention of also indigenously maintaining these arms as well. Had Bhutto gone through with this, its quite possible that Pakistan, like Iran, would consist of two military wings: a Peoples Army and the older, British-US trained Army. (I referenced Iran because they have a Revolutionary Guard and formal Shah era military too). While Bhutto never managed to create his Peoples Liberation Army similar to the PLA in China, perhaps due to his early ouster or perhaps due to nervousness from the Pakistan military about a parallel ‘peasant army’ that outnumbered them, he did manage to have his own mini-Cultural revolution as well when he purged the civil services of their traditional bureaucratic manpower and opened them up to the lower-middle classes. A move that has long been criticized by some as the seeds of destruction for the Pakistani civil service in terms of quality and by others as a major egalitarian move that reduced elitism in the country. Zulfi withdrew Pakistan from Britain’s Commonwealth of Nations and U.S.- dominated SEATO. Then he flew to China in early February, where he drank many toasts to the health of Chairman Mao Tse-tung and Chou En-lai, to “the further development of friendship and co-operation between Pakistan and China,” and “to “Afro-Asian solidarity.”35 By that time Bhutto had either imprisoned or retired many of Pakistan’s bureaucratic “Brahmins,” members of the vaunted Civil Service of Pakistan (CSP), the highest echelons of the administrative framework that had held Pakistan together from its inception, managing most of the ministries and departments of state. “People say that 2,000 Government servants have been retired,” Zulfi told his by-now-cheering audience in Lahore. “But they were sucking the people’s blood. They were parasites. There was a clamour for a purge. But when it took place, there have been complaints. We are in the midst of a revolution. . . . We must root out corruption. . . . Poor people will get justice. . . . Mao Tse-Tung said that sometimes the wind comes from the West, sometimes from the East. In Pakistan the wind blows from all sides.” - Zulfi Bhutto of Pakistan, Stanley Wolpert On the foreign policy front, Bhutto saw India as a socialist partner (once the Kashmir dispute was resolved), in contrary spirit to the nationalist military that saw it as their existential enemy in the brutal aftermath of the 71 conflict. And he made multiple calls for his African-Asian proletariat brotherhood that included Pakistan, China and India in a pan-socialist project. And Bhutto also clearly sided with China against the USSR which he saw as an expansionist power with eyes on Balochistan. During the Sino-Soviet split aftermath at least, he clearly threw Pakistan behind China. A decision whose benefits we would reap decades later once the USSR collapsed and China emerged as the rising power. How much of Bhutto’s beliefs were actual Maoist doctrine, and how much were wreathed in the flames of populism is fairly unclear. But Bhutto’s admiration of Mao and his inspiration from Maoism was incredibly clear to the people of that time and heavily documented. And it’s unclear whether Pakistan would enjoy its current deep relationship with China in the absence of Bhutto’s long architecting of the relationships foundations: From his prevailing upon Ayub Khan to cede disputed peaks to China in the early 60s to this long relationship building with China throughout the 70s. The Pakistani military had always been cool towards the idea of stronger ties with their large socialist neighbor, laying their eggs clearly in the US basket for strategic cover and allianceship. Had it not been for Bhutto, Pakistan’s earlier disputes with China would have persisted and might even had led to serious tensions, the likes of which provoked the 62 war between China and India. Its quite possible the military may have offered up Pakistan as a strategic second front against China as well to the US. All of this was avoided because of Bhutto’s long admiration for Mao and Maoism and his machinations, first as Foreign Minister and later as Prime Minister, to bring Pakistan closer to China. After Bhutto’s hanging by Zia, the military inherited the Chinese close ties the same way they inherited Bhutto’s nuclear program. And by then the foundation of the relationship had been set strong and deep enough for the US and British trained military to be immersed in pro-Chinese sentiments. Quite a quirky oddity if considered closely: the idea of Sandhurst trained Military Officers holding fond views of Communist China. An idea unthinkable back then in a world where the often Colonial trained and organized militaries of the third world were often used to launch coups by the CIA and Western bloc against democratically elected leaders suspected of socialist sympathies. The military still did the coup part. But were at the same time filled with officers and rank and file that used and trained and worked with Communist Chinese military and political systems. Even as they transitioned from a US trained, somewhat secular military into a more religiously inclined, Islamic ideology based military. With China’s rise into the world stage, Pakistan’s ties with China have underwent a somewhat significant evolution: somewhere in the 87–89 period, Chinese foreign policy became that of a rising world power rather than an ideological state. And Pakistan began to be seen as a strong diplomatic partner with a good history rather than the ‘iron brother’ ideologically sympathetic state of the Mao-Bhutto era. The relationship is still friendly, just more formal as China takes on the responsibilities at a world stage as a Global partner rather than just a regional one with regional stakes alone that is centered around Pakistan. The relationship between both countries is based on too strong a foundation thanks to the Bhutto-Mao era. And it would take a lot to unravel it. But it was a foundation laid very carefully over a long time and not just an accidental product of circumstance or the fact that a common rival existed. It was carefully cultivated and manually established by a Maoist sympathizing Foreign Minister turned PM. Before China, there was Iran which Pakistan sought to court as a strategic, regional counterweight to India. And the Iranians, under the Shah were a true military power to rely on. Only problem was: Pakistan had no Shah admirers or big fans of Iran in positions of power at the key moments needed to make such an alliance happen. And there was no concerted effort to develop such ties by important individuals in Pakistan the way an attempt was made with China. When the Shah proposed a common federation between Iran, Afghanistan and Pakistan with Iran as the leader, Ayub and his cronies were open to the idea of being led by the Iranians as a common nation. But the process never went through because either no one worked on it in a consistent manner or because the 65 war rattled the Shah about how unpredictable the Pakistanis were as partners and he withdrew the offer himself. Showing how you can have two countries in a natural path towards a closer relationship only for it to be scuttled because of blunders by one side. By every definition in the book, Iran should have been our China. It was culturally, linguistically, geographically, politically and militarily far more aligned with Pakistan and they were in the same global camp as well. Ayub even sent advisers to Iran to learn how their constitution could be imported into Pakistan. But politics is messy. And chance rises where least expected. The fact that we ended up with China instead of Iran as our closest regional partner is perhaps the strangest yet most wonderfully curious chapters of our history. And a testament to how complex and strange foreign policy is and how individuals in power can decide how millions of people think about millions of other people and who loves who and who hates who. People can like each other fine. Indians and Pakistanis abroad get alone quite well. But foreign relations between nation states are stories that emerge from the actions, words and thoughts of national leaders and the immense government machinery they lead. And Pakistani-China relationship is such a product. And those relationships at the top are what ripple their way to the bottom. And thus, today, Pakistanis view China more positively than many of their more similar cultural and social neighbors. The common rivalry with India is not a strong basis for Pakistan and China’s friendship. India could vanish into thin air tomorrow and the basis for Pakistan and China’s current strong foundation would remain in place due to its careful cultivation over 2 decades by Bhutto. If the common rivalry with India was a keystone of the relationship, it would have meant that Pakistan and China quickly established friendly relations as soon as Pakistan went through a first round of hostilities with India. But this didn’t happen. The military and anti-communist lobby of Pakistan was too strong and actually sided with the US against China in the initial few years of our existence. Only upon the rise of Bhutto through the ranks and up into the position of Foreign Minister and later PM did a thaw occur. And he had to fight anti-communist elements within the Pakistan army(who were cool to the idea of any warm ties with Red China) to convince them to cede key peaks to China in the Kashmir region thus avoiding any border tensions with China and allowing him to smooth the relationship between his own country and country of the man he drew inspiration from: Mao. On 9 September 1976, when news of Mao’s death reached him, Zulfi knew he had lost his strongest supporter in the Third World. “Men like Mao Tse-tung come once in a century,” Bhutto emoted, “perhaps once in a millennium. They capture the stage and write the pages of history with divine inspiration. ... Chairman Mao . . . was a giant among giants. . . . [T]he son of revolution, its very essence, indeed, its rhythm and romance, the supreme architect of a brilliant new order shaking the world.” It was a eulogy the likes of which he hoped would be written about him. “He remains immortal, his thoughts will continue to guide the destinies of people and nations until the sun sets forever.” - Zulfi Bhutto of Pakistan, Stanley Wolpert

title: My Colombian friend told me that Colombia is a poor country. It is not good to live there. Is that really the case? Can someone tell me about the benefits and disadvantages of living in Colombia?
post_text: Colombia is a country with a complex socio-economic landscape, and opinions about living there can vary widely depending on individual experiences and perspectives. Here’s a balanced overview of the benefits and disadvantages of living in Colombia: Benefits of Living in Colombia Natural Beauty : Colombia is known for its stunning landscapes, including mountains, beaches, and rainforests. Places like the Amazon, Andes, and Caribbean coast offer diverse outdoor activities. Cultural Richness : The country has a vibrant culture, with a rich history, music (like salsa and cumbia), festivals, and art. Cities like Bogotá, Medellín, and Cartagena are cultural hubs. Cost of Living : Generally, the cost of living in Colombia is lower than in many Western countries. Housing, food, and transportation can be quite affordable, allowing for a comfortable lifestyle. Warm Climate : Colombia enjoys a tropical climate, with warm temperatures year-round, especially in coastal and lowland areas. Friendly People : Colombians are often described as warm and welcoming, making it easier for newcomers to feel at home. Improving Infrastructure : Major cities have seen improvements in infrastructure, public transportation (like the Medellín Metro), and healthcare services in recent years. Disadvantages of Living in Colombia Security Concerns : While security has improved, crime rates can still be high in certain areas, particularly related to theft, drug trafficking, and gang violence. It's important to stay informed and choose safe neighborhoods. Economic Disparities : Colombia has significant economic inequality, with stark contrasts between wealthy and impoverished areas. This can affect access to resources and opportunities. Political Instability : Colombia has faced political issues and conflict, including the legacy of civil war and ongoing challenges with drug cartels. This can lead to uncertainty in certain regions. Bureaucracy : Navigating the legal and bureaucratic systems can be challenging, especially for foreigners dealing with visas, permits, or business regulations. Healthcare Access : While urban areas generally have good healthcare, rural areas may lack access to quality medical services. The healthcare system can be complicated to navigate. Language Barrier : Spanish is the primary language, so not speaking it can pose challenges in daily life and work, although English is spoken in some tourist areas. Conclusion Living in Colombia can be a rewarding experience, offering a unique blend of culture, natural beauty, and affordability. title: What is your routine to get stuff done?
post_text: I’ve spent the last 10+ years honing and tweaking my system to enhance my ability to get things done. What I’ve learned? The secret to being productive isn’t finding the right methodology or the best tools, it’s embedding the habits that support you in consistently doing the work you need to do to achieve your goals. For me, this looks like: Theme your days This one comes straight out of Jack Dorsey’s playbook. The Twitter and Square CEO has themes he uses to guide his days and make it easier to stay on track with what’s happening at both companies. I’m not pretending to be as busy as Jack, but I do manage several different products across a number of businesses and I’ve found it really helpful to theme my days. At the moment, my week looks like: Monday: Business Strategy Tuesday: Product Development Wednesday: Customers & Partnerships Thursday: Market & Competitors Friday: Reflection and Planning Saturday: Family & Friends Sunday: Personal Growth By batching my tasks and objectives across the week according to these themes I’ve found myself achieving much more. Capture everything If there’s one thing to take from David Allen’s Getting Things Done it’s this. One of the most powerful productivity habits is capturing absolutely everything in a trusted system so you can get it off your mind. It’s easier said than done, though. As someone who’s been practicing GTD for over a decade, I still find myself thinking “I’ll write that down later” and forgetting something that could have been hugely important to one of my projects. If you want to get things done, make ubiquitous capture your cornerstone habit. Without it, everything else will come crashing down. Separate the actionable and non-actionable Not everything you capture is actionable. You need to make the distinction between stuff you need to do something with and stuff that you want to keep for reference. A lot of GTD/productivity implementations have both within the same system but I’ve found this muddies the waters too much. Your todo list and your notes app aren’t the same thing. Choose a tool for each and keep them separate. Bucket your to-dos by time and energy GTD’s original idea of applying location and device-specific contexts feels almost obsolete in our perma-connected world. Most of the time I have everything I need for any task at my fingertips. What I don’t always have, though, is the time or mental energy to do them. Instead of categorising your next actions by “@computer” or “@anywhere” start bucketing them according to the amount of time and energy you’ll need to get them done. I apply the following tags to everything on my todo list: Agendas: stuff I need to pick up with different people Braindead: when I’m feeling burnt-out and need something easy to work on Calls: any phone calls I need to make Dashes: tasks that will take less than 30 minutes Downtime: tasks I can knock off my list when I’m waiting around; at the doctors, in a queue, on the bus etc Errands: any errands I need to run Focus: the “big ticket tasks” which need my undivided attention for a couple of hours or so Home: everything I need to do at home Office: everything I need to do in the office Planning: any pre-planning I need to do (for meetings, outlining projects and the like) Thinking: stuff I just need to do some thinking about before I commit to action Timebox your calendar According to classic GTD your calendar is sacred ground that should only contain tasks and activities that need to happen on a specific day or at a specific time. That doesn’t necessarily work, though, if the next action you could take is almost always going to be “absolutely anything off my todo list.” Just like theming your days helps add structure to your tasks and priorities, timeboxing your calendar into buckets like “focus time”, “tactical work” and “reading & research” make it easier to choose exactly what you should be doing next. Set SMART goals There’s no point in putting effort into getting things done if you don’t know what you’re doing them for. Make sure you’re getting off the runway and paying attention to your wider horizons. Set SMART goals for your 1–3 and 3–5 year objectives and make sure you’ve got projects and tasks in place to help you deliver them. If you’re not working towards some clearly defined outcomes, then all you’re really doing is building a clever system for busywork. Review your system regularly David Allen says if you’re not doing your weekly review then you’re not doing GTD. Make it a habit to review your system on a regular basis and don’t be afraid to make changes if something isn’t working. Use other people’s productivity systems as guides and carve out your own path for getting things done.
