title: How is Jiujitsu better than Tai Chi?
post_text: In my opinion, Tai Chi is best learned for changing your body. There are changes that can take place where the soft tissue becomes more elastic. There are certain capabilities that come with that, but you still have to translate that into an advantage. Jujitsu can offer a lot, in terms of positioning, strategy, and techniques. When combined with the changes to the body — in such a way where those techniques and strategies take advantage of those body changes— it sounds practical to me, if you are willing to invest your training time into it. The kind of changes to the body that Tai Chi makes are not unique to Tai Chi. Many other Chinese arts generate some or even all of those benefits. Tai Chi’s techniques rely on those changes … so if your body has not sufficiently changed, those techniques are not going to be as useful. To look at it a different way, Bajiquan forked from Chen Taijiquan a while back and went its own way. It has a lot of short ranged techniques like Taijiquan, and retains those body-changing training methods. But many Bajiquan practitioners also train in Pigua, and they are often taught together. This is because Pigua focuses on techniques at the mid-range, and has evolved with Bajiquan to complement each other. No single strategy or fighting method will work under all circumstances against all people, all the time. While the mindset and principles can be applied broadly, perhaps even in a different context, you will also run into limitations that may be better approached with something else. Lastly, if you wanted to stay in the Chinese “family” of arts that can complement Tai Chi, check out chin na (which is really a broad classification of techniques around joint and structure manipulation) and shuai jiao (essentially, wrestling).

title: How much money do I need in my savings account to retire at 50 and live off of the interest for the rest of my life?
post_text: It depends on your lifestyle. Some people can enjoy retirement by taking full advantage of activities that don’t cost money like spending time in the library while spending very little, living in an old, small home that is paid off, no car, enjoys cheap grocery staples like dried beans and oatmeal with no fancy restaurant meals, etc. Others may enjoy splurging on nice cars and exotic vacations. Your annual retirement income requirement might range anywhere from $2,000 on the low end to $100,000 on the high end. Look at how much you are spending annually right now and budget how much you need to spend in retirement to get an estimate on how much you need to retire. Convert that amount to a future value at age 50, allowing 3–4% inflation. For example, if you need $50,000 a year in today’s dollars in retirement, and you are 35 years old right now, you need $50,000*(1.04)^15 = $90,047 annually when you are 50, allowing for 4% inflation rate to be conservative. Now multiply that amount by 50. So $90,047*50 = $4.5M. 50 times your annual income requirement allows you to live on 2% of the principal each year, which is a conservative withdrawal rate to avoid running out of money in retirement. Now, you don’t want that money languishing in a saving account, because your principal will gradually lose purchasing power to inflation. You need to invest that money in stocks, ideally a low or no cost total stock market index fund and simply live off the dividends. If you insist on putting your money in savings account only and living off the interest, you’d need a lot more than $4.5M to retire at 50. That’s because the savings accounts pay only 2% interest without principal appreciation, while inflation can average up to 4% and you need to budget for a long lifespan like living up to 100 just in case so you don’t run out of money. I did a bit of calculation and figured that you will need $19.4M at age 50 just to maintain the same purchasing power in retirement starting at age 50 up to age 100. That is almost 5 times more than if your money is in stocks. In sum, estimate your annual retirement income needs in future dollars. Multiply that amount by 50 if you are investing your money in a stock index fund, or by 250 if you leave your retirement savings in a saving account.

title: Is Wikipedia a reliable source for research papers in college (USA)? What are some alternative sites that come close to its database size and reliability level?
post_text: The problem isn’t Wikipedia — it’s with using general purpose encyclopedias at all, doesn’t matter if it’s Wikipedia or Encyclopedia Britannica. Those are good sources for high school papers, but by college you should start relying on better sources from specialists. In terms of accuracy, Wikis are generally seen as unstable because they are open source. Literally anyone can edit most entries. But at the same time, when Wikipedia was compared to Encyclopedia Britannica on a number of entries, it was comparable in accuracy. Furthermore, some Wiki entries are in fact written by specialists who are doing a public service by contributing their expertise in that way. title: How does the Israel Defense Forces integrate individuals with physical or mental disabilities since everyone has to serve in the military?
post_text: First of all, not everyone has to serve. Large parts of the population, primarily Arab or Ultra-Orthodox Jews, are exempt, as are people who migrated to Israel after the age of 22 in the case of men and 20 in the case of women, although they still can volunteer. However, the IDF does exempt those it deems unfit from service for physical or mental reasons under  Profile 21 , the lowest profile in the IDF’s medical profile system. The classifications change every now and then. For example, after the death of a soldier serving in the Military Police from an allergic reaction to eating food with nuts, the IDF put nut allergies under Profile 21 in 2016. And it’s also common for those seeking to get out of military service to fake psychological unfitness to get exempted. Draft-dodging in Israel is now more common than it used to be, and the IDF likely tolerates it to some extent because it’s already a bit bloated. That being said, even those exempted from service under Profile 21 can apply to volunteer for service in non-combat positions if they wish. In particular, there are a number of volunteers on the autism spectrum who end up serving in intelligence positions.

post_text: I am thinking that cities are going to have a hard time. Even after COVID-19 passes, companies realize they can have most of their workforce doing their stuff at home, if not every day, than most days. People are going to move to the suburbs, exurbs and even rural areas with good internet connections — they no longer need to be that near the city. They probably won’t want to be too far, but an hour and a half commute one or two days a week is doable. As people move out and property values drop, taxes will have to increase, which will start the cycle anew. Some cities have income taxes, and will experience the same issues. Policy wise, there’s going to be more effort to extract money from suburbs and other areas for urban areas as this issue furthers itself. Transit systems will experience lower ridership but relatively fixed costs, so they’ll have problems. There’s going to be almost a full scale war waged against zoning / public school districts in various states around the country. Probably won’t end too well. Retail is going to have a difficult time — people will buy stuff online, but Walmart, Target etc. will continue to do well. A few malls will buck the trend, but many malls will enter a death spiral as a few merchants pull out, which will cause foot traffic to drop and thus more merchants to pull out. Many professionals will be able to relocate to where they want to live, not where they have to live. If you like skiing, there’s no reason not to live near a resort, even if your job is a thousand miles away, because you can do it remotely. There’s likely going to be a push for a higher minimum wage. Covid didn’t kill automation, it’s still going to be happening, and a minimum wage increase might be the final thing that pushes automation. title: If a transgender woman saved your life, would you still have negative views of transgender women?
post_text: You likely mean well, but anything anyone might answer in response to this question suffers from the same problem that already plagues trans folks in this arena — it’s entirely speculative. The  idea of folks being transgender  already prompts too many folks to engage in pure speculation as to whatever they imagine being transgender must entail, and from that speculation, to develop strong opinions  about people they have never met  and know next to nothing about. I know a few transgender folks well (myself included), and am acquainted with or otherwise personally aware of a number of others. To my knowledge, none of them have saved my life (unless you count my own part in finally coming to the realization that staying closeted was killing me, and might well have finished the job had I not ultimately acted). More to the point, much as tends to be the case with cisgender folks I know, I find that while I have very positive views of many of them, I have somewhat less positive views of a few. What I don’t have is  any particular view  of the vast majority of folks (trans or otherwise) whom I simply have never met or otherwise encountered in any meaningful way. If one of those folks I’d never met happened to save my life in some sort of emergency situation, I would certainly be grateful. Their actions would also seem to indicate something of a positive nature about them as a person, but honestly, I’d still not have a great deal to go on there unless I ended up spending more time with them afterward, and got to know them better as a result. So really, I think  this sort of speculation  isn’t all that fruitful. What  might  be useful for folks to ponder — and especially folks who imagine themselves justified in holding a negative view of so many trans people they’ve never actually met — is the growing probability  they have encountered trans folks  in their daily lives without ever even knowing it. And  they’ve formed views of those people  based on things it turns out actually matter when it comes to our day-to-day interactions with one another. The cheerful waitress who made your last restaurant visit a particularly pleasant experience might have been transgender. The person who went out of their way to open a door for you when they spotted you laden with groceries might have been transgender. The delivery driver who not only gets your order to your door on time, every time, but never forgets that you like  two extra containers of special sauce , might be transgender. Maybe some of you have come across one, or two, or even a few folks who are transgender (or else whom you thought were), either in person or on the internet or TV, and didn’t particularly care for something they said or did, or even just their overall appearance. I’m not going to tell you that couldn’t happen. What I am going to say, though, is that extrapolating any such distaste grounded in anecdotal experience to a whole bunch of people you  haven’t  encountered   and don’t know the slightest thing about is irrational at best. But if you just can’t keep from speculating about the rest of us trans folks you  haven’t met , then allow me to suggest speculating, not so much as to how you might feel in the extraordinary case that one of us happened to rescue you from dire straits, but the far more likely scenario that that you  may well have encountered  one or more of us in the course of the many smaller, but still meaningful interactions we all have in our day-to-day lives — and already formed an entirely positive view of us. When it comes to people in general, maybe not every person you ever meet will strike you so positively, but you know that some inevitably will. You already know this sort of thing can and does happen  with people  all the time. Transgender people  are people.  Even if you’re presently carrying around negative views as to the  idea of a person being transgender , and imagined that necessarily requires your holding a negative view of all transgender folks, the reality is that  real, live transgender men and women  can and often will absolutely come across to you in completely the same positive sort of way. Some of us may well already have done so. Then all you have left to decide is whether you’d rather hold onto a distaste for an entire group of people you’ve never met, born entirely of speculative assumptions about them, or else form your views about people as the individuals they are. I’m not here to tell you, or anyone else what to do — but if the shoe were on the other foot, how would you prefer other folks formed their opinions about  you ?

title: Were there any black US soldier during the WWII?
post_text: Yes, there were many Black soldiers who served in the U.S. military during World War II. Approximately one million African Americans served in various capacities, including combat roles, support positions, and as part of segregated units.  Notable contributions included: Tuskegee Airmen : This group of African American pilots and aircrew members served with distinction in the Army Air Forces. They were the first Black aviators in the U.S. military and played a crucial role in escorting bombers and conducting air combat missions. The 761st Tank Battalion : Known as the "Black Panthers," this unit fought valiantly in Europe and was awarded a Presidential Unit Citation for its bravery. The 92nd Infantry Division : This all-Black division, also known as the "Buffalo Soldiers," fought in Italy and earned several awards for its service. Despite facing racial discrimination and segregation within the military, these soldiers made significant contributions to the war effort and helped pave the way for the eventual desegregation of the U.S. Armed Forces in 1948.

title: Why was Yugoslavia bombed by NATO in 1999, and which countries bombed it?
post_text: Look at this As you can see, Serbia has a very interesting geostrategic position. Due to geography, the two natural land communications that connect Greece and Turkey and with this the Middle East with the rest of Europe pass through Serbia. Plus the Danube River. Due to the geography of the Balkans, especially the Western Balkans, it is very problematic to build really usable communications and bypass Serbia in the process. Essentially, Serbia controls the three main land lines connecting the rest of Europe and Asia. This is the main reason why Austria-Hungary attacked the Kingdom of Serbia in 1914 (WWI). This is the main reason why the great powers are not eager to allow the former Kingdom of Yugoslavia (of which Serbia was a part) to be a neutral country in WWII. This is the main reason why after WWII Yugoslavia was allowed to choose its own side. To be a kind of buffer zone. All the great powers wanted to control these communications, but they did not want to enter into a new war. Allowing Yugoslavia to choose was the only solution acceptable to all. This was the main reason why NATO attacked Yugoslavia (FRY). They were able to do this because it was a monopolar world at the time. This was the main reason why the Republic of Serbia is still under enormous pressure from the Collective West. In 1999, they failed to achieve their main goal. All these communications bypass Kosovo. But they hold something in their hands with which they can blackmail the Republic of Serbia. And they do it abundantly. And they will continue to do this in the future. If this were still a monopolar world, they would find some excuse for a new aggression against the Republic of Serbia, like in 1999. But luckily for Serbia, that is no longer the case. The new aggression would have very serious consequences for the "Western World". Especially of an economic nature. And not because of Serbia as Serbia. Because some big economic powers do not want this to be a pattern that could threaten some of their vital interests in some other parts of the world. Especially because this has already backfired to the West in their face with the situation in Ukraine. Where Russia uses the same pattern and the same excuses. Of course, as a major economic power, China is interested in these communications as part of the new Silk Road. That is why they are gradually increasing their presence in Serbia through companies controlled by the Chinese state. They are not (yet) as aggressive with their presence, but the trend is obvious. But their presence is not the main problem that would cause them to enter into a serious economic war. The Strait of Malacca is. Because they wouldn't want some fool (read USA) jeopardizing 60% of their trade (and 70% of China's fuel) with some foolishness that someone might do here using the same pattern. Some say this aggression was due to natural resources. True Kosovo has some amount of this. But these are not some resources that the "West" cannot find in some other places in significantly higher quantities and at a lower price. So that's not the reason. At least not the main reason. Some say this is because of the "humanitarian situation" (which, by the way, was caused by "the West"). But you have much worse humanitarian situations before, during and after this where the "West" did not react. So this is not a reason either. This whole thing has nothing to do with Kosovo as Kosovo. It was just an excuse to try to take complete control of these communications. This did not work in 1999, which is why the Republic of Serbia is still under constant pressure from the West. Although the Republic of Serbia has signed some agreements where they have access to these communications even in a military sense, the pressure is still very strong because they want physical control (boots on the ground). At this moment, the Republic of Serbia is a neutral sovereign country and that is simply not possible at this moment. Without war of course. And this is the main reason why the Republic of Serbia will continue to be a target for economic and political pressure from the West and for anti-Serbian propaganda. This is not something new. This has been happening since ancient Rome. In Serbia, you have a saying that all this is happening (so frequent wars here) because we built a house in the middle of the road... Which is kind of true.

title: What are your top 5 weirdest and creative recipes?
post_text: Here's a delicious recipe that has been a favorite for years. Just typed it up for my grand niece who is collecting recipes. Sandy and Pat’s Upside Down Burrito Pie – serves 4-6 Ingredients Non-Stick Pan - the right size to line with tortilla (see below) 2 tablespoons butter 5 flour tortillas big enough to fill pan (10″ or so) 1 can (10 oz) Green Enchilada Sauce, heated ½ can (15 oz) refried beans, heated – more if you have room 2/3 cup sour cream ½ cup sliced black olives 1 ripe avocado, sliced ½ tomato, thinly sliced – use a whole one if small 1½ cups grated Monterey Jack cheese (2 cups if you have room) 2-3 tablespoons sliced green onions Hot sauce of your choice (optional) Tips: It’s important that the pan is deep enough and the right size to hold the tortillas. The plan is to build each layer of the pie over the other in the pan, with the tortillas holding each layer of the ingredients so they don’t spooge out and make a mess in the pan as the next layer is put on top. As you build it, gently press down each new layer to form good contact with the layer below. Cooking temperature is important – the pie should heat through so that the cheese in the second layer melts, while the top layer of sour cream gets warm, but does not curdle. This should all happen such that the bottom tortilla that is lining the pan browns, but does not burn. This may take some practice! Directions: Set stovetop to low heat – to avoid burning the first tortilla while the dish heats through Melt butter in pan – roll to coat all of the inside Lay in the first flour tortilla – should come part way up the sides of the pan. Turn to make sure that the bottom side of the tortilla is coated in butter In even layers, Add the green onion, then half cup of cheese. Top with 2 oz enchilada sauce Lay in the second flour tortilla. In even layers, add beans, remainder of cheese, and 2 oz enchilada sauce Lay in the third tortilla – add avocado, tomato, 1 or 2 oz of enchilada sauce. Salt and hot sauce to taste Lay in the fourth tortilla – add sour cream, black olives, 1 or 2 oz enchilada sauce, sprinkles of hot sauce to taste Cover with the fifth tortilla. Put a lid on top (goal is to make the pan filled, but not overflowing) With a knife, trim any excess tortilla sticking out from the pan lid Simmer on low until you can smell it toasting, and the top of the pie is slightly warm to the touch Remove from heat, carefully insert knife or spatula along one side – check that the first (base) tortilla is getting crisp and golden. Return to heat if needed When crust is golden and pie is slightly warm on top, run a spatula around the edge of the pie so it releases cleanly. Place a serving plate on the top of the pan. Then, while holding the plate in place, quickly and carefully invert the plate and the pan together. Carefully remove the pan. Cut into serving portions with a large sharp serrated knife (to avoid crushing the pie while cutting). Serve with any remaining enchilada sauce on top. Rich, decadent, and delicious.

title: How did WWII veterans typically deal with PTSD after the war?
post_text: Drac Smith’s answer provides a good list of ways veterans who might have suffered from what today we call PTSD dealt with those symptoms. Of that listing, ranging from motorcycle clubs to self-medication, the most common means was almost certainly just dealing with it. I’ve known quite a lot of WWII veterans, from my dad and uncle, to those of friends to include German vets as well, some of whom underwent severe combat, imprisonment, etc. Among these, a father of a close Army buddy of mine whose dad described landing at Normandy and crossing Europe on his belly, to keep out of the way of German machineguns. The father of another Army buddy whose dad served as an Army AA artillery officer in the Pacific. The father of a German woman I knew well fought on the Eastern Front, was captured by the Soviets and spent many years after the war in a Soviet POW camp. A client of mine, and the father of a law school classmate, who as a navigator on a B-17 was downed over Germany, captured, and almost starved to death in a German POW camp. The father of a close German friend who fought at Stalingrad, was lucky to get out on one of the last evacuation flights from the pocket, and went on to fight in Normandy and the Western Front. A German bar owner who was infantryman in a Waffen SS unit on the Eastern Front late in the war. My uncle who fought in the Huertegen Forest in a US infantry division. My father who swept mines for the US Navy. The father of an Israeli relative who served with the British Army in Africa. The father of one of my best friends growing up who as a Marine fought in the Marianas. Of all these men, the only one that I think suffered from what today might be called PTSD was the last fellow, who had a drinking problem and died intoxicated in a car crash in the early 1970s. The others all seemed to handle whatever psychological trauma they suffered on their own, without any obvious behaviors that today would be regarded as indications of PTSD. How representative of WWII vets this is I do not know, and obviously I did not know all these men equally well. But my feeling is that whatever PTSD they suffered they simply dealt with without seeking assistance, not that any such assistance necessarily would have been offered to them at the time anyway other than for the most obviously severe psychological symptoms.

title: What is meant by NFT?
post_text: So what is NFT? Before that, I would like to quickly explain you the difference between a  fungible  asset and a  non-fungible  asset. Fungibility In simple words, fungibility refers to something replaceable or exchangeable. An asset or a good (ex- Gold or Silver) is a fungible asset if you can replace or exchange one part of it with another indistinguishable part. Gold, Silver, Wheat, Currencies, Oil, are all fungible goods. You can also consider fungible goods as common items that are not very rare, unique, or collectible. Non-fungibility It is exactly the opposite of fungibility i.e. something unique and irreplaceable. An autographed book or a rare old coin is non-fungible as they both can’t be easily replaced. Consider non-fungible goods as rare and unique items. Back to NFTs So  NFT  stands for  non-fungible token  now you might have an idea what it is. Like any other non-fungible asset a non-fungible token or NFTs are basically something unique and irreplaceable. In simple words they are nothing but an unit of data stored on a very complicated piece of technology known as  blockchain . BTW blockchain is the same technology Bitcoin, Ethereum, Monero and almost every other crypto currency works on. So NFT is nothing but Data stored on blockchain but now you might wonder what that data actually is. That data can be anything digital as photos, videos, e-books, Gifs, audios and so on. There isn’t any limit (as far as I know) on what can be an NFT. Although physical stuff can also be an NFT but for now most NFTs are digital. What’s the difference between an NFT and a Cryptocurrency like Bitcoin? Well, its complicated and confusing. Both an NFT or a crypto at their core works on similar technology i.e blockchain and have very similar working principles. That’s why non tech heads find it hard to distinguish between both. But in simple language a Crypto currency is the virtual version of real money whereas NFTs are virtual version of collectibles not a currency neither they can be used to buy or sell stuff. You can buy an NFT with Bitcoin but in most cases buying a Bitcoin with an NFT is not that easy. All Bitcoins (or any other crypto) have a fixed value which means 1 BTC = 1 BTC. But that’s not the case with NFTs. Every NFT is unique and no two can have same value. As value of an NFT is determined by an underlying asset. Every token carries different underlying assets thus have different values but that’s not the case with cryptos. Cryptos do not carry any asset and every crypto in circulation on a blockchain is same thus all have same value as well. If you have more questions regarding NFTs I have also written an Article on them. You can check it out  here .

title: How long does it take for an outdoor cat to get used to being an indoor cat?
post_text: The time it takes for an outdoor cat to adjust to being an indoor cat can vary significantly based on several factors, including the cat's personality, age, and previous experiences. Generally, the adjustment period may take anywhere from a few days to several weeks. Here are some key points to consider: Initial Adjustment : Cats may initially show signs of stress or anxiety, such as hiding, vocalizing, or trying to escape. This phase can last from a few days to a week. Gradual Adaptation : Over time, most cats will start to explore their new environment and become more comfortable. Providing a safe and stimulating indoor space can help facilitate this process. Environmental Enrichment : Offering toys, climbing structures, and scratching posts can make the indoor environment more appealing and help the cat adjust more quickly. Routine and Patience : Establishing a consistent routine for feeding, playtime, and interaction can help the cat feel more secure and settled. Individual Differences : Some cats may adapt quickly, while others may take longer—up to a few months. Patience and understanding are key during this transition. If you have specific concerns about your cat's behavior during the adjustment period, consulting with a veterinarian or a feline behaviorist can provide additional guidance.

title: Can you tell me about an early historical figure that you find interesting that many people probably don’t know about?
post_text: Have you heard about this fellow called the prophet Mani? He was a third-century Mesopotamian who became the founder of what was at one point the world's most widespread but now extinct religion - Manichaeism. He grew up in what was likely a Christian community but believed he had a divine twin (possibly Jesus) who asked him to preach a religion that would correct the mistakes of the past ones. He wrote all his teachings down into a book so there would be no disagreements, gathered disciples and spread their teachings from the Roman Empire through Persia (and later, others would take it as far as China). He was also known as a master painter, and is reported to have painted all his teachings as well as writing them so more people could have access to them and understand them. His reputation as a miracle worker and healer endeared him to the Sassanian Kings of greater Iran and became a court advisor and was allowed to spread his teachings - much to the anger of competing Zoroastrian priests. Unfortunately, he would eventually fall out of favour and be martyred. His followers persevered for a few centuries in the Near East despite near constant persecution by everyone, and last until the early 15th century in China and Central Asia (where they would eventually fade into Buddhism). Anyways, his religion was pretty interesting / odd in some ways (worth looking it up) but one of the things that really stands out was its emphasis on vegetarianism for all followers - which was unheard of in a lot of places where it spread (even Chinese Buddhists thought they were crazy for not eating meat). Also the only ritual we know they performed was basically a ceremonial (vegetarian) feast where the lay people fed the monks (and nuns) who lead the community with a portrait of Mani seated nearby at a table. They believed doing so would free all the souls of living beings trapped in matter (and who were reincarnated in food) — which is basically sending souls to equivalent of Heaven by feasting with friends. Not bad.

title: How can I get a free cell phone if I have a low income and I am disabled?
post_text: Lifeline is the FCC's program to help make communications services more affordable for low-income consumers. Lifeline provides subscribers a discount on monthly telephone service, broadband Internet access service, or voice-broadband bundled service purchased from participating providers. Lifeline typically provides up to a $9.25 monthly discount on service for eligible low-income subscribers. Subscribers may receive a Lifeline discount on either a wireline or a wireless service, but they may not receive a discount on both services at the same time. Lifeline also supports broadband Internet access service and broadband-voice bundles. FCC rules prohibit more than one Lifeline service per household. Lifeline is available to eligible low-income consumers in every state, commonwealth, territory, and on Tribal lands. To participate in the Lifeline program, consumers must either have an income that is at or below 135% of the  Federal Poverty Guidelines  or participate in certain federal assistance programs, such as the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program or Medicaid. You can see if you are eligible by reviewing the information available at  lifelinesupport.orgOpens in New Window  (see "Do I Qualify?"). More info on the program / application process  Lifeline Support for Affordable Communications A lot of providers advertise low cost service through the Lifeline program. Q Link Wireless advertises that it “provides you with FREE monthly data, minutes, and unlimited texting courtesy of the goverment funded Lifeline Program.” Note, it doesn’t say free phone, so it may not be entirely free. And, Assurance Wireless, “a federal Lifeline Assistance program brought to you by Virgin Mobile,” advertises “discounted or free phone service through the Lifeline Assistance program. Assurance Wireless provides eligible consumers with free monthly data, unlimited texting, free monthly minutes plus a free Smartphone.” Since they’re all through the Lifeline program, I do not know if there is any difference. title: Why does Lee Kuan Yew occupy such a hallowed and godlike status in Singaporean culture and history?
post_text: Many thanks to Erik Fair for the excellent edits :-) Mr.  Lee Kuan Yew  is certainly respected. Not sure about hallowed or godlike status. Here's why: Totally dedicated to  Singapore  - Under his leadership, the nation was transformed from a basket case to a developed nation. All this in a span of 25 or so years. He fought the communists in a vicious death struggle. Think this affected him deeply and he remained vigilant and view any plots through the lens of his experiences. Walked the talk - Mr. Lee understood the corrosive nature of corruption and worked hard to stamp it out. Ministers and the Old Guard were not spared. He remained so incorruptible that when some challenged him and his family over a property deal, even the opposition stood up for him and said that there's no corruption and the matter was closed. Selected the right people - He surrounded himself with capable men and women to get the job done. Visionary - Seemed to be able to predict trends and get ahead of them. Some excellent policies: Limiting of Racial Mix - By setting limits on where various races could stay (public housing) this preventing the rise of racial enclaves e.g. Molenbeek, Belgium, Melbourne, Sydney, Paris, London, etc. There are some areas in these cities that even the police fear to tread. We don't have these in Singapore thanks to his foresight. Public Housing - By enabling citizens to own their own home, this creates a stake in the nation. CPF - This encourages self reliance, responsibility and prudence. It also helped build up a large national reserve which puts Singapore in an advantageous financial position. National Parks - By encouraging planting of trees and creation of parks, it makes Singapore a much more attractive and pleasant place to live. Contrast this with some Malaysia towns and cities where all the trees are cut down and there's no shelter making and the sun beats down on all the open areas. Public Transport - Saw the need for a good public transport system and invested SGD 4B into the MRT system. Limits on Cars - Singapore roads although congested, flows relatively freely and averts the grid lock that one see in cities like Bangkok, Manila, etc. Meritocracy - Firmly believed in the right man or woman for the job. Pluralism - He made it a point to speak in Malay, Mandarin and English. This is to ensure that all the races are given equally respect and recognition. How many leaders can and will do this? His son Mr.  Lee Hsien Loong  follows in his footsteps and this makes him very popular. Policy U-Turns - Not afraid to admit mistakes and make policy U-turns if necessary e.g. the 2 child policy. Widely respected - Trusted by key Chinese and US officials, Mr. Lee was able to navigate the cold war successfully. Totally dedicated to his wife - Those who know Mr. Lee say that after she passed on, he was a broken man. The couple is a model for Singaporeans to emulate. Point of view: How one conducts themselves in private is also how they conduct themselves in public. Meaning, a person who remains faithful to his wife is one that is faithful and trustworthy. Stepped Down from Power - How many leaders do this? Instead we see many examples of leaders that cling on to power to the detriment of their nation e.g. Venezuela, Zimbabwe, South Africa etc. Mr. Lee Kuan Yew was not perfect but he was certainly rare and enlightened. Singapore is blessed to have had his leadership. This is why he is much respected. Rest in peace Mr. Lee Kuan Yew.

title: How are the companies managing to deceive the deceivers in the battle against hackers?
post_text: Hi there, “ To deceive the deceivers ” - nice one! I assume it’s not as simple as that and with the quote above, “HoneyPots” came to the mind first. A cyber honeypot is a sacrificial computer system that’s intended to attract cyberattacks, like a decoy. It mimics a target for hackers, and uses their intrusion attempts to gain information about cybercriminals and the way they are operating or to distract them from other targets. There are two primary types of honeypot designs: Production honeypots —serve as decoy systems inside fully operating networks and servers, often as part of an intrusion detection system (IDS). They deflect criminal attention from the real system while analyzing malicious activity to help mitigate vulnerabilities. Research honeypots —used for educational purposes and security enhancement. They contain trackable data that you can trace when stolen to analyse the attack. There are three types of honeypot deployments that permit threat actors to perform different levels of malicious activity: Pure honeypots —complete production systems that monitor attacks through bug taps on the link that connects the honeypot to the network. They are unsophisticated. Low-interaction honeypots —imitate services and systems that frequently attract criminal attention. They offer a method for collecting data from blind attacks such as botnets and worms malware. High-interaction honeypots —complex setups that behave like real production infrastructure. They don’t restrict the level of activity of a cybercriminal, providing extensive cybersecurity insights. However, they are higher-maintenance and require expertise and the use of additional technologies like virtual machines to ensure attackers cannot access the real system. By monitoring traffic coming into the honeypot system, one can assess: where the cybercriminals are coming from the level of threat what modus operandi they are using what data or applications they are interested in how well the security measures are working to stop cyberattacks Feel free to visit a previous answer about changes in cybersecurity happenings in the last decade here -  NitinS's answer to How has cyber security changed in the last decade? title: Why is Belgium important to the EU?
post_text: Located at the crossroads between Latin and Germanic Europe, Belgium is surrounded by the Netherlands, Germany, Luxembourg, France and the North Sea close to the United Kingdom. Belgium is home to NATO and the European Union. 60% of Europe’s purchasing power is within 500 kilometers, as Belgium is centrally positioned– broadening Greater London to the Netherlands and parts of France and Germany. The country is a central logistics hub of the European market. Despite its small area of 30,700 km², Belgium boasts about 800 European distribution centers (EDCs) – the highest concentration of EDCs in Europe. The Port of Antwerp is the 2nd largest port in Europe and 15th largest globally. The Euro tunnel provides essential links to the UK, making Brussels an even more attractive location. Thus, Belgium is a vital transportation hub in Europe for anyone trying to reach the European consumer market of 500 million people.

There is some controversy on how useful this index is and results sometimes vary but it provides a general idea of how nutritious a fruit is: The sugar content of fruit can be measured by the Glycemic Index. title: How much money is enough to travel Europe?
originally_answered: How much money should I save for travelling around Europe?
post_text:
Obviously, it depends where you go, how long you plan to be there and what time of year. But, I'll try to give examples from my experiences this last summer/autumn, and I hope they prove useful.  GETTING THERE  Probably the most important part, but certainly not the hardest. It takes time and diligence, but consider all options. Once you're there, you'll find traveling through Europe to be pretty easy.  My example: I wanted to go straight to Spain. The flight there was $800. So, I flew to Paris for $440, stayed for awhile, flew to London for $70, stayed for awhile, and then flew to Barcelona for $100. After Barcelona, I took a train to Valencia for $20, stayed a couple days, then took a six-hour bus to Madrid for $5, stayed a few days and then flew to Milan for $75. So... $800 to fly straight to Barcelona vs. $710 hopping around first. If you're planning on seeing as much as possible, just get your one-way ticket there and make your plan as you go.  I also found round-trip tickets to be more expensive (sometimes) than looking for individual one-way tickets.  I took Icelandair from Denver. The cheapest places to travel into were Copenhagen and Paris. The Layover in Keflavik was only 1.5 hours. I wish I had taken advantage of the "Up to 7-day Layover" in Reykjavik that Icelandair offers... next time though ;)  HOSTELS 
I was not staying in the cheapest hostel every time, but it was usually close to it. I tried to balance location/rating when possible. Do you want to be in the city center, or one block from the train station? These are prices (give or take) that you could expect to pay: London- August 1st = $38/night
Valencia- September 5th = $14/night
Athens- October 21st = $12/night
Bucharest- November 24th = $12/night
Prague- November 2nd = $5/night
Bratislava- November 5th = $9/night
Budapest- November 7th = $15/night
Budapest- November 13th = $13/night
Warsaw- November 14th = $19/night
Warsaw- November 20th = $27/night
Copenhagen- November 21st = $45/night Tips for hostels:
 Request the bottom bunk when booking. You will be much more comfortable not having to climb into bed.  Use an app like  Hostel World . Check reviews, ratings and location before you book. I found deals on hostels that were only a 15-20 minutes from the city center by bus/train. Consider the bus/train would only be ~€1, so it was a great deal!   Check amenities. Every hostel I stayed in had WiFi, but some only had it in certain common areas, and not in the rooms. Also, if you're lucky, they will have on-site laundry!  Have a longer USB cord handy. Not every room has a plug right next to your bed.  The bigger the dorm room, the cheaper the bed. 12-16 bed rooms offer the best price. Hopefully you're not a light sleeper.  Have a small towel that dries quickly.  Have a small lock  
Hostels will likely be where you stay most, but  Air B&B  can be a good deal sometimes, especially if you have travel partners. I had a couple great experiences with Air B&B over the four months of my travels.  If you're interested in  Couchsurfing , I recommend doing research on it for the countries that are more expensive (i.e. The UK, Scandinavia etc.), because this is when it will really matter most. Briefly, create/complete your profile now, start going to local Meet-ups, gain references, host if possible and test it out close to where you live. This is a community built on trust, and you would be wise to prove you are trustworthy. Also, I recommend giving your host a small gift or offering to help with groceries and small chores :)  PLANES, TRAINS & AUTOMOBILES So, the myth is that buying a Eurorail pass will save you money... If you are trying to budget, there are many more options to consider.  Before I get to that, I would like to point out one VERY important thing when considering which mode of transportation is best.  Let's say you find a one-hour flight from Milan to Rome for $30. Let's say you also find a four-hour train for the same trip that costs $35. You would likely choose the plane because it costs less and it's much faster. Here's the problem though: it will cost more and take longer! Airports are rarely near the city center, and will require transport to & from both. There goes the $5 you were saving... Now consider the 45-minute bus ride to the airport, checking in an hour early for your flight, waiting at the gate, the actual hour of flight, navigating the new airport, finding transport to the city center... You're looking at almost the same amount of time if not more! Also, some train tickets are good for all day, but if you miss a flight...  Lastly, you have to consider Time vs. Money. The same trip could have been done for €5 on Megabus, but it would have taken ten hours and you will have lost that whole day. Lots to think about. Anyway...  GoEuro  is an app that is (almost) perfect for comparing planes/trains/busses/rideshare at the same time. In my limited experience, it works best in Western/Southern Europe, but you can still find use in Eastern/Northern.  Megabus  seems to be the cheapest way most of the time, but make sure you have a pillow (hint* keep the one from the flight you took to get to Europe). Most rates I found are only €5! Great for a budget.  Trains  may be tricky at first, especially because some cities have multiple stations, so make sure you're at the right one. Check to see if your ticket is good for all day, or if it is time specific. The best priced tickets are usually non-refundable, so you don't want to make a mistake. Also, if you are not assigned a seat, you may want to line-up early to get a good seat.  Planes  can be surprisingly cheap. I actually flew from Milan to Athens because the flight was only $33!? The train would have taken almost a whole day and would have cost $125+! I recommend  Kayak  first for flights. You will probably end up flying budget airlines such as  EasyJet ,  Ryanair  or  LOT .  BlaBlaCar  is a rideshare. Say someone is driving from Prague to Vienna. They can list open seats of their car, and charge you to ride along with them. I didn't always find this to be reliable, but it is certainly an option to consider.  FOOD So, this one is pretty easy, but I'll go through it real quick. Find a market close by, make some sandwiches and buy a few snacks to keep in your backpack. Get a thing of water, and you should be set. This will save your budget. Some countries will have food that is really affordable and pinching pennies isn't completely necessary (Spain, Greece, Hungary), but others will crush your wallet.  WORK It is possible to do work while you're traveling. Of the 19 weeks I traveled, I spent thirteen with free accommodation and food. Websites like  Workaway  and  helpx  made it possible for me to stay somewhere in exchange for 25-30 hours of work each week. I would highly recommend researching these sites and potential hosts. The best part is that you will immerse yourself into their culture and meet new people! You will see and do things unlike most tourists :)  MONEY  Now, the hard part.  First and foremost: Get a card from your bank that is "Chip + pin" or "Chip + sign". Already have a chip? Good, you'll need it. But if you don't, I HIGHLY recommend getting a Charles Schwab HYI (High Yield Investment) Checking account. This account carries no minimum, and you will not be charged ANY ATM fees! Carrying cash is dangerous, and if you need to exchange currency, you will be charged and lose money. I kept as little cash on me as possible, and since I didn't have to worry about ATM fees, it was a no-brainer to only take out a little at a time.  If nothing else, you must have a card with a chip though. It's standard in Europe, and the only time I could use my non-compliance credit card was when I was booking transportation or hostels online.  Budgeting will be up to you though...  I walked everywhere all the time. Don't take taxis! They will rip you off, and kill your budget. Figure out the bus/train/metro, because that will come in handy, but walk as much as possible! You'll find so many things along the way and save money!  Careful of  tourist traps ... They're everywhere and they see thousands of you everyday. Just Google "Tourist Scams". Here's a pretty good result: https://www.ricksteves.com/travel-tips/theft-scams/tourist-scams Tourist traps aren't just people on the street scamming you either... I use the London Eye as a perfect example. If you want to ride the "ferris wheel", it will cost you £25 (roughly $37). You could pay that much to go to a Six Flags! Go to the Portrait Museum (free) or the British Museum (free) and save your money!  Coinpurse  seems kind of silly, but they have so many more coins in Europe, and having a small little purse will keep you from pulling a wad of change out of your pocket every night.  Currency converters  or a small calculator are handy if you're not the best at math. The exchange rate can be confusing, and it's smart to know how much something costs.  Budgeting  comes down to the individual though. I like coffee and wine, but those can start add up over time... Do you smoke? Do you eat a lot? Do you need nice 4-star accommodation? If you're trying to see as much as possible while spending as little as possible, you must have discipline. I was able to do work exchange, so my accommodation/food budget was fairly low. I also saw twelve countries, so my transportation expenses were pretty high.  If you crunch your budget, don't go out to bars, eat cheap and really squeeze the most out of every dollar, you could probably get by on a budget of ~$150-250/week. If you do the work exchange to eliminate food + lodging, you could get by for significantly less. I worked a Vineyard in Piedmont, Italy for five weeks and spent a total of ~$300! Keep in mind that it would be impossible to get by in Copenhagen or the UK on that budget... So, if you plan to travel there, you'll have to save/budget money from somewhere else.  Feel free to follow up with me, as I would be happy to help answer any questions you may have. I'm sure I've left something out, and I will likely update this answer in the future. Best of luck in your travels, and have fun :)

title: Do any Chinese people have Spanish names and Spanish accents?
post_text: Sure. There are a good number of ethnic Chinese in Latin America and the vast majority speak the language of the country they live in to some extent, with many speaking it fluently. If they were born there or grew up there, they probably have a good Spanish (or Brazilian, etc.) accent. If they immigrated there as adults, probably they are less likely to have acquired a good accent. Do any have Spanish names? Some will have taken Spanish names for purposes of school, work, etc. Some may have Spanish names because they were born there and their ethnically Chinese parents gave them a popular Spanish name, possibly in conjunction with a Chinese name as well. Having two names in this way is a common practice among Chinese in the US too, a Chinese name and an American name. Some Chinese-origin families may have lived there for decades and basically gone native in many ways. Maybe they still celebrate the lunar New Year, but also celebrate local holidays and customs and see themselves more as part of the community than as newcomers to it. How well a group gets integrated with the larger community can depend on whether there is an ethnic enclave that they fit into. Sometimes people form closer relationships with others of similar background and tend to socialize more with them. It's not always just a matter of how long one has lived in a place. Integration into a community may not be integration into the whole community as much as finding one’s place among friends, who may be of similar origin. When I taught ESL, I occasionally had Asian, sometimes Chinese, students who had grown up in Central America and were now living in the US.

title: Is CBD oil the same as hemp oil?
post_text: No, they can’t be considered the same. Hemp oil is an umbrella terms that is used to describe both hemp seed oil and CBD oil. However, Hemp seed oil and CBD oil are two wholly different products. The former is made by cold-pressing the hemp seeds and contains ample amounts of nutrients including fatty acids, vitamins and minerals. However, comes with no cannabinoids. It is typically used in foods and skincare. The CBD oil, on the other side, is a thick liquid extracted from hemp flowers using C02 extraction process, containing cannabinoids and terpenes. It is a type of health supplement that is consumed in liquid form or taken as capsules, vaped or used in topical formulation.

title: Why is my cat peeing outside and inside the litter box?
post_text: There are so many possible reasons for it, none of us responding here can address them all. But everyone is correct—you need to get your cat to the vet to determine if it’s medical or behavioral. Medical reasons can include a UTI, but one of my cats with a history of inappropriate peeing does it whenever something is wrong in her life. The first times it happened, it took four vet visits before a different vet in the practice looked in her mouth and saw she had tooth resorption, which is very painful. Six extractions later, and it stopped for a year. Then she had impacted anal glands, and again the inappropriate peeing stopped when that was addressed. Only once was it a UTI. But she’s also done it when I tried change the brand of litter to one I liked, but she didn’t. And it’s been a constant challenge since one of the other cats started bullying her and ambushing her in the litter box and elsewhere. Other people sometimes have problems with their cats marking walls and such when there are stray cats outside that get them upset. So you need to be something of a sleuth, but you really need to start with the vet.

title: Where is low risk in the stock market or in mutual fund investments?
post_text: Low Risk for Stock Investing is identifying companies that have growth and expansion for this year and several more years but are still at bargain prices. There are 5 levels of price trends within most stocks from 2020. This range is from the highest highs of 2020 before the pandemic began (OR the highest high of the stock before it began its business bear cycle before the pandemic began. Most bear business cycles began in 2018 for thousands of stocks. The lows of March 2020 are the low level. Repeat the highest high of January or February 2020 (unless the long term trend was downward prior to 2020) to the LOWS of March is the 5 level tier of trends. The lowest level is when a stock is near the March 2020 lows STILL at this time. Most of these companies are NOT bargains but at risk of hostile take overs, Corporate Raiders who will buy sufficient shares to take the company over and then sell the assets, pay secured debt holders, leave investors with nothing, and pocket the profits. This is not a level that is a buy low situation. It is a very high risk level. The next tier up is a trading range or sideways pattern that moved up to about 30% above the low of March but is still a long ways from the highs of 2020 or the highs before the business cycled down in its normal bear business cycle. There are some stocks in this group that are beginning to show breakout patterns which are ideal also for long term investors as well as traders. This group will show patterns of 3 attempts usually before the breakout to a higher level. What you are looking for on the charts is Institutions buying the stock. Buy Zone technical patterns and Buy Side Institutional accumulation patterns. The 3rd tier up is in the middle range of the low to high levels previously described above. This is another strong area for good lower risk investing this year. It is probably the most ideal for risk averse investors. Again you are looking for sideways trends with 3 attempt or more breakout to test the resistance of the range highs. This can take several months or even a year to break. That means if the pattern developed in 2020, NOW is the time to start watching for those breakout patterns ahead of the 1st quarter earnings season. Level four is higher risk. This smaller group of stocks are at or near the highs of 2020 which were speculative highs before the pandemic. The market was poised for a correction well ahead of the pandemic. That just triggered a rapid decline. This group is smaller than the other tiers and price is speculative in many instances. There are a few stocks worth considering BUT the caveat is those companies were already in a downward bear business cycle starting in either 2017 or 2018. When the March price collapse occurred that was the final 3rd leg down for that corporation. When this is the the trend present, then the previous all time highs are still a long ways above the current price level. You can see this on weekly charts. These stocks have less risk and good potential as revenues and earnings have improved in 2020. The highest tier at this time, is now a few hundred stocks out of the 5800 stocks listed on the US exchanges at this time that ran up speculatively due to heavy concentrations of retail guru-led investors all buying at the same time. These companies are well-known and overly popular and many investors refuse to believe these companies won’t keep going and going up. This level tier is above their all-time highs, running at angles of ascent of price that are far too steep to sustain long term. A correction is inevitable at some point. However the caveat is that speculation can and does go beyond all technical patterns and totally beyond common sense in regards to risk before it implodes. So many will keep running as if it will never stop. ALL STOCKS in speculative mode will correct. Either the stock will run down in price OR it will run down briefly and then enter a long term trading range that can last for years. Neither is a good investment for long term as ROI is negative to minimal.

title: What makes Disney Plus successful?
originally_answered: Why will Disney Plus succeed?
post_text: There are many reasons behind the success of Disney Plus (i.e. over 28 million subscribers after less than 5 months of operation). For my answer, I will focus on three factors: Strategy, Implementation and Luck. Strategy: The Walt Disney Corporation had a great strategy that they have been developing for years. They would focus on families with kids and fans of the intellectual properties they already possessed. Disney+ will primarily be the “exclusive” streaming home of beloved Disney, Pixar, Marvel and Star Wars content. In addition to their vast library, they will make a few, buzzy Disney+ originals (e.g. The Mandalorian, High School Musical: the Musical: the Series, The Imagineering Story) that can spearhead their marketing campaign. They restructured their company so that the Media Networks and Studio Entertainment segments will provide the content that the Direct-to-Consumer & International (DTCI) segment will monetize. DTCI was allowed to forego easy money from content licensing so that they can harness pent-up demand via Disney+. They acquire both BAMtech and 21st Century Fox to fuel their streaming ambitions. Implimentation: Some parts of their implementation went better than expected. They launched their campaign with a big D23 discounted plan for avid fans. They also convinced Verizon to both pay for Disney+ subscriptions and provide such subscriptions free to their planholders. Not only were they able to stream their content earlier than expected, they were also able to add newly acquired content from 21st Century Fox (e.g. National Geographic, The Simpsons) into the service. Despite multiple setbacks (e.g. Comcast forcing them to sell their Sky PLC shares, wrong aspect ratio for The Simpsons, many glitches during opening day), Disney+ had a brilliant launch in Netherlands, U.S., Canada, Australia and New Zealand. Luck: The Mandalorian was a huge hit, exceeding all expectations. No one expected the online sensation of Baby Yoda overshadowing the finale of the Skywalker Saga. The poor launch of Apple TV+ weeks prior, made Disney+ launch even more newsworthy by comparison. While Disney marketing is far from infallible (e.g. resulting in high profile flops like Dark Phoenix and Solo: A Star Wars Story), many of their media campaigns became viral, setting multiple bloggers and influencers buzzing about Disney+. Walt Disney Studios scored an unprecedented 7 billion-dollar hits in the same year, making their library more prominent than ever. I personally don’t know if any company can duplicate the launch success of Disney+. Even Disney themselves maybe unable to duplicate it. I just hope they continue keeping the service worthy of such popularity.

title: What effects can Social Media have on public opinion?
post_text: That’s a very interesting question. I think we saw the power of social media in societies with strict freedom of expression rules during the Arab Spring. Thanks to Facebook and Twitter, protesters were able to gather, spread the word among them at first and then to the rest of the world. Prior to social media, the Arab Spring would have probably not taken such great length. I also believe that it allows subgroups that are discriminated against and threatened to voice their opinions and to gather. For example, I saw this documentary about a heavy metal band in Iran where the lead singer is a woman! They are absolutely forbidden to play in public as this musical genre is deemed “evil” and the lead singer would probably end up in jail. But thanks to social media, they are able to show the rest of the world who they are and that’s how I heard about them, all the way in France. Lastly, I think that social media allows groups and populations that do not have a voice in international/public affairs to be heard by being carried by other groups. For example, the Syrian refugees probably don’t have easy access, or access at all, to Facebook and Twitter but thanks to the incredibly viral power of some Tweets and Facebook posts, the rest of the world is able to know what is going on and (hopefully) take action. 15 years ago, we would have known about it very differently and we would have probably seen less international support. Hope this helps!

title: Should no questions be asked to a spiritual master?
post_text: The whole point of approaching a spiritual master is to receive spiritual knowledge. One should ask relevant questions to the spiritual master. The spiritual master will always welcome inquiries from a sincere disciple. The disciple should never accept anything blindly. He must approach the spiritual master to have his doubts cleared. Doubting is a function of the intelligence, and doubts can be removed by proper knowledge and intelligent reflection. Krishna says: Just try to learn the truth by approaching a spiritual master. Inquire from him submissively and render service unto him. The self-realized souls can impart knowledge unto you because they have seen the truth.  —Bhagavad-gita, 4.34 Srila Prabhupada explains: The path of spiritual realization is undoubtedly difficult. The Lord therefore advises us to approach a bona fide spiritual master in the line of disciplic succession from the Lord Himself. No one can be a bona fide spiritual master without following this principle of disciplic succession. The Lord is the original spiritual master, and a person in the disciplic succession can convey the message of the Lord as it is to his disciple. No one can be spiritually realized by manufacturing his own process, as is the fashion of the foolish pretenders. The Bhagavatam (6.3.19) says,  dharmam tu saksad bhagavat-pranitam : the path of religion is directly enunciated by the Lord. Therefore, mental speculation or dry arguments cannot help lead one to the right path. Nor by independent study of books of knowledge can one progress in spiritual life. One has to approach a bona fide spiritual master to receive the knowledge. Such a spiritual master should be accepted in full surrender, and one should serve the spiritual master like a menial servant, without false prestige. Satisfaction of the self-realized spiritual master is the secret of advancement in spiritual life. Inquiries and submission constitute the proper combination for spiritual understanding. Unless there is submission and service, inquiries from the learned spiritual master will not be effective. One must be able to pass the test of the spiritual master, and when he sees the genuine desire of the disciple, he automatically blesses the disciple with genuine spiritual understanding. In this verse, both blind following and absurd inquiries are condemned. Not only should one hear submissively from the spiritual master, but one must also get a clear understanding from him, in submission and service and inquiries. A bona fide spiritual master is by nature very kind toward the disciple. Therefore when the student is submissive and is always ready to render service, the reciprocation of knowledge and inquiries becomes perfect.

title: Which country has no borders?
post_text: No existing country. But this question reminds me of John Lennon's fantasy in  Imagine  and some of the weed-induced dreams people used to have as children of the sixties, when a simple and simplistic explanation seemed to contain the answer to all of humanity's woes. What it ignores, however, is the impact of civilization, particularly the sort of "clash" of civilizations that is real and not easily wished away. For starters, the second largest religion in the world is Islam. It has its own economic basis (no usury) and its legal system, mostly based on a book that allows no compromises. Would Sharia Law work for the whole as well as it seems to work for the Arabian Peninsula? Or would the Arabian Peninsula recognize that it would be just as easy to adopt some sort of vanilla ethical/legal system? Globalization has introduced changes that are lowering trade barriers, removing some of the passport regulations as in the Schengen area, and allowing the free movement of financial instruments around the world, but, in order to allow the absolute free movement of peoples, countries like Norway or Sweden or Germany, with generous social welfare systems, would have to either dismantle the system or face the possibility that they would be over-run with immigrants from those places that have no similar system. If we are to move towards a system of global harmony and free movement, it will have to be the sort of incremental movement we see today. That one recognizes, for instance, that there are dangers inherent in free movement. It recognizes that scale matters -- what Norway can offer to 5 million citizens is not necessarily what can be offered to seven billion citizens of the world. The best we can hope for is incremental improvements of the sort we are beginning to see in Africa or have seen in China in the last 20 years. By the way, what would happen if we had a vote and the people of the world chose some sort of communist totalitarian system as the single worldwide choice?

post_text: STOCKS DECODED PART 1 SENSEX(SENSitivity indEX) is a measure of performance of our stock market. Sensex was started with an arbitrary number 100 on Jan 1 1979. Ever wondered what this index represents ? Sensex is computed from the performance of 30 of the biggest companies of India.And the rise and fall of these companies are directly proportional to the rise and fall of Sensex. If these 30 top companies cumulatively grow by X% then Sensex will also rise X%.So this index depicts the health of our economy. And how this index value is calculated? Free floating market capitalization method  is used for this purpose.Suppose we have 2 companies,Co A and Co B- Co A has 100 shares out of which 90 are available for general public (called  free floating shares ) and 10 are owned by company management. Each share is valued at Rs 100. Co B has 1000 shares out of which 800 are available for public and 200 for company management.Each share is valued at Rs 10. Co A has a total value= Total market capitalization  =total no of shares*value of each share=100*100=Rs 10000 Co B has a total value = Total market capitalization =total no of shares*value of each share=1000*10=Rs 10000 Co A has a total free floating value= Total free floating capitalization =total no free floating shares*value of each share=90*100=Rs 9000 Co B has a total free floating value= Total free floating capitalization =total no free floating shares*value of each share=800*10=Rs 8000 So the total free floating capitalization adds up to=9000+8000=Rs 17000(of A and B) Now suppose we say that the amount of 17000 is equal to 100 Sensex point for reference then we calculate the Sensex points with this point based on the gain/loss of the company. So now if these 2 companies  free floating capitalization  becomes 170000 in 20 years, then Sensex will indicate 1000 . title: Why are Italy and France the top selling wine nations in the world?
post_text: Because they are not. Spain is the top wine seller in the world, in the last year Italy edged over Spain for the first time in a long time and France is below both in third place.   Italy and France  seem  like the top wine sellers because a big chunk of the planet seems to rejoice in utter ignorance about Spain, and because they are actually top wine producers themselves (no denying that), just not the top 2. Spain is by far the country on the planet with the most vineyard soil, although being sunnier and drier usually our soil produces less wine per squared meter than the wet French countryside, but it doesn't matter because the advantage in soil is such that we still produce more wine than Italy and France.  And it also doesn't matter because since our name is Spain no one will have a clue about it,  there's no Spaniard in movies drinking wine with a beret dipping bread in mayonese next to a painting from Picasso. Vineyard in France Vineyard in Italy Vineyard in Spain Even though Picasso was Spanish, mayonese is a sauce taken by Richelieu from the town of Mahón located in the Spanish island of Menorca, and berets are Basque-Navarran-Aragonese shepard hats (present in France to be fair, exactly on their border with Spain).  C'est le Hollywood! Spanish   kids  (Navarran) in the  Running of the Bulls,  wearing the traditional  red beret  in Spanish  “boina"  that my grandpa and my great-grandpa wears and wore (in other colours) Despite this,  or because of it , France and Italy are the ones that make the most money from the wine they sell. France goes from 3rd wine seller to being the top profitter with twice Italy's income and thrice Spain's. Italy also has a lot more income than Spain despite producing less too, Spain “only" comes third in income from wine sales in the world. The reason is obvious: marketing (not necessarily French marketing), marketing makes you associate wine with France and Italy, so the French can sell you their wine nicely priced and you will feel fancy drinking it. Again, ot the French fault, it's a combination of things, like those who go around saying French is a lot more complex and refined than Spanish, it's not the French's fault it's a combination of ideas floating around from several sources. Spanish things aren't refined, that's not an adjective that goes with it in most customers' minds and wine is supposed to be refined, my family drinks it daily in plastic water bottles,  but beyond wine-countries it is fancy, and the Spanish brand isn't  like the French and to a lesser extent the Italian brands are. Los Cigarrales,  right outside Toledo in the background with vineyards all around it And it's not just with France, actually  the same happens with olive oil,  one out of every two drops of it on the planet are Spanish olive oil, and the other drop is the rest of the planet combined and a little of Spain's too. Yet your average Joe in most places thinks of Italy when he thinks of olive oil, can you imagine any product in the world in which a country controls over half the production?  And yet that product is associated in pop culture to another place?  The difference here is that the surplus in production is so stark that the higher price at which Italians can sell their olive oil due to the world thinking it's “their thing” doesn't get to outweigh that, like it does with wine. Olive fields  in southern  Spain , covering all there is to see in the horizon Either way the reason why these countries are the main producers of wine becomes quite obvious when you actually complete the list of top producers: Spain, Italy, France, Chile, Australia, the United States… What's in common?  Mediterranean weather. This map that looks like the Roman Republic got colonies These are countries with large fields to grow wine located within warm-moderate weather zones. Spain and Italy are almost entirely covered by Mediterranean weather, France is largely covered but the uncovered part is still within warm-moderate weathers, Chile, Australia and the US happen to be in the limitted list of countries around the world  to have sizeable Mediterranean weather areas , which happen to be the main producing areas within those countries. Beyond that the culture around wine built in Italy, Spain and France over the centuries makes those three considerably richer in varieties, partly also from the sheer larger production and larger number of vineyards, because the Mediterranean weather extends over the entire country instead of just a fraction of California and Valparaíso. There is a culture and tradition around wine in Spain, Italy and France that is just a lot more commercial among the other top producers. In fact, of the other top producers, the one with the most wine culture arguably is Chile, precisely because it's Hispanic, or in this case we could simply argue it's Latin since the list includes France and Italy. I once saw a video of a Chilean YouTuber in Spain saying “ we have a lot of wine culture in Chile really, does Spain also have good wine ", this sentence shows two of my point in one: the utter ignorance about Spain (asking if wine is a thing in Spain) and that Chileans have more of a culture around it. French president  drinking wine in a wine fair Monument to  wine makers  in  Jerez de la Frontera,  a wine town in southern Spain home of  Sherry Wine Portugal is also hanging there among the top 10 producers in fact, only that the country is smaller and it is not the most wine-centred part of the Iberian peninsula either, the wine production tends to be along mid-course valleys of rivers in warm-template weathers, which all fall within Spain in Iberia. The Balkans don't have Mediterranean weather penetrating inland like Spain or Italy, only Greece in the southern tip is all Mediterranean weather, but it is too mountainous for large vineyard zones. They do have better olive oil production because those grow better in hot Mediterranean zones and they adapt better to hard terrain, which is a reason why olive trees—unlike vineyards—desert France and blossom in Spain in such numbers (vineyards are more in Spain too but they don't  desert  France) because olive trees like it warmer, they are not as tolerant of grey skies and rain as vineyards are. title: If Trump is impeached, will he have to leave office?
post_text: Other answers probably say this, but just to make sure it’s clear: Under the Constitution, the House conducts hearings in various committees and decides whether to write articles of impeachment and send them to the Senate. When they do that, the president is  “impeached.” That’s just the first step toward removing the president, however. The Senate then has conduct hearings, and then vote to  “convict”  the president before she or he can be removed. So that’s what happened to Bill Clinton. He was impeached but not convicted. Nixon wasn’t even impeached. He resigned before the House could vote on articles of impeachment. The process is involved, and lengthy. It isn’t easy to remove a sitting, duly elected president, nor should it be, in my opinion.

A Christmas or two later, we took the older brother (Andrew) and the baby brother (John) to our town’s entertainment district which was beautifully lit and decorated, and offered horse drawn Santa rides. We climbed into the wagon (sleigh) with other families after patting the horses (reindeer) and started clopping down the street with Santa “ho ho ho’ing”. About halfway down the street, four year old Andrew calls out, in a voice firm with belief and expectation, “Santa, when will we fly into the air?!?” All the adults spontaneous laughed, telling Andrew he had made their day. Andrew of course pouted at not flying into the sky. John,of course, was a different kid than his brother (isn’t that always the case?). He was a wise old man from birth on. Somewhat introverted and a rule follower (works in Compliance today). He struggled here and there through middle school, not always understanding the joking and social cues of other kids. One day he came home, sat his backpack down, and in a very firm voice pronounced, “I want this family to know that I, John, am just a serious guy in a foolish world”. title: Does medical practice need practice management software?
post_text: Yes, medical practices need practice management software. If you do not want to run behind accounts receivables and break your head on claims rejections, you do need a practice management software.
