title: Why is Transthyretin so prone to forming protein aggregations?
originally_answered: why is Transthyretin so prone to forming protein aggregations?
post_text:
What is Transthyretin (TTR)? 
Transthyretin (TTR) is one of the many proteins known to aggregate  in vivo . It is a fully functional protein, involved in binding and  trans port of  thy roid hormone,and  retin ol binding protein/vitamin A complex.  It has a very distinct quaternary structure (homotetramer, a dimer of dimers).  Why is this relevant? because proteins that have distinct quaternary structures are not, generally, prone to aggregation.  Which brings us to the following question: if they are not prone to aggregation, why and how do they aggregate?  There are two types of diseases associated with the aggregation of TTR
 Mutational TTR/Inherited  amyloidogenesis : at least 100 point mutations in TTR have been identified and implicated in autosomal dominant disorders. These mutations are known to destabilize the quaternary or tertiary structure of TTR. However, there are studies that show that the mutations that destabilize the structure the most, are not the ones that cause the protein to aggregate, so we don't yet know the inter-relationship between mutations, destability and aggregation. WT TTR  amyloidogenesis : these are diseases associated with formation of amyloid plaques by misfolded wild type(WT)  TTR. 
I am going to focus on WT TTR in this answer. Can a fully functional, folded TTR aggregate? 
No, TTR is an example of a protein that has to undergo conformational changes in order form aggregates or  become amyloidogenic. Essentially, TTR has to misfold (how?) and become less stable, to interact with other less-stable misfolded structures, so that it can form a more stable aggregate.  What happens when TTR undergoes conformational changes? 
Misfolding or partial unfolding of TTR is said to expose large stretches of  hydrophobic residues in partially unfolded conformation. The exposure of hydrophobic patches, causes misfolded monomers to come together due to an entropic hydrophobic effect. (NOTE: TTR has lots of bets sheets, and sheets in general are stabilized by hydrophobic contacts and hydrogen bonding, as opposed to hydrogen bonding driven alpha helix) 
 How does TTR misfold and aggregate? 
 TTR aggregation proceeds by mechanism called downhill polymerization reaction. TTR (the homodimer) must dissociate into monomers, and the monomers must become partially unfolded/misfolded, and the partially misfolded monomers aggregate efficiently as the aggregated trimer is more stable than the aggregated dimer and so on. TTR aggregation does not need a "nucleus formation", and is only limited by the tetramer disassociation. 
 
 What is the difference between TTR aggregation and other aggregation processes? 
 Nucleated polymerization  :the widely accepted mechanism to explain aggregation is the nucleation driven process, where multiple chains interact to form a nucleus, which is the rate limiting step and then the process of amyloid fibril formation is almost downhill. (example: polyglutamine) Nucleated conformational conversion : many monomers rapidly interact to form an amorphous aggregate (mostly disordered), and then they rearrange themselves in a slow process of fibril formation. (example, A-beta (slightly controversial), prion protein sup35) Whereas TTR aggregation is a completely new mechanism (downhill polymerization), this is probably because amyloid beta is intrinsically unstructured and does not acquire a tertiary fold as opposed to TTR with a quaternary fold 
References:
 From Delineating the Molecular Mechanism of Aggregation Linked to Pathology to a Regulatory-Agency-Approved Drug 
 Transthyretin: the servant of many masters 
 Transthyretin Aggregation under Partially Denaturing Conditions Is a Downhill Polymerization†

title: Why are there so many vegetarian recipes with faux meat?
post_text: I sort of think I know why. I’ve been vegetarian for much of my life, when I was a kid my mother (also vegetarian) used to use a ton of the meat substitutes. She grew up on a farm and ate home grown meat until she was in her late 30s, when she joined the Seventh Day Adventist church. To her, meals didn’t feel like a full meal without something resembling meat as a center dish. Dinner without the hearty main (meat) dish just didn’t fly right with her taste buds. She’d work for hours on end hunting for and trying out meat substitutions. So, what about me? Raised without meat, I don’t like fake meat. Never developed the taste for it. Even though I ate meat as an adult, I never really liked it that well. It was “ok” but really, I’d rather have something else please? So my theory on the fake meat thing for many vegetarian recipes? Its because like my mother, a lot of people who weren’t raised vegetarian feel unsatisfied without meat. I doubt it's just the protein or fat, I think it's umami. People taste umami through taste receptors that typically respond to glutamate, which is widely present in meat. They’re used to having that umami taste of meat. And if you aren’t raised with it there’s less craving for it and other things satisfy you.

This required the use of wood to burn the bricks. For the following few thousand years after that the woodlands were cut to use the wood as fuel for the kilns. title: How does European club soccer work? There's the UEFA Champions League, but also the Europa League, Super Cup and FIFA Club World Cup. What's the difference? Can you explain it to a very casual fan?
post_text:
There are differences between those tournaments. It goes like this: UEFA Champions League (UCL) : The teams participating is the top clubs in their respective leagues. Number of clubs per country is determined by the coefficients of the countries in Europe. 
E.g.: 
England (Premier League) may have 3 or 4 teams participating. (3 qualifies to group stage, 1 goes to playoff)
Italy (Serie A) may have 2 or 3 teams participating. (2 qualifies to group stage, 1 goes to playoff) The coefficients changes every year, based on the performance of clubs in the competition. There are 3 qualifying rounds before the playoff is played. The 10 playoff winners will join 22 qualified teams to complete the roster of the tournament. The tournament works like FIFA World Cup, but UCL teams faces their opponent via two leg matches on a home-away basis except for the Finale. UEFA Europa League (UEL) : The Europa League is the second tier of European club tournaments. The teams participating is the domestic cup winners in their respective countries & next club that has been chosen for UCL. If the cup winners is participating in UCL, extra slots is given to the cup's runners up. Clubs that lost in UCL final playoffs will automatically qualify to group stage.
E.g.:
England (Premier League) 5th rank club and UCL playoff loser (if any) goes to group stage, 6th rank plays in playoff & FA Cup winners will play in 3rd qualifying rounds. Also, the clubs that placed 3rd in their UCL group stage will have second chance to play in round 32 of UEL. Like UCL, UEL also uses two leg matches on a home-away basis except for the Finale. UEFA Super Cup : The Super Cup is like the "Charity Shield" of UEFA. This cup participant is between the Champions League winner vs Europa League winner. This is usually played at the start of the next season. This cup is held to prove the true champions of Europe. FIFA Club World Cup : This tournament gathers the champions of each continental in order to determine the greatest club of the world. This tournament is usually held around December each year. There are 6 champions together with the host country's domestic league champion will participate. It started with a playoff between OFC (Oceania) champion vs host country's club champion. The winner will participate in the quarter finals with AFC (Asia), CAF (Africa) & CONCACAF (Americas) champions. Winners of quarter final will battle against UEFA & Copa Libertadores champions. Winners of semi finals goes to the finale. All champions mentioned above are their respective Champions League winners. That's how it works. Hope that helps. P.S.: Please Wiki around to get more info, especially on the qualification part. It's quite hard to explain here.

title: How do I start with stock trading?
post_text: You need to start with something to get somewhere. You need to start trading to learn trading. And the reality is that you never stop learning in stock market. Through out your life, you are a student. Only difference is that you get better with every trade. Every trade you take has something to teach you. You just need to learn that. And the best way to learn is to be in the market. Many people suggest to do paper trading first. But that is of no use. Real trading involves emotions, your mood, your instant trading decision and many more thing. It’s very easy to hold on to profit/loss on paper. But the real experience you get only after stepping into the market. Trade small. No matter if you lose or win, you will be learning something. Start with buying or selling 1 share. That won’t put a dent to your pocket. People argue that we need huge capital to make profits out of the market. But the real truth is if we can’t make profit with 1k how can you expect yourself to make profits out of a 10L account. I could give few suggestions that might help you: Always try to risk the amount of money you can afford to lose. Risking 1K in 1L account is fine but risking 10k in 1L account isn’t a good idea. Just 10 bad trades and you are back to ground zero. No matter what, always try to save your capital. Making profit comes next. At first try to save your ass. Even a newbie can make profit but trading is all about saving that profit till the end of the month. Try to cut your losses fast. People tend to do opposite. They will carry or average that one losing trade and will cut off the profitable one as soon as possible. Book loss, accept the loss & learn to live with that loss, market isn’t going anywhere. It will again open tomorrow. Try to have an edge in the market. There gonna be some days when you might not understand what is it doing. Be a spectator that day instead of jumping in a trade and then losing it all out. No trade is also a trade. Don’t try to get rich in a single trade. Plan your trade and trust your plan. Before punching the order have your target/stop loss & plan B ready. People come into the market to cover up the losses they made earlier and later end up losing more. Don’t have that mentality, trade to make profit be it small or big not to recover your old losses. You can't change the past, but you can certainly learn and make better decisions in the future. Knowing what to trade is different thing and managing that trade is another. Your real skill is tested once you are in the trade. That is the thing you need to work upon. Knowledge is overrated in the market. But risk management is underrated. 60% is knowledge. Rest 40% is risk management. Instead of following the so called pundits of stock market try to learn on your own. At least start with something, you will end up somewhere. Don’t trade the news, that news is already in the market. It is just that you don’t know it. And at last remember this: “Your biggest lessons will come from your biggest pain.” Thank you!

I'm certainly no expert, but during the time I lived in Okinawa, the local citizens tended to identify first as Okinawan in my opnion.  That's not to say they don't consider themselves Japanese.
 
I draw a rough equivilancy to the American southern states.  Many from outside the U.S. and even those in the north of the country might refer to American citizens by the term "yankee."  Southerners would definitely not identify with that term and in fact would find it to be somewhat insulting.  There's a reason for the term "damn yankee" in the south.  There's great patriotism in the American south, but southerner's associate "yankee" not with the American Revolution, but rather with the U.S. Civil War, which is a sore subject, even now.
 
I realize this isn't a direct equivalent to the Okinawan situation.  However, I think the citizens of Okinawa do have a similar view of their fellow Japanese citizens to the north sometimes.  The Civil War comparison is a pretty apt one.  
 
Okinawans feel like they have gotten short shrift for a few centuries now.  They don't appreciate many of the decisions made on the "mainland" that have far reaching ramifications on their little island.  Hence the tendency to identify as Okinawan first.
 
I hope I've represented them accurately.

title: What is the best way to travel from Shinjuku station in Tokyo to Kyoto, Japan (by public transportation)? How much time will it take? What are some things to do on the way there/back home?
post_text: To travel from Shinjuku Station in Tokyo to Kyoto by public transportation, the most efficient option is to take the Shinkansen (bullet train). Here's a detailed guide: 1. **Shinkansen (Bullet Train):** - **Time:** The Nozomi Shinkansen is the fastest option, taking around 2 hours and 20 minutes. The Hikari Shinkansen takes about 2 hours and 40 minutes. - **Procedure:** Purchase a Shinkansen ticket at the JR East Travel Service Center or use a Japan Rail Pass if you have one. - **Departure:** Shinkansen depart from Tokyo Station. You can reach Tokyo Station from Shinjuku by JR Chuo or Yamanote Line, taking about 15-20 minutes. 2. **Things to Do on the Way There:** - **Bento:** Grab a traditional Japanese bento (boxed meal) at Tokyo Station for the journey. - **Scenic Views:** Enjoy the picturesque landscapes as the Shinkansen speeds through the countryside. 3. **Kyoto Station Arrival:** - **Time:** The Shinkansen arrives at Kyoto Station. - **Explore Kyoto:** Visit Fushimi Inari Shrine, Kiyomizu-dera Temple, or stroll through the historic Gion district. 4. **Things to Do on the Way Back:** - **Souvenirs:** Pick up souvenirs at Kyoto Station before your return journey. - **Relaxation:** Reflect on your Kyoto visit and enjoy the comfort of the Shinkansen. 5. **Return Journey:** - **Departure:** Board the Shinkansen back to Tokyo from Kyoto Station. - **Arrival at Tokyo Station:** Once back in Tokyo, consider exploring Shinjuku Gyoen National Garden or indulging in local cuisine. 6. **Alternative Option (if available):** - **JR Thunderbird Express:** If you prefer a more leisurely scenic route, you can take the JR Thunderbird Express, though it takes approximately 2 hours longer than the Shinkansen. Always check the latest schedules and consider making reservations for the Shinkansen, especially during peak travel times. This detailed journey ensures you experience both the efficiency of Japanese high-speed rail and the beauty of the landscapes along the way.

title: What are some tips for a better mental health and life?
post_text: Mental health   is your  emotional, psychological, and social well-being . It helps in determining how we handle stress, connect with others, and take decisions. Mental health is essential right from childhood and adolescence through adulthood. There is nothing more valuable than a  peaceful and sound mind. As per certain research, some factors are the basis of achieving optimum mental health. Your diet  - What you feed your body is the most important factor in achieving both physical and mental health, and here Vegetarians have an edge. It has been found that people who consume plant-based food are likely to live a happier and longer life without any mental health issues. Value yourself - Don’t let others define you. Each individual is different and unique and gifted, so don’t compare yourself with other people. Many mental health issues arise when we try to judge and compete with others. Take care of your body(Exercise) . Any physical activity that brings momentum to your body can greatly contribute to reducing your stress and anxiety. Exercising releases happy chemicals called endorphins which boost your mood and mental health. The water -The brain is made up of 73%water. Research has linked dehydration to anxiety and depression. Dehydration causes brain function to slow down. Water has natural calming properties. It gives clarity to the mind. Connect to nature  -By simply connecting to nature makes you vibrant. Try to walk in the woods, get more sunshine, and more outside air and see the difference in your mood. Nature acts as a soothing balm to our brains. Balancing  is essential. Inculcate habits and hobbies that allow you to destress. Little things like gardening, painting, knitting, solving puzzles, playing an instrument, and writing can be great stress busters that detach you from your regular mundane job. Rest  - Don’t try to become a robot-like machine that works non-stop. We need to rest. Rest and sleep are our recovery mechanisms. In research, it has been found that we cure ourselves of many diseases when we are asleep. Surround yourself with good people,  your go-to people. title: Should elections be based on popular vote?
post_text: Nope, not at all. I know this answer will not be very popular since the electoral college vote just got someone elected who will probably go down as the worst US president in US history, but bear with me for a bit. First off, if the public is extra-decided for a president or against another and one candidate gets a popular vote advantage of, let’s say, 5%, that person will definitely get elected based on current trends. Now, I know theoretically  someone can win the presidency with little over 20% of the popular vote  but that is statistically impossible given the current trends. Now, the US is actually a federation of states and when talking about elections you must think about what the states want and make sure small states don’t get ignored too easily. That is still possible now because the number of electors in each state is dependent on population but that’s ok, because you want some kind of a balance as well and don’t want to go as far as a small minority dictating. By using electoral votes and not popular vote, you make sure the politicians pay attention to issues happening across the country and not just in large places. This is particularly important when you’re talking about a country of a vast size and encompassing over 300 million people. If a couple of states face economic difficulties, politicians can easily ignore them in favour of large areas that are generally more prosperous. But with electoral votes, you know that you can’t just ignore some states that are small, because they can overturn you if there is enough commitment from the people. Let’s take the terrible election that happened recently as an example. Donald Trump has lost the popular vote but won the election because he flipped Michigan, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin. I don’t think it’s a secret that these states have lost a lot as an effect of globalisation. While I still think the country as a whole advanced a lot because of it, it did leave a percentage of the population behind. Nowadays, you can’t get a middle-class job without a Bachelors and if you are a manual labourer, tough luck for you. These are all problems that would have never been in the spotlight as much as they are now if this election was won just by the 200k extra votes that Clinton had. Would the democratic party have actually worried that much that their candidate just won by a razor thin margin? Probably not. I think that now US politics will lean more towards the left because of this and find better metrics to improve such as the number of part-time vs. full-time jobs created, real income growth per household, etc. Right now, the only metric the government showcases in its job report is the unemployment rate which isn’t a clear indicator of progress. Let me point this straight. If you’re trying to find culprits for Trump’s election, you have a billion other stuff to look at that are much more relevant. A lot of things have gone wrong with the US system which prompted this to happen. However, popular vote in a country comparable to the whole EU block will not solve your problems, it will only make them invisible for a while longer.

title: What are the advantages/disadvantages of a reverse mortgage?
originally_answered: What are the benefits and drawbacks to reverse mortgages? Someone just called my mom to peddle one.
post_text: A reverse mortgage is about a change in lifestyle. If someone does not have enough savings on hand and monthly income to be able to enjoy life and do the things they want to do, a reverse mortgage may make perfect sense. I am working with a client right now that is 87 years old and owns her home free and clear. Her only income is Social Security of about $1,200 a month. Because she receives so little income, she does not qualify for any traditional refinance. Her family discussed it with their attorney and their attorney reached out to me. Her home is worth about $200,000 and by structuring the loan with an initial disbursement of $25,000 to clear up some outstanding bills, she will receive about $1,200 additional every month from the reverse mortgage. She never has to make a monthly mortgage payment but she still has to pay her real estate taxes and home owner’s insurance policy from her SSI income and the reverse mortgage monthly disbursements. This loan will change her life. title: Why do humans cook food when animals do not? Why are animals OK not cooking food?
originally_answered: Why do humans cook food?
post_text: Cooking (by heat or chemical) acts to denature proteins and break starches into sugars. It also breaks down some fibers that would otherwise be hard to digest. In this way, cooking improves our ability to digest and receive nutrients from the food we consume. No animal eats as wide a range of foods as humans do (excepting domesticated animals). We are able to eat this wide range of food because we developed cooking and are now able to derive nutrition from foods that we would not be able to eat raw. And, as you mention, many foods last longer if they have been cooked first. It took tens of thousands of years for humans to develop the varied methods of cooking we now employ and to incorporate all of the foods we now eat. During this time we also "domesticated" most of the agricultural plants we now cultivate. Grain yields and the multitude of variations on Brocoli/Cabbage/Cauliflower/Kohlrabi were all developed by centuries of breeding and selection. As for animals "cooking", there are some examples of food preparation by animals. Inedible parts are removed (shelling nuts). Carrion eaters let the carcass decompose some first, making it more easily digested for them. Some monkeys wash their food before eating. Chimps have been known to pound palms with objects to make the fibers digestible. Cooking, in fact, is thought to be the one things we learned that started us on the whole course of history leading to tool-use, agriculture and civilization. If other animals cooked (with heat), there would probably be more than one intelligent species; assuming one was not killed out by the other. There are many books on the history of cooking and some of them are fascinating. You should check them out!

title: Why are American people not interested with football games?
post_text: American people are used to sports where performance and results are more closely correlated. Here are some examples: (For the purposes of this answer, I will refer to American Football as “football" and real football as “soccer.” It's just faster to have a one-word name for each sport) Football is a game for everyone. You can be tall and skinny and make a great wide receiver. If you're short and stocky you might be a fullback. Big all around? Lineman is your calling. Genetics won't prevent you from finding a place on your high school team is you want to play badly enough. In soccer, though, it's all about speed. A guy who is 140 kg is going to be at a huge disadvantage, even if he's fit. It's just too much weight to move around the pitch, and you HAVE to be able to move all over the pitch, no matter what position you want to play. Luck. Luck matters in every sport. There will never be a sport where a lucky bounce at the right time doesn't occasionally determine the winner. But in soccer, where games often end 1–0 or 1–1, one lucky bounce and ANY POINT during the match is very likely to change the result. In football, you might see a team score a lucky touchdown and get 7 free points, but games almost never end 7–0. As long as the lucky bounce doesn't happen in the last few minutes of the game, the other team can easily recover. This creates a better sense of fairness in the game — if your team gets a bad break early on, you don't have to spend the next 80 minutes hoping they can somehow get an equalizer. Fractional scoring. In soccer, one team can dominate possession, play nearly the whole game in their opponent's end, and still not quite be able to get one in, and the game will end 0–0. In football, if that happens, the team will at least be able to kick a few field goals and build up a meaningful lead. They will definitely have a harder time “putting the game away" if they can't score any touchdowns, but their advantage will at least show up on the scoreboard. In soccer, if you can't get one all the way in, nothing else matters. The penalties in soccer are ridiculous. One penalty call (correct or incorrect) can essentially give a goal to one side. That's HUGE! Since teams often only score one goal in the whole match, that means the refs are often responsible for ALL the scoring in match! There is also a massive disparity in fouls. If a foul is called just outside the box, it's basically nothing — a free kick and maybe a 1/20 chance to score a goal. But if that same foul occurs one meter closer to the goal? Hoooo boy, that's a penalty kick. And not even by the player who was fouled either — they get to send their best PK specialist out to take it, so that's like 95% odds that it will be a goal. There are also only 3 different levels of foul: regular, yellow card, and red card. In football, there are (in theory) more than 100 different levels of fouls. The most common levels are 5 yards, 10 yards, or 15 yards, but there is also loss of down for some fouls in addition to the yardage, and there are spot fouls as well (where the ball is moved to wherever the foul occured. Many defensive fouls come with an automatic first down, while some do not. Ejection is also possible. So the refs have a bunch more tools to work with. And the penalty is generally the same no matter where the foul occurs on the field. The biggest penalty that can be assessed is for defensive pass interference, which is a spot foul (can theoretically be as much as 98 yards). If a defender commits DPI 21 yards from his goal, the ball will be placed at the 21 yard line. If another defender later commits DPI 20 yards from his goal, the ball will be placed at the 20 yard line. If another defender later commits DPI one yard from his goal, the ball will be placed at the 1 yard line. There is no MASSIVE difference in penalty for two fouls that occured a meter apart. Lastly, as much as we like to bitch about the refs in football, they impact the game far less than they do in soccer. This is kind a combination of all of the above reasons, but nobody likes it when refs decide the game, so I'm going to repeat it. In football, refs have far more tools to work with as they try to call a fair game, and when they do mess up it's usually not as damaging to the team that got screwed.

title: What if I stopped eating sugar for a month, could that make any change in my appearance?
post_text: Eliminating “sugar” is currently a popular trend in health diets. There is some solid science behind it. Specifically, lowering your daily intake of sucrose, and fructose apparently reduces the amount of inflammation in the arteries, and also decreases overall insulin levels. Insulin stimulates lipid storage in adipose (fat) cells. (Side note: Insulin also stimulates protein accumulation in muscle cells.) A reduction in arterial inflammation is likely to reduce your risk of cardiovascular disease. A reduction in insulin levels is likely to lower the rate of fat deposition. Yes, you could achieve a change in your appearance after one month of reduced sugar intake. However, the only change you could possibly notice would be if you lost a significant amount of fat. A low sugar diet can help you do that, but the change will be much more noticeable if combine that with other weight loss techniques such as exercise and overall calorie reduction. A lot of these responses are anecdotes about people who cut out soda pop, or candy. That’s a healthy move. However, fruits are also very high in sugar regardless of how natural they may be. So if you want to cut sugar, you have to minimize fruit intake as well. An apple is much better for you than a candy bar (with rare exceptions), but to be really serious about your diet means being aware of the composition of everything you eat. Hope this helps.

title: What are the most important psychological facts that everyone should know?
post_text: Perception is subjective: Each person perceives the world differently, based on their past experiences, beliefs, and emotions. We have limited attention span: The average attention span of a person is around 8 seconds, which means we need to make the most of every moment. Our memories are not perfect: Memories are not always accurate, and they can be influenced by our emotions and beliefs. Our thoughts create our reality: Our thoughts and beliefs shape our experiences and how we perceive the world. Emotions can be regulated: Emotions are not always under our control, but we can learn to regulate them through mindfulness, meditation, and other techniques. Social connections are essential: Human beings are social creatures, and having meaningful social connections is essential for our well-being. Our self-talk matters: The way we talk to ourselves can affect our mood, self-esteem, and overall well-being. Change is possible: We have the ability to change our thoughts, behaviors, and habits, and create a better life for ourselves. Gratitude is important: Practicing gratitude has been shown to have numerous psychological benefits, including increased happiness, optimism, and life satisfaction. Self-care is vital: Taking care of our physical and mental health is essential for our overall well-being, and should be a priority in our lives.

title: Why don’t American trains go as fast as European trains?
post_text: American passenger rail service gets far less of a subsidiary per mile of track, or per passenger mile, than trains in other developed countries. They have to travel over tracks that are maintained in satisfactory condition for freight trains. The railroad can order the passenger train to stop on a siding on a single-track line and wait until a freight train has passed. I regularly rode on Amtrak in the 1970s, riding each week back and forth between my college town and my home. I had a chance to get to know the conductor a bit, since his “office” was a seat in the club car. He said that the maximum speed was 90 mph, which was the same 50 years earlier. Back then mail trains had contracts for high speed long distance delivery of mail, which benefitted the passengers, and the railroads kept the tracks in good shape. But in the 1970s as soon as the train got up to 90, they would arrive at an Ill-maintained section with a “slow order,” limiting the train to 15 mph. Then it would take a while to get back up to speed. Many countries have rail lines dedicated to high speed bullet trains, with elevated track. In the US, trains are mostly at the same level as roads, with grade crossings every mile or closer. Frequent accidents cause long delays.

title: Why is Buddhism called a religion? Isn't it more closer to atheism? What should buddhism be classified as?
post_text: Here’s the thing: Atheism is not the opposite of religion. Atheism is the lack of belief in deity. Yes, belief in deity is a very common aspect of religious belief, but it is not the only aspect of religious belief, and it is not even a necessary aspect. A religion is any set of beliefs dealing with the purpose of life, the origin of the universe, the basis for human morality, etc., usually involving spiritual reality and some sort of revealed truth. Some religions are theistic in nature. Some religions are atheistic in nature. Similarly, some religions involve a belief in karma, while others do not. If I do not believe in karma, does that mean that I am not religious? Not necessarily. As for Buddhism, some Buddhists are, in fact, theists because they believe in one or more deities, to whom they pray. For some Buddhists, the Buddha is a deity, and they may worship other deities as well. Conversely, other Buddhists are, in fact, atheists, though they still necessarily believe in spirits and/or objective morality that cannot be empirically proven by any scientific means…and are therefore religious. It would be a mistake to say that Buddhism is “like atheism”, because, as any knowledgeable atheist will tell you, atheism is not a belief system, but is simply the lack of a specific belief. Buddhism, however, is a belief system, and many Buddhists are atheists.

Her family would be falling apart and it would be her fault, or everyone would think that it is her fault for letting that happen. post_text:
Push them into  lakes .
We have over 98,500 lakes larger than 2 acres (8,100 sq m), and hundreds of thousands of lakes all named lakes included. With our 450,295 square kilometres (173,860 sq mi) country size we are big (third-largest country in the European Union) but always with a lake nearby. These areas usually also have barbecue grill sites. Most if not all counties have maps over their such sites. Here is one. Just look how suitable docks for pushing children into the lake from: As mentioned not all lakes are small and cute like that one. Some are quite big. title: What does Hinduism say about eating meat?
originally_answered: Is eating meat against Hindu culture?
post_text: Theories grounded in yoga hold that since what you eat gets assimilated by the body and hence eventually becomes a part of you, the gunas of what you eat will affect your mind, behavior and life force. Thus, for those who need to act with passion/generate anger (kings, warriors, fighters etc.) meat is not necessarily prohibited, but for everyone else it does more harm to the spiritual process than good. Bhakti based systems hold that you cannot eat anything without offering it to your God (Krishna or Rama or anyone else) first and there are conventions (the Tamil word is aidheegam - convention is not exactly the same, but is the closest thing English offers) around what can be offered. For most deities except certain forms of Shakti and for clan leaders/ancestors who have achieved deity status, meat is not offered. But again these are conventions and can be broken in exceptional circumstances (for example offering meat to Chenchu Lakshmi and Narasimha by the Chenchu tribals of Ahobilam). Many vedic theorists hold that only animals that are killed in sacrifices are the ones that can be eaten. But you also cannot use weapons to kill an animal, you must enable the animal to die in a way that allows the animal to go to heaven or achieve moksha. This means either get the animal to voluntarily offer its life to propitiate the devatas or kill the animal by uttering a mantra. The argument this is that neither of these is feasible in Kali yugam - which is why animal sacrifice is not allowed in Kali yugam and consequently eating of animals is also not allowed. Nobody has been able to explain clearly to me whether this rule applies only to Brahmins or everyone. Coming to the matter of culture, meat eating is not culturally taboo in Hinduism. Several meat eating groups exist and have done for a long, long time. What is against Hindu culture is taking meat eating to an extreme. Hindu culture encourages moderation rather than prohibition - so while you may see several meat eaters, most people will have one day a week or one week every quarter or something like that when they avoid meat. You will also see that the quantity of meat taken in India is less since Hindus also take a number of vegetarian food options.

title: How can cancer be detected without going to the hospital?
post_text: SOME lesions on the skin, can be, IF a Dermatologist, removes the lesion, and sends it out for a biopsy, by a Pathologist. This happens IF the Dermatologist, can surgically remove the entire lesion, or part of the lesion. Depending on the biopsy results, a patient with a skin cancer, can have the MOHS Procedure done. This method of preserving non-cancerous tissue, was developed in the 1930’s, by Dr. Frederick Mohs, giving it his name. The part of any raised tumor still there, after the biopsy, is removed. Before this, a “numbing medication,” (local anesthetic), is injected. The MOHS procedure begins, where the Doctor removes the lesion, layer by layer. EACH layer is examined under a microscope, to visualize any cancer cells. IF there are cancer cells, another layer is removed. This continues, until there are no more cancer cells visualized. This method saves tissue, especially useful for areas that are cosmetically important, such as those areas on the face. This could be on the ear, eyelid, nose, lip, etc. Basal Cell Carcinoma, and Squamous Cell Carcinoma, are the types of skin cancers, that are removed by this method. These examples, are just some cancers whose detection, and diagnosis, can be done, without going into a Hospital.
